question: Reveal character through what the character does in the dramatized action itself, rather than telling the reader who they are.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: the action itself reveals an aspect of Sally’s character—she’s a pleaser but she’s also impulsive.

question: Check the causality of your story: action is “this happened, then that,” plot is “this happened because that”—rewrite the sequence so later events happen because of earlier ones.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Action refers to the events that happen in a scene and in the narrative as a whole—this happened, then that happened. Plot, however, is action with a cause-and-effect relationship—this happened because that happened.

question: Find an alternation between scene and summary, showing and telling.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: like most of us you’ll want to find an alternation between scene and summary, showing and telling, somewhere on the spectrum of predominance.

question: Create tension by setting a character's appearance against their actions, and let the disparity make the reader wonder.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: There is already a tension in this scene caused by the disparity between this woman's appearance and her actions. You can use disparity between appearance and actions in your own work to increase tension and therefore reader interest.

question: For each scene, ask what it is really about, what is at stake, and how it contributes to the piece.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Ask yourself the following questions: What is this scene really about? What is at stake in the scene? How does this scene contribute to the piece as a whole? Once you have established a clear intention you will know what needs to be cut, what should stay, what should be developed further, or even if the scene should be there at all.

question: Stop polishing and just start at a place, a moment, a scene, or a voice that excites you.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Therefore, any way in is a good way in. You can’t let yourself get stuck in rewrite perfectionism before you find your subject and your story. Just start at a place, a moment, a scene, or a voice that excites you.

question: Check whether your beginning sets up a contrast with what unfolds later, so the early lightness or forgiveness makes the coming darkness land harder.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: the beginning provides a playful, nearly lighthearted contrast (everyone forgives Oblansky his “peccadilloes”) to what will happen when Anna falls in love and has an affair.

question: If you're writing a crime drama, start with the crime or its discovery in scene before pulling back into summary to introduce the detectives.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: if you’re writing a realistic crime drama you might want to start with the crime itself, in scene, or the discovery of it, in scene, before you duck away to introduce us via summary to the detectives who will pursue the case, friends or family members of the victim, and even the victim’s background history.

question: Check your opening against the general demands of beginnings: does it draw readers into the world through setting, situation, or character, and give them a reason to keep reading?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: By general demands I mean that they give us an opportunity to be drawn into the world of your story (through well-evoked setting, situation, or character) and give us a reason to keep reading (character, voice, conflict, suspense, etc.).

question: If the beginning still doesn't work, move it to another juncture: write a scene or summary that occurs before or after your current opening, or try starting from a different character's point of view.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Perhaps you’ve begun your piece too early or too late (as Tolstoy did in his early drafts of Anna Karenina) in the narrative. Consider beginning at another juncture—try writing a scene or summary that occurs before or after your current beginning. Or, if you are writing fiction, try starting with a different character’s point of view.

question: Don't force your beginning early—accept that many writers only find their true opening after the draft is finished, when plot and ending are known.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Many writers don’t get their beginnings until they’ve finished their draft.

question: Open with an unanswered question, presented through showing or telling, so the reader keeps going to find the answer.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Each of these questions invites the reader to keep going to find an answer.

question: Answer for yourself the questions readers bring to your opening: what world have they entered, what and who matters, why they matter, and who is guiding them through the tale.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: When readers approach a story, they consciously or unconsciously are trying to figure out what world they’ve entered, what and who matters, why they matter, and who is guiding them through this tale. You won’t be able to help them figure this out until you’ve answered these questions for yourself.

question: Start your piece with scene or summary—either can work—as long as the opening meets the general demands of beginnings and the specific demands of your tale.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You too can effectively start your piece with a scene or summary, as long as they each meet the general demands of beginnings and the specific demands of your tale.

question: Before you craft the final version of your first pages, pin down what's at stake in the piece and what its themes are—until you know, the perfect beginning can't come.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Until you have a fairly solid idea of what’s at stake in your piece and what the themes will be, it’s very difficult to craft the perfect beginning.

question: If you've shaped your beginning to set up what will follow but aren't satisfied, rephrase it in the other narrative mode—switch scene for summary or vice versa—to get the needed distance or closeness.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Once you are sure of your own intention, and you know that you’ve shaped your beginning to set up what will follow, but you are not satisfied with your attempt, try switching scene for summary or vice versa. Sometimes a change in narrative mode will give the needed distance or closeness that your piece requires.

question: Open with a character whose presentation and true nature conflict—the tension between what she presents and who she is draws the reader in.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: A paragraph later we learn that Scarlett’s demure demeanor doesn’t hide her lusty and willful true nature, and the tension between what she’s trying to present and who she actually is draws us in.

question: In a story set in an alternate reality, spend time establishing the world in summary before introducing characters and situations, so the fantastic elements are easier to accept.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: you might very well want to spend some time creating the world in which your story will take place before characters and situations are introduced, through the use of summary.

question: After a stretch of fast-paced action, give readers breathing space with a slower section—scene or summary.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: When a lot of fast-paced action has occurred, it’s only natural to give readers some breathing space with a slower section, be it scene or summary.

question: Keep digressive reflection to about a paragraph, then bring the narrative elements back into play—don’t interrupt the story for too long.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: But the digression only lasts for a paragraph before the author starts to bring the narrative elements back into play. The author is careful not to interrupt his novel for too long.

question: Open a story with a brief omniscient reflective passage—a paragraph or two—then slide into the mind of the protagonist.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Sometimes an omniscient reflective narrator can be used briefly as a device to begin a story before introducing or sliding into the mind of the protagonist, and it often only lasts for the first paragraph or two.

question: Rewrite any character whose wisdom or behavior doesn't fit their age and experience.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: On a less obvious level, lack of credibility can occur in situations such as when children are preternaturally wise or always smarter than their parents, like those TV sitcom kids who talk with the ironic smarts of little Jon Stewarts or David Lettermans.

question: Analyze a scene from a writer you admire: map how it is built and how it shows rather than tells, then apply that structure to your own scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can analyze how their scenes are built and discover how they show rather than tell in their scenes.

question: Rewrite any dialogue where characters speak outside their own idiom, keeping each voice true to how that person actually talks.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Dialogue also sounds stilted when characters speak outside of their own idiom.

question: Cut cliché, sentimental images from your scenes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: And be very careful about using such cliché and sentimental images phrasings as “a single tear ran down her cheek.”

question: Check your scenes for continuity contradictions and fix them.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: First there’s the simple problem of lack of continuity, as they say in the movie business—one scene contradicting another.

question: When you are moved by a scene you've written, ask yourself whether the emotional intensity feels earned — does it match the level of intensity you actually felt?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: When you are moved by something you read, ask yourself if the emotional intensity in the scene feels earned. Does it match the level of intensity of emotion you felt when reading?

question: Create a brief scene in which conflict between two characters is apparent.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Create a brief scene in which conflict is apparent between two characters. The conflict can be small, say, over a choice of restaurant, or large, such as a divorce.

question: Eavesdrop on a conversation you can hear but not see, then write the dialogue so the speakers' relationship, power dynamic, and individual voices come through their words alone.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write down as much of the dialogue as you need to establish the relationship between or among the speakers. Is there a power relationship? What is the nature of the information being passed? Is it merely chat, is someone trying to persuade, is there a conflict or does one of the speakers have an agenda? Can you individualize the speakers from their words alone?

question: Identify the agenda and any conflict in the exchange.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write down as much of the dialogue as you need to establish the relationship between or among the speakers. Is there a power relationship? What is the nature of the information being passed? Is it merely chat, is someone trying to persuade, is there a conflict or does one of the speakers have an agenda? Can you individualize the speakers from their words alone?

question: Rephrase the obvious comparisons in your work with fresh, surprising similes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write a list of ten similes that are fresh and surprising.

question: Rewrite a scene from a different point of view — if you wrote it in third person, switch to first, or change the point-of-view character — and see what the shift reveals.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Rewrite the parent and child scene, above, from a different point of view. If you wrote in third person, rewrite it in first person. Or change the point-of-view character from child to parent or vice versa.

question: Choose one detail of appearance, gesture, voice, or action for each character that reveals something important about them, and write a scene in which those details carry the characterization.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Go to a public space and choose one detail (of appearance, gesture, voice, action) for each person you observe that reveals something important about that person. Write a scene in which details reveal character.

question: Rewrite one of your scenes in a different season and time of day, and consider how time and setting affect mood and tone.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Then rewrite that scene in the morning, mid-summer. Consider the way time and setting affect the mood and tone of the two versions.

question: Write a scene in present tense, then rewrite it in past tense, and compare how the tense shift alters the tone.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write it in present tense and then rewrite it in past tense. How do these tense shifts alter the tone of the scene? Which works better here? Why?

question: Rephrase dialogue that delivers exposition the characters would already know, making it sound like natural speech.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Dialogue sounds false whenever it contains information that the characters would already know but the writer inserts as exposition, as in “My mother, Geraldine, would be very happy to come to your house for dinner Uncle Joseph.”

question: Rewrite your first-person narrator's attitude so they come across as self-aware rather than self-pitying or self-aggrandizing, so readers trust the emotions and facts.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: To be credible, a memoir narrator writing from an adult perspective must be self-aware.

question: Signal an unreliable narrator deliberately, or don't use one at all: don't risk the reader's trust by making your narrator too self-regarding or too villainous to believe.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: But these are cases in which the author deliberately invites you to mistrust the narrator. In most novels and memoirs, trust between reader and narrator is essential. Don’t risk losing that trust by making your narrator either too self-regarding or too villainous to believe in your scenes.

question: Cut or summarize any scene in which no important events or interactions ensue — nothing that reveals character or advances plot or themes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If a narrator or character takes her car for an oil change and no important events or interactions ensue, you could and probably should just skip the scene and summarize it.

question: Scan your work for passages where you've taken on the style and mannerisms of a writer you admire, and rewrite them in your own voice.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: you’ll need to be on the lookout for instances in your work when you’ve taken on the style and mannerisms of writers you admire.

question: When a scene does little to heighten complications or further plot or themes, summarize it instead of dramatizing it — keep a quiet scene only as setup for what comes later.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: if the scene does little in terms of heightening the complications or furthering the plot or themes, consider summarizing instead.

question: Read your dialogue aloud; wherever you stumble over the words your characters are speaking, revise the line.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: read your dialogue aloud. If you find yourself stumbling over the words your characters are speaking in your scenes, it’s time to revise.

question: Articulate the difference between sentiment and sentimentality in your work — name where genuine emotion ends and the attempt to manipulate the reader begins.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: What is the difference between sentiment and sentimental? I think of it as the difference between real sugar and artificial sweetener. Sentimental scenes are as artificial as Sweet’N Low.

question: Rewrite any death or parting scene that relies on tearjerker conventions, so the emotion feels earned.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Generally the sentimental death scene requires the dying person to be an angel of some sort—already artificially sweetened—or to have a deathbed conversion to goodness. Frequently last-minute forgiveness is featured.

question: Ask of each scene whether it moves the plot forward, reveals character, and engages the reader emotionally; cut what drags with unnecessary details or pointless dialogue, or start the scene sooner or later.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Do my scenes move the plot forward? Do they reveal character? Do they engage the reader emotionally? Do they drag on and show unnecessary details, pointless dialogue, etc? Should they be started sooner or later?

question: Write your summaries to carry your narrative voice—voice is often best displayed in summary, not buried in the information.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Much of that novel is carried by Bridget’s witty voice, and narrative voice is often best displayed in summary.

question: Replace a random detail in a summary with one whose associations reinforce the character or situation you are writing about.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The point here is that the details you use in your summaries shouldn’t be random.

question: Expand a flat summary with concrete specifics that let the reader infer more than facts alone.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: From both versions we understand that the mother cared for her children. But in Allende’s version, we know that the mother went to the trouble of heating stones in a fire to warm their hands.

question: Replace an overused detail with a fresh image that makes the subject vivid.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You don’t want to write about a hunched old lady or verdant landscapes. These details are devalued by their overuse. If your old lady has the posture of a wilting flower, you’ve made her vivid and your summary enlivened.

question: Choose details of behavior or appearance that expose your character's inner life.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: To reveal character through summary detail in your own work, choose features of behavior or appearance that expose a character’s inner life.

question: Go through your summaries and make each detail do more than one job: reveal character or further theme, not merely inform.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: When possible, allow your detail to do more than one job. Ask yourself if the details you use in your summaries serve to reveal character or further themes.

question: Add sensory detail—sights and sounds—to a flat summary until it reads as vividly as a scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: At night we slept in boggy rooms where headlight beams crawled up and down the walls and mosquitoes sang in our ears, incessant as the tires whining on the highway outside.

question: Animate one summary detail with a simile to make it memorable.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Not only does Updike put elephant plants into this summary, but he uses a simile—they sat like faithful dwarfs!

question: Add a detail that raises an unanswered question to create tension in the summary.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Tension is created when a detail raises an unanswered question.

question: Audit each concrete detail in your summaries: besides giving information, does it advance the theme?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Besides giving concrete information, do your details advance theme?

question: Rephrase narration with everyday, repeated phrasing to give it a conversational, informal quality.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The repetition of “before that” has an everyday quality, as does the informal phrase “a lot.”

question: Shift your first-person narrator’s language from simple to more complex over the course of the work to show growing age or sophistication.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: In first-person narratives, a shift from simple to more complex language over the course of a story can demonstrate a change in the narrator’s age and/or sophistication.

question: Set your summary’s tone through word choice and sentence structure: ordinary words for an informal, conversational feel.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Diction (word choice) and syntax (sentence structure) can help set the tone of a summary.

question: Replace clichéd metaphor or simile in your summaries with fresh symbolic language that suits the material it illustrates.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Symbolic language—metaphor and similes—is as useful in summaries as it is in scenes as long as it is fresh and not cliché.

question: Cut each interjection of an older, wiser perspective unless it furthers the reader’s understanding of character and situation in an essential way.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: But remember that each time you interject an older or wiser perspective, you are interrupting the narrative flow. What would make an interjection or juxtaposed perspective worthwhile? It must further the reader’s understanding of characters and situations in an essential way.

question: Question the placement of each older-narrator interjection: could the information sit elsewhere, or must it interrupt the younger narrator’s story right here?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Ask yourself if there is a better place for inserting the information that the older narrator will provide. Does it need to go right here in the midst of the younger person’s story? Why?

question: Layer your first-person narrative so summaries reveal how your narrator sees the world at different ages and stages of maturity.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Narrative layering refers to a first-person work in which the narrator is seen at either a younger and older age, or from a more naïve as well as a more experienced perspective.

question: Check whether you are using irony or humor to avoid emotion on painful material, and rewrite so the fear stays visible underneath the jokes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Ask yourself if you are using irony or humor as a way to avoid emotion. Sure, Lorrie Moore uses humor very well in her story excerpted above, but she always lets us see the fear underneath the jokes.

question: Establish your piece’s tone and mood deliberately in your summaries, where they first take hold.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Summaries are often the place where tone and mood get established, particularly when scenes are allowed to unfold without much interior commentary within characters.

question: Name your intended tone with a precise adjective, then check that the wording actually produces it.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The tone of a piece can be urgent, dismissive, judgmental, ironic, sentimental, mocking, harsh, alarmed, sympathetic, and any other number of adjectives that describe and qualify experience.

question: Cut or temper any tone that detracts from or overwhelms the material it is meant to carry.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: One of your purposes in choosing a particular tone is to create a mood in your reader, and the mood will be spoiled if the tone detracts from or overwhelms the material.

question: If you address a harsh, judgmental tone directly to “you,” reconsider: such address risks making readers turn away.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The tone forces the reader to examine her own prejudices and assumptions, but when this harsh tone is addressed to “you” there’s a danger of making readers turn away.

question: Rephrase a line so its tone shifts, and find the wording that carries the meaning you intend.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: A big brother could tell his bored little brother “Go fly a kite,” with a tone of enthusiasm and encouragement, or he could say, “Go fly a kite” and mean “get lost.”

question: Make sure change occurs in your scene—in characters, in circumstances, or in the reader’s perceptions—since change is the essence of narrative.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: And change—in characters, in circumstances, and in the perceptions of readers—is the essence of narrative.

question: Keep choppy scene-to-scene jumps without setup when you are portraying the disjointed thought patterns of a distraught or mentally ill character, or stacking scenes like an album of memories.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Choppiness is fine if you’re portraying the disjointed thought patterns of a distraught or mentally ill character, or stacking up scenes like an album of memories.

question: When you rearrange chronology with flashbacks or out-of-order events, have an important reason: it must serve the piece more than it disrupts.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: In any case, when an author chooses to rearrange the chronology of a scene with flashbacks or taking events out of order, there should be an important reason for that choice. It must serve the piece more than it disrupts.

question: Hunt out and cut clichéd language—sparkling eyes, jet-black hair, loving someone more than life itself—tired language flattens and kills even exciting scenes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: No matter how exciting the action in a scene might be, tired, overused language will flatten and kill it. When eyes sparkle or twinkle, when hair is jet black or a man loves his girlfriend more than life itself, we know we are in the hands of a lazy or inexperienced writer who hasn’t taken the time to find fresh language.

question: List every way you could show your character’s desire—through gesture, speech, inner thoughts—and cut any that feel too familiar, stereotypical, or clichéd.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Then think of all the ways you can show that desire—through gesture, speech, inner thoughts—and discard any that seem too familiar or expectedstereotypical or clichéd.

question: When your story is truly action-based and the action is rising toward a dramatic climax, let fast sections follow on each other’s heels until the climax is reached.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: However, if your story is truly action-based and the action is rising toward a dramatic climax, it’s okay to allow fast sections to follow on each other’s heels until the climax has been reached.

question: Recast a close-third-person passage in first person (or vice versa) to test the difference in intimacy—close third stays within the perceptions of a single mind.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: It wouldn’t be terribly difficult to recast this in first person, nor would it make an enormous change in effect because the thirdperson narration above is close third, meaning it stays within the perceptions of a single mind.

question: Consider organizing a creative nonfiction piece nonlinearly, relying on thematic or imagistic organizing principles rather than strict chronology.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Creative nonfiction probably uses nonlinear narratives more often than fiction does, relying on thematic or imagistic organizing principles.

question: Combine interior thoughts, actions, and dialogue in the same scene instead of letting them work in isolation to reveal character.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Interior thoughts, actions, and dialogue don't have to work in isolation to reveal character. You can combine these elements effectively.

question: Find scenes that dramatize information not worth that much space and compress them into summary, so the remaining scenes carry the emphasis.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: A work comprised of scenes alone, especially a long work, can be a welter of dramatic renderings, many of which provide information that doesn’t deserve to take up that much space.

question: Compress the spans of time that do not need examination into a single sentence of summary, and save scene for the spans that require careful attention.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: can be compressed with summary such as “Over the next two years Ralph saw his father only a few times.”

question: Use concrete experience as a ladder to great abstractions, and when the reflection has gone far enough, return to the most precise observations of the world around you.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: She uses the concrete as a ladder to great abstractions. Yet when she’s gone too far for you, she comes back to the most precise observations of the world around her.

question: Check whether your conflicts develop as the piece moves on—intensify and further complicate the initial conflicts rather than leaving them static, and make their resolutions satisfying.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Think about the conflicts operating in your own work. Do they develop as the piece moves on or do they remain static? What ways might you intensify and further complicate the initial conflicts? Does the resolution of these conflicts feel satisfying?

question: Let conflict reveal character—keep scenes whose only purpose is displaying a trait rare, since too many of them lose the reader.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The development of conflict and character go hand in hand because conflict reveals character.

question: Decide whether your piece is light entertainment or basically serious with touches of irony, and stay consistent.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You must decide if your piece is going to be light in tone, a piece of entertainment, or basically serious with a few touches of irony, a few laughs. What won’t work is if you keep wavering between intentions—using your characters for humorous effect and then expecting people to be moved by their loves and losses.

question: Wield contradiction deliberately: let a character’s words, thoughts, and behavior disagree for effect, but not so much that the character reads as schizophrenic.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Contradiction is a useful tool but one that must be wielded carefully.

question: Make each turning point grow naturally out of what comes before it—readers won't believe a change that comes out of thin air.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You want your readers to believe in the turning point, and they won’t if it comes out of thin air.

question: Cut any scene that doesn't ultimately move the piece forward—a scene without conflict must at least serve as setup for conflicts to come.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Scenes without any form of conflict can still be useful—they can serve as setup for conflicts to come, for instance. But if they don’t serve a purpose that ultimately moves the entire piece forward in a significant way, perhaps they shouldn’t be scenes at all.

question: Cut unnecessary conversations and irrelevant background exposition from your scenes—they slow the pace until the reader loses sight of what’s at stake in the scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: But you don’t want to bog down your scene with unnecessary conversations or irrelevant background exposition, slowing it down to such a degree that the reader loses sight of what’s at stake in the scene.

question: Cut any summary that explains what a scene has already made obvious; let the scene evoke the most significant events.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: I still resent, as most readers would, a narrative in which the author explains what a scene has already made obvious—reporting rather than evoking the most significant events in the characters’ lives. That sort of summarizing leaves the reader far removed from the action and emotions of the characters; it’s alienating and dull.

question: Ask the same defining questions of your older, wiser narrator that you asked of the younger self.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Who is the adult or older narrator now? Ask the same questions of your “wiser” narrator.

question: Define the differences between your narrator’s older and younger selves: is the younger self naive, hopeful, full of illusions, given to excesses? Pin down its nature.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: First, you must define the differences between the narrator’s older and younger selves. Ask yourself, is the younger narrator/ character: Naïve? Energetic? Hopeful? Full of illusions? Given to excesses? Does she drink too much? Jump from relationship to relationship? Submissive with authority?Impoverished? Abused? Happy-go-lucky? Whatever the nature of the younger narrator/character, you need to pin it down.

question: Find the flat, generic descriptions of your characters and rephrase them with individuating details that reveal nature.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If I write "The old lady sat on the park bench" I'm describing directly but not revealing anything about her character. But I can add to the description to individualize this old lady and give you a glimpse into her nature. I might dress her quite elegantly, with a neat, upswept coiffure, a fashionable tailored jacket, and expensive shoes with heels.

question: Name each scene's central desire and the obstacle that thwarts it—desire plus obstacle is what creates narrative tension.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Either way, it involves characters having desires and those desires being thwarted by obstacles of some kind. These desires and the obstacles thrown in their way create narrative tension.

question: Keep symbolic details concrete and grounded so the symbolism never overwhelms the story—and avoid so many significant details that the scene turns heavy-handed.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Most remarkable to me when reading this story is that every detail is both concrete and significant, so the highly symbolic nature of Erdrich’s prose never overwhelms the story being told. It is always grounded, always believable.

question: Sort your concrete details, keeping those that carry meaning for the character in this particular scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: First, let’s distinguish between ordinary concrete details such as a brown dog, a ceramic cup, a hose on the lawn, the building on the left—and details that carry greater meaning. All of the details mentioned above could be significant in a particular scene. If seeing a brown dog reminds a character of the time her father ran over her beloved pet, a brown dog is significant in that scene.

question: Use details to do more than create a believable world: they can carry themes, reveal character, and heighten or provide drama.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: At their best, details do more than just create a believable world in which the story or essay or chapter exists. Details can also carry themes, reveal character, heighten or provide drama.

question: Mark the places where you get bored reading your own draft and the holes where it rushes; work out why each drags or races, then cut or add so the narrative moves forward smoothly and compellingly.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Where do you get bored reading the draft? Where are there holes? Mark those places and consider them carefully. What can you cut or add to make the draft move forward in a manner that is both smooth and compelling?

question: Ask yourself whether your use of dialect relies on stereotypes that diminish the humanity of any character—stereotyping only weakens the work.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Ultimately you must make your own decision about your writing, but at the least you should ask yourself if you are using stereotypes and therefore diminishing the humanity of any character, which will only weaken the work in the end.

question: If you avoid writing dialect, establish each character’s speech habits through word choice and rhythm instead.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: There are some authors who insist that dialect should never be used and that a writer must establish characters’ speech habits through the use of word choice and rhythm.

question: Audit each dialogue passage: does it move the scene forward, heighten tension, put forth themes, or reveal character? Cut words or lines that do none of these.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Ask yourself, as you look over your dialogue, what it’s doing for the scene? Does it move the scene forward, heighten tension, put forth themes, reveal character? When you read it aloud to see how it sounds, check for words or lines that could be cut.

question: If a passage of dialogue exists only to deliver background, cut it and present that background through narrative summary instead.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If expository dialogue serves no purpose in the scene besides exposition, it is usually better to present the background through narrative summary, which will be discussed in Section II.

question: When background is carried through dialogue, give it a function in the scene and a reason the character tells that history now.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: When background is carried through dialogue there has to be a reason for that background to be revealed in the scene. It has to have a function in the scene and there needs to be a reason that the character is telling that history now.

question: Make your dialogue seem as though it is generated naturally from the events transpiring, even though you are selecting and shaping it to your own ends.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The dialogue must always sound believable—it must seem as though it is generated naturally from the events transpiring, even though you are selecting and shaping it to your own ends.

question: Check each line of dialogue against its context: when speech doesn't fit the setting and events around the character, that disconnect shows the reader something important about her.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Study how your character's speech fits the setting and the events around her; if there is a disconnect between the two, you've just shown your reader something important about your character.

question: Write dialogue that is natural to the individual: ask what this character would say at that moment, in that circumstance.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Second, it’s not enough that your characters speak in a natural manner in general, it must be natural to them as individuals—what would she say at that moment, in that circumstance?

question: Give your dialogue more than one job in the scene—reveal character, tip off region or class, expose themes, heighten drama, provide background—never let it be mere “color.”

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: It can also tip off the reader to identifying characteristics such as region of origin, social class, education level, mood of speaker, whether or not someone’s been drinking, etc. Dialogue can expose themes, heighten the drama, provide background, and occasionally add humor. It should do more than just one of these in a scene.

question: Make sure your reader always knows who is speaking: use dialogue tags unless actions and description show the speaker, so no one has to read back.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Dialogue tags are essential unless you are able to show through the actions and description who is speaking. It’s very frustrating when a reader has to read back to see who is talking when.

question: Infuse your dialogue so it echoes the themes of your piece.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: How might you infuse your dialogue so it echoes themes in your piece, as the diner owner’s wife does above when she discusses mistrusting people in the excerpt above?

question: Digress in your reflection from the personal to the historical or informational to make the narrative more layered and thought provoking.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Reflection that “digresses” from the personal to the historical or informational can make a narrative both more layered and more thought provoking.

question: Cut any setup summary that pretells something the following scene will show—if the summary reveals what happens, it weakens rather than strengthens the scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If your summary pretells something that the scene will show, it will weaken rather than strengthen the scene.

question: Before a dramatic scene that is focused on the immediate actions and words of the characters, add setup summary so the reader understands more about the characters than the scene itself can show.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: This kind of summary as setup is particularly helpful with dramatic scenes that require the reader to understand more about the characters than the scene shows because the scene is focused on the immediate actions and words of the characters.

question: Rewrite events so they are dramatized rather than reported: ground the reader in place and give the illusion of real time passing.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: To be truly engaged in the lives of characters, events must be dramatized rather than simply reported; for dramatic impact we must be grounded in place and experience the illusion of real time passing, which only occurs in scenes.

question: Before lifting your story into big summarized abstractions, supply the specificity of concrete details so the reader trusts you.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The reader has come to trust O’Brien through the specificity of the concrete details he has supplied. The particularized summary and the focused scene have set us up for the more abstract picture of these soldiers, and all the soldiers like them, who carried the burdens of the war.

question: Denote a character's emotional state through action or dialogue—a nervous gesture instead of a line that tells us they are nervous.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: It’s usually more vivid and more affecting when emotional states can be denoted by action or dialogue in scenes rather than by authorial telling.

question: Choose scene or summary point by point by asking whether you want to engage the reader’s emotions or intellect—there is no formula for how much to show and how much to tell.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: There just isn’t a formula for how much to show and how much to tell. You have to take into consideration whether you want to engage the emotions or the intellect of your reader at various points in the piece.

question: Trim your mid-scene summary to only what is needed to convey the character's emotional base and emotional shift, since every interruption of forward movement costs momentum.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Whenever forward movement is interrupted you pay a price in momentum lost. So you want to add only enough summary within the scene to allow us to understand the emotional base and the emotional shift.

question: Give your characters recognizable yet complex emotions, and render the experience as it happens in time, complete with sensory detail, so the reader goes through it with them.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Scenes create an emotional connection for the reader by making characters and events seem real, and by giving characters recognizable, though complex, emotions. The “real” feeling comes from the reader going through the experience with the character as it’s happening in time, complete with sensory detail.

question: Check that your piece delivers significant change—in character, narrator, or the reader's perception—by the end of your story, essay, or book.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: There is significant change (in character, narrator, or reader’s perception) over time by the end of your story, essay, or book.

question: Shape your ending to leave a sense of closure—if not complete resolution—and ideally to linger in the reader's mind.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: they must leave your reader with a sense of closure, if not complete resolution, and, ideally, they should linger in the reader’s mind.

question: Check whether you reached your ending before your final paragraphs—if so, cut off the last paragraph or page or two.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: I’ve often found that students have reached their ending before their final paragraphs and all they need to do is cut off the last paragraph or page or two.

question: If the ending isn't working, switch scene for summary, try ending earlier or later than you do now, or add a scene or summary to see where it takes you.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Just as with beginnings, if you aren’t satisfied with your ending, try switching scene for summary and vice versa. Or try ending earlier or later than where you end now. Add a scene or a summary to your current ending to see where it takes you.

question: Choose an ending built on reflection, epiphany, pointed action, or a haunting sensory detail—each contains a resolution, and don't worry whether it's scene or summary.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Reflection, epiphany, pointed action, haunting sensory detaileach of these successfully brings the tale to conclusion. Each contains a resolution. Half are scenes, half summaries.

question: Cut the neat-bow wrap-up: an ending that ties off every detail gives closure but won't stay with a reader.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You don’t want to wrap up every detail in a neat bow at the end. That kind of ending gives closure, but it won’t stay with a reader.

question: Match the ending's tone and content to everything that came before, whether you cast it in scene or summary.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Whatever you choose—scene or summary—as an ending, it must be suited to what’s come before in terms of tone and content.

question: Create a character using summary: include interior thoughts, external description, summarized behavior, and narrative commentary.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Create a character using summary; include interior thoughts, external description, summarized behavior, and narrative commentary.

question: Write a page of summary that condenses thirty years in the history of a family — and make it interesting.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write a page of summary that condenses thirty years in the history of a family. Make it interesting!

question: Insert a passage of summary into one of your scenes to deepen the reader's sense of the character.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Now, insert summary into the scene of this woman in the parking lot to deepen our sense of the character.

question: Write a paragraph of summary in which the narrator establishes a tone of irony, then rewrite the same paragraph shifting the tone to straightforward and pragmatic.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write a paragraph of summary in which the narrator establishes a tone of irony. Rewrite the same paragraph shifting the tone to straightforward and pragmatic.

question: Write two paragraphs of summary with narrative layering: the first in the voice of the narrator as a child, the second in the same narrator's adult voice.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write two paragraphs of summary with an eye to narrative layering—one paragraph in which the narrator is a child, the second in the voice of the same narrator from an adult perspective. The older, wiser voice should illuminate the younger, more innocent or naïve passage.

question: Practice the scene-summary ratio: write a page where summary dominates and scene appears briefly, then a page where scene dominates and summary appears briefly.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write a page in which summary dominates and scene appears briefly.

question: Write a paragraph of summary in the voice of a reflective narrator who has just read an old love letter.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write a paragraph of summary in the voice of a reflective nar-rator who just read an old love letter.

question: Take a scene you've written and follow it with reflective summary, letting the narrator or character reflect on what just happened.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Take one of the scenes you’ve written earlier, from these exercises or your own work, and follow it with reflective summary.

question: Select a published scene that contains interspersed summary, remove all the summary embedded in it, and read what remains: what has been lost, and has anything been gained?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Select a published scene that contains interspersed summary. Remove all summary embedded in the scene and read what remains. What has been lost? Has anything been gained?

question: Write a few paragraphs of summary that display the use of repeated time.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write a few paragraphs of summary that display the use of re-peated time.

question: Write a paragraph of summary about a childhood outing, using vivid sensory detail throughout.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Write a paragraph of summary about a childhood outing in which you use vivid sensory detail.

question: Raise dramatic tension in a scene by opening it with setup summary before the action begins.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Use setup summary to raise dramatic tension in a scene about a woman who has lost her car keys in a darkened parking lot on a city street.

question: Insert a brief expository description into a scene to add texture, symbolism, or a momentary slowing of pace—keep it short enough that it does not interrupt the scene for long.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Whatever the purpose, and we can’t know without a longer sample, the expository insertion adds texture without interrupting the scene for long.

question: If your story turns surreal or fantastic, ground it in a seemingly realistic setting first—place the bizarre within the believable so the interplay makes the setting function.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Pullman has grounded his fantasy in a seemingly realistic setting, and it is within that grounding that he positions the bizarre fact of people possessing personal animal-like daemons.

question: In first-person narrative, notice which details your narrator selects—those choices automatically reveal the narrator’s character.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The details in a first-person narrative, be it fiction or nonfiction, automatically reveal the character of the narrator because the first-person narrator has made the choice to notice and select those details that have meaning to him.

question: Keep your reader located in time through every flashback—use time markers on entry and draw attention back to the ongoing action on return, or readers give up.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The important thing is that you keep your reader located in time; it’s very frustrating for readers when they can’t figure out what’s happening when and they’re likely to give up on your story.

question: Drop the announcing verbs 'remember' or 'recall' from flashback entries so the move feels less like a device.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Try not to use verbs such as “remember” or “recall,” as in “Dave remembered the last time he’d run over a squirrel … ” to announce a flashback. “The last time Dave had run over a squirrel … ” functions fine without the verb “to remember” and is less obviously a device.

question: Include a flashback only when its payoff outweighs the forward momentum it costs, and anchor it to a real connection with the ongoing scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: In writing, you want the flashback to have a connection to the ongoing or surrounding scenes. It shouldn’t be random—there has to be a good reason to go into a flashback as it stops the ongoing action. Flashbacks should provide information essential to readers’ understanding of the current scene. The payoff for including them must outweigh the cost of losing forward momentum.

question: Shift the verb tense to mark the move into a flashback—present to past, or a few past-perfect verbs when the scene is already in past tense.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: A verb change is important. If you’re writing your scene in the present tense, a simple shift to past tense lets us know we’ve moved back in time.

question: Cut any passage, fast or slow, that does not contribute to the forward movement of the whole.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: All aspects of the piece, whether slow or fast, must in some way contribute to the forward movement of the whole.

question: In revision, keep your language fresh—but don’t hype it to the point where diction and imagery distract from the scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: That’s not to say you should hype up language to the point of absurdity so the diction and imagery distract from the scene. But, in the act of composition and revision, work to keep your language fresh.

question: Weigh the costs of interrupting your narrative before jumping into the future tense; use it occasionally to telegraph information that changes how the reader judges the current characters and action.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: It can be useful, occasionally, in telegraphing information that will be important to the reader's understanding of the ongoing scene. As with flashbacks, it's important to weigh the costs of interrupting the narrative against the possible payoffs such as giving readers a sense of prescience and informing readers of events that will change the way they judge the "current" characters and action.

question: Set your scene-to-summary ratio by genre.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: if you are writing a fast-paced, action-packed political thriller, you probably will want to keep most of your summary limited to just what the reader needs to know about the characters and the background of the political situation so readers can follow the story, with a little summary-as-connective tissue between scenes thrown in. Romance writers tend to focus on scenes because their readers’ primary goal is sharing the emotions of the protagonist. Science fiction writers generally include considerable exposition to set up the parameters of the imaginary worlds their characters live in. But they too depend on scene for the important events.

question: In a thriller, keep summary to what readers need plus connective tissue between scenes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: if you are writing a fast-paced, action-packed political thriller, you probably will want to keep most of your summary limited to just what the reader needs to know about the characters and the background of the political situation so readers can follow the story, with a little summary-as-connective tissue between scenes thrown in. Romance writers tend to focus on scenes because their readers’ primary goal is sharing the emotions of the protagonist. Science fiction writers generally include considerable exposition to set up the parameters of the imaginary worlds their characters live in. But they too depend on scene for the important events.

question: In romance, favor scenes that share the protagonist's emotions.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: if you are writing a fast-paced, action-packed political thriller, you probably will want to keep most of your summary limited to just what the reader needs to know about the characters and the background of the political situation so readers can follow the story, with a little summary-as-connective tissue between scenes thrown in. Romance writers tend to focus on scenes because their readers’ primary goal is sharing the emotions of the protagonist. Science fiction writers generally include considerable exposition to set up the parameters of the imaginary worlds their characters live in. But they too depend on scene for the important events.

question: In science fiction, use exposition to establish the world but scene for the important events.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: if you are writing a fast-paced, action-packed political thriller, you probably will want to keep most of your summary limited to just what the reader needs to know about the characters and the background of the political situation so readers can follow the story, with a little summary-as-connective tissue between scenes thrown in. Romance writers tend to focus on scenes because their readers’ primary goal is sharing the emotions of the protagonist. Science fiction writers generally include considerable exposition to set up the parameters of the imaginary worlds their characters live in. But they too depend on scene for the important events.

question: Plant early references or parallels that foreshadow major events to come, so the momentous scene lands with greater meaning.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: To lay the groundwork for future scenes in your own work, consider the possibilities for foreshadowing major events to come, through references or parallels that will have greater meaning when those more momentous scenes occur.

question: In your setup summary, establish the character's routine with markers of repeated time so the scene that follows disturbs a recognizable pattern.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: By using summary first—including markers for repeated time such as “never” and “always”—to set up the scene, I’ve established the tedium and hectic, disorganized nature of Marie’s life before the action begins.

question: Carve conflict that is less overt: let a character's hidden emotions and motives come through to the reader without stating them.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Unlike in the Amy Tan scene in which a child screams “I don’t want to be your daughter,” the wife is less overt about her emotions and her motives, but the message comes through to the reader.

question: Do not rush from major plot point to major plot point; let the story pause long enough for the reader to learn something about the human condition along the way.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: A good story hits these major plot points but allows us to learn something about the human condition along the way.

question: Express humor through reflective summary—irony, absurdity, exaggeration, odd juxtapositions, sarcasm—where it can’t be voiced in a scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Summary gives a writer the opportunity to express humor through reflection, apart from actions or speech.

question: When your humor criticizes the reader, include yourself in the criticism—criticize “us,” not “them”—or the reader will feel attacked rather than laugh.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Sedaris manages to be critical of us as Americansand us is an important word here, because if he were critical of readers and didn’t include himself, we’d become annoyed and resentful rather than laugh.

question: Integrate any inserted history or place description into the overall intention of the story so it echoes the events within the scenes rather than arriving at random.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The insertion of history or place description can’t be a random choice; it must be integrated into the overall intention for the story. That place or family history might in some way echo the events that occur within the scenes.

question: Before deciding how much scene and summary to use, get clear on what you wish to accomplish in the overall work; your proportions depend on what’s at stake and what you want to emphasize.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You can’t know how much scene, how much summary to use if you aren’t clear on what you wish to accomplish in the overall work. Your proportions of scene and summary depend on your being aware of what’s at stake in your piece and what you wish to emphasize.

question: Before shaping a character's thoughts, name what you want to accomplish in the scene—then shape the thoughts (or your narrator's) to show exactly what you want them to.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: It always comes back to intention—knowing what you want to accomplish in your scene, then shaping your character's thoughts (or choosing your narrator's, in nonfiction) so they show what you want them to.

question: In fiction, use internal monologue to show what lies beneath a character's behavior and appearance—don't waste the opportunity that playwrights and screenwriters don't have.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The ability to delve into a character's interior world is fiction's gift to writers—something playwrights and screenwriters can't do and memoirists and personal essayists can only do for their narrator. If you're writing fiction, don't waste this opportunity to show what is beneath the surface of behavior and appearance.

question: Try a turning point with no direct confrontation: a character quietly coming to an important decision or seeing the truth about a situation without voicing it.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Turning points can occur without direct confrontation. A turning point scene might be wholly internal, as when it leads up to a character making an important decision or coming to see the truth about a situation without necessarily voicing that awareness.

question: Check whether your reflective narrator judges the younger self too harshly—heavy judgment can spoil the reader’s experience.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If you answered that your reflective narrator feels very judgmental toward her younger self, this too can spoil the experience for your reader.

question: Weigh which narrative voice your scene needs: the limited voice has immediacy, while an older, wiser voice can interpret and comprehend even mid-action.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The limited voice has immediacy; an older and/or wiser voice can interpret and comprehend even in the middle of the ongoing action. You must weigh which effect is desired.

question: If your essay is meditative, moving by association rather than plot, let it depend on reflection—a lot of it, as long as it stays relevant and well written.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: if you’re writing a meditative rather than a narrative essay, which might move by association rather than a chronology of action, the piece will depend on reflection rather than plot, so a lot of reflection (as long as it is relevant and well written) will not be a problem.

question: In memoir or personal essays, choose your details with intention: what you describe reveals what matters to your narrative persona, sets the mood, and hints at themes.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: For those of you writing memoir or personal essays, be aware that the details you include always reveal what’s important to your narrative persona, and they go a long way toward setting the mood and hinting at themes.

question: Check that each metaphor and simile makes sense within the context of the scene—the image must fit the material that contains it.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You’ll want to make sure that the metaphors and similes you choose fit the material that contains them.

question: Keep the narrative and your characters primary—technique must serve them, not the other way around.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: it’s crucial to remember that your narrative and your characters must be primary; technique must be in their service, not the other way around.

question: Vary the intensity of your conflict scenes—if every scene runs at full blast, readers grow exhausted and numb.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Not every conflict scene has to be earth-shatteringly intense; in fact, readers would become exhausted and perhaps even numb if all scenes offered only the constant barrage of (usually violent) conflict that Hollywood blockbuster movies provide.

question: Establish mood through concrete details that combine into a tone, rather than naming the mood outright.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: the silliness of an adult breaking an ankle on a playground slide, and the ridiculous tippy espadrilles all combine to suggest that the story might be ironic or perhaps playful.

question: Cut any dialogue where a character announces the meaning of the story too directly—characters who serve as mouthpieces for the author lose believability.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: As for letting your dialogue carry themes, that too is tricky as once again you don’t want your character to announce the meaning of the story too directly—whenever characters serve as mouthpieces for the author their believability dwindles.

question: Examine the movement in your scene and distinguish physical from emotional movement: does a character change, or does the reader’s perception of the characters change?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Examine the movement within your own scenes and see if you can distinguish physical and/or emotional movement. Is the emotional movement in your scene within a character (has anyone changed over the course of the scene) or is the emotional movement supposed to occur within the reader, who has a new perception of the character(s) and their situations?

question: In creative nonfiction, make sure your narrator's inner world is on the page and that her thoughts are sufficiently revealing of her character.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If you're writing creative nonfiction, make sure your narrator's inner world is on the page and that your (narrator's) thoughts are sufficiently revealing of your (narrator's) character.

question: To make your narrator sound like a child (or any persona), choose not only the words they would use but also the details they would observe.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If you want your narrator to sound like a child, you must not only choose the words a child would use but the details that a child would observe.

question: Insert summary at a natural pause in the action or dialogue of a scene—such as when a character says something the narrator or protagonist needs to reflect on—rather than mid-momentum.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: An example of a good place to insert summary in a scene is a natural pause in action or dialogue, such as when a character says something that the narrator or protagonist needs to reflect on.

question: Don't stack multiple flashbacks in one scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Taken all together, multiple flashbacks are confusing and counterproductive.

question: Filter extra memories elsewhere in the story.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Taken all together, multiple flashbacks are confusing and counterproductive.

question: If you are writing historical fiction or a period piece, use old-fashioned omniscient narrative reflection to intentionally mimic the style of an earlier time.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: For those who are writing historical fiction or period pieces, this sort of “old-fashioned” narrative reflection might serve you well if you wish to intentionally mimic the style of an earlier time.

question: Let your intrusive reflective narrator strike a pose of omniscience tempered with self-deprecating modesty.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: This reflective narrator who insists on intruding on the story strikes a pose—that of both omniscience and self-deprecating modesty.

question: Open with a brief, vividly rendered scene that hooks the reader, then follow with the background summary.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If Wolff had started off with all that background about traveling the West with his mother, I would not have been half as interested as I was after that quick glimpse, that shocking event in the scene that opens the book. I’m hooked, and now I can step back to get the context.

question: If your older narrator feels detached from the younger self, figure out the younger person's motives to reconnect the two selves.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: You’ll have to find a way to connect the older narrator to his or her younger self or the retrospective reflection won’t have depth and power. One way to overcome detachment is to figure out the motives of the younger person—why was she that silly or he that cruel?

question: Remember that pace comes from time, not form: a scene can be slow because it mimics a deliberate progression of time, and a summary can be rapid because it compresses time.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: a scene doesn’t mean speed just because it contains actions, nor does a summary necessarily indicate slowness; scenes can be slow because they are mimicking a deliberate progression of time, and summaries can be rapid because they are compressing time—minutes, days, years.

question: Where you want distance from events, use past tense or past perfect to give both teller and reader breathing room.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The past tense and past perfect give a bit of distance from events—they imply that the narrator is telling the story either soon or long after it happened. They provide breathing room for the teller of the tale and the reader.

question: If the narrative voice and point of view don’t come naturally, try different versions of the scene and keep the one that best serves your intention.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If the narrative voice and point of view don’t come to you naturally, it’s worth trying different versions to see which works best according to your intention for the scene.

question: If your scene needs a moment-by-moment feel, consider present tense.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If your scene requires a moment-by-moment feel, consider using present tense.

question: Where you want events to feel like they are happening in the very moment of narration, write the scene in present tense for immediacy.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Present tense adds immediacy—events are happening in the very moment they are being narrated.

question: When a character receives shocking or confusing information, try present tense to show the character's disjointed response.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If you intend to relay shocking or confusing information to a character, to show that character's disjointed response, you might try using the present tense.

question: Identify the scene at the center of your story—the event everything else spins around—and make sure it is the event you dramatize.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: the center around which the general life of these soldiers, their day-to-day existence, spins. It is the underlying source of all terror. It is the cruel joke, the happenstance—killed while peeing. It is the primal scene, in essence, of the story, the one that must be returned to.

question: Achieve humorous put-downs through the extremity and absurdity of your examples, but never put down the reader—imply you share the assumptions and the wit.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Bryson accomplishes his put-down of this particular place by the extremity and absurdity of his examples. But he doesn’t put down his reader—he implies that we are all buddies here and that we share his assumptions and his wit.

question: Insert a quick summary mid-scene that gives the reader a much fuller sense of the characters' situation and shapes the interpretation of the scenes that follow.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: With those few summarizing words, midscene, we’ve been given a much fuller sense of this family’s situation.

question: Read your dialogue aloud as you work—or have someone read it aloud to you—and rephrase anything that does not sound convincing.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Most important: Read your dialogue aloud as you work to see if it sounds convincing. Better yet, if you can, have someone read it aloud to you.

question: When you follow a scene with reflective summary, make the reflection deepen understanding of the scene or take the reader beyond its events—never restate what the scene has already shown.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The important thing with this technique is that the reflection must deepen our understanding of the scene or take us beyond the events of the scene rather than restating what the scene has already shown.

question: Cut any reflection that doesn't repay the momentum it costs.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Reflection, like flashbacks, slows the action. It interrupts the narrative’s forward movement. So any reflection you add to your story must be worth the loss of momentum, in terms of adding insight or interest for the reader.

question: Cut a follow-up reflection that is obvious, general, or obscure, keeping only what adds something important for readers.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Your follow-up reflection must not only be fresh in that it doesn’t restate what has been well shown in the scene but it also can’t be obvious, general, or obscure lest your reader wonder why you bothered with it at all. Consider if you have something important to add that will engage readers and enlarge the scope of the story.

question: Rewrite any character reflection that floats in a vague narrative ether so it happens in the moment, inside the scene.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Even when Margaret reflects on dentists and suicide, she is reflecting in the moment, within the scene and not in some vague narrative ether.

question: Let your narrative voice tell the reader not just what happened but why it happened or what it means.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: a reflective narrative voice acts as guide and interpreter through a tale; it’s a voice that says it’s not enough to know what happened, I’ll attempt to tell you why it happened or what it means.

question: After a reflective passage of large abstractions, move quickly into the specifics of your story.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Of course he’s speaking in large abstractions and you wouldn’t want to read (or write) a book made up only of abstractions, and Dickens certainly gets into the specifics of his story soon after this reflective introduction.

question: Add reflective summary at points where a distinct narrative voice can ponder and comment on the action or characters.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: It is through reflective summary, or reflection, that we get to hear a distinct narrative voice that ponders and comments on the action or characters.

question: Write reflection that raises ideas your story will then live out, so the reader is intrigued and hungry to see how the story answers them.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Dickens reflects in a manner that gets you intrigued so you are hungry to find out how the story will live out the ideas raised by his introduction.

question: Ask of your dialogue: do the word choices reveal where each character comes from geographically or economically, and what mood they are in?

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Do your characters speak with a regional idiom? Is there any way that their choice of words could tell your reader where they come from geographically or economically? Can you tell the mood of your characters from the manner in which they speak?

question: Check for redundancy between channels: once a character has thought something internally or said it in dialogue, do not repeat it in the other form.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Remember not to repeat in dialogue what your character has thought internally and vice versa—once is enough.

question: Make a resolution scene believable—it must grow naturally out of the characters and actions that precede it and must not feel sentimental, forced, or tacked on.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: The trick with the “happy ending” resolution is that it can’t be sentimental or forced. The scene of the resolved difference must be believable; it must grow naturally out of the characters and actions that precede it and must not feel tacked on.

question: Match the resolution's scale to the work that precedes it—highly dramatic work earns a dramatic resolution, a small personal story wants a quiet one.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Resolution scenes must fit the work that precedes them—if the work is highly dramatic we expect a dramatic resolution scene—for instance, a critical battle in a war story; if the work is small and personal, as in “Cathedral,” then the resolution should be quiet as well.

question: Consider a subtle resolution—the real resolution can be an emotional realization that precedes the story's final, more obvious event.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: Resolutions don’t always have to come with the finality of death or happy endings or divorce; resolutions can be less obvious, more subtle.

question: Build your retrospective story or memoir on the distance between the older, wiser narrator and the younger self as character.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: That distance between older, wiser narrator and younger self as character is an essential part of a retrospective story or memoir.

question: When a character makes a pivotal decision in a scene, insert summary that reveals the process of reasoning behind it.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: We’d know that the narrator decided not to go to war but we wouldn’t know why. The summary inserted into this scene plays a very important role in revealing character motivation and transformation.

question: Make your summaries richly detailed—a summary rendered with rich detail reads as fully dramatized and keeps the story from flattening.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: I had mistaken the proportions of scene and summary in these memoirs because both of these authors made their summaries so richly detailed.

question: Ask whether you are letting your narrator off the hook: be completely honest in assessing both the younger and older self.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
source.quote: If your narrator reflects on his earlier self in too rosy a light, honesty can be sacrificed, leading to the reader losing confidence, trust, and ultimately interest in the narrator and story. Ask yourself, are you letting your narrator off the hook? Have you been completely honest in your assessment of the narrator both younger and older?

question: Don’t force resolution into every scene: a scene can raise a problem the narrative resolves further along, or introduce themes developed later.

source.author: Laurie Alberts
