question: Check your opening: does it immerse the reader in heightened experience, emotional or intellectual, more rewarding than the life around him?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Successful writing immerses the reader in heightened experience—emotional, intellectual, or both—more rewarding than the life around him.

question: Invert a familiar phrase in your first sentence to produce two attention-getters in half a sentence.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We don't think of judging saints. And Orwell inverts the usual 'innocent until proven guilty,' producing two attention-getters in half a sentence.

question: Run your draft's first paragraph through a checklist: does the first sentence trigger curiosity?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Does your first sentence trigger curiosity to make the reader want to continue? What will the reader see in that first sentence? Have you focused on an individual? Have you given us a visible characteristic of that individual? Have you portrayed the individual doing or saying something? Is there a startling or odd fact that will trap attention?

question: Ask what the reader will see in your first sentence.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Does your first sentence trigger curiosity to make the reader want to continue? What will the reader see in that first sentence? Have you focused on an individual? Have you given us a visible characteristic of that individual? Have you portrayed the individual doing or saying something? Is there a startling or odd fact that will trap attention?

question: Check that you have focused on an individual with a visible characteristic doing or saying something.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Does your first sentence trigger curiosity to make the reader want to continue? What will the reader see in that first sentence? Have you focused on an individual? Have you given us a visible characteristic of that individual? Have you portrayed the individual doing or saying something? Is there a startling or odd fact that will trap attention?

question: Ask whether there is a startling or odd fact that will trap attention.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Does your first sentence trigger curiosity to make the reader want to continue? What will the reader see in that first sentence? Have you focused on an individual? Have you given us a visible characteristic of that individual? Have you portrayed the individual doing or saying something? Is there a startling or odd fact that will trap attention?

question: End an ominous sentence with a run of short, monosyllabic words to strengthen the feeling.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: 'Daring death' is an omen. And the rhythm of the words at the end of the sentence is designed to strengthen the ominous feeling in 'the next snow fell.'

question: Position your narrator in a relationship to the main character that itself raises questions the reader wants answered.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The fact that the narrator is Sammy's boss also piques the reader's curiosity. Will the narrator continue to put up with Sammy's drive? Will Sammy get fired? Will Sammy succeed, and if so at what and how will he do it?

question: Treat your nonfiction opening with the goal of sparking the reader's interest enough to engage him in reading the rest.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: At the beginning of a piece of nonfiction, the goal of the writer is the same as that of a writer of fiction: to spark the reader's interest sufficiently to engage him in reading the rest.

question: Mint a novel comparison for a familiar object.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A novel comparison also makes a good hook: At the Academy Awards, the entrance to the Shrine Civil Auditorium is flanked by four giant Oscars quite, or so it seems to me, like sullen art deco Nazis. The sentence might have been improved by omitting 'or so it seems to me' but the comparison is startling and strong nevertheless.

question: Trim the hedging that weakens your comparison.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A novel comparison also makes a good hook: At the Academy Awards, the entrance to the Shrine Civil Auditorium is flanked by four giant Oscars quite, or so it seems to me, like sullen art deco Nazis. The sentence might have been improved by omitting 'or so it seems to me' but the comparison is startling and strong nevertheless.

question: Seduce the reader leisurely by planting omens that something is going to happen.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: There are, however, more leisurely ways to seduce the reader, through omens.

question: Check your opening paragraph against the three goals: does it excite the reader's curiosity about a character or a relationship, introduce a setting, and lend resonance to the story?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The ideal goals of an opening paragraph are: 1. To excite the reader's curiosity, preferably about a character or a relationship. 2. To introduce a setting. 3. To lend resonance to the story.

question: Revise your opening until the curiosity goal is strongly at work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The ideal goals of an opening paragraph are: 1. To excite the reader's curiosity, preferably about a character or a relationship. 2. To introduce a setting. 3. To lend resonance to the story.

question: Replace the flat, abstract name for a character trait with an original, concrete word.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: 'thirsty,' an original way of saying Sammy was hungry, meaning ambitious.

question: Try opening with pseudo-candor — a disclaimer that does the opposite of what the reader expects.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Both examples entice with a slight surprise because they do the opposite of what we expect. Both seem to be disclaimers. Each is a cover-up for a fault. They both might be characterized as pseudo-candor, which can be as effective as candor.

question: Try a quiet first sentence that intrigues through implication rather than shock.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Here's a quieter—yet intriguing—opening sentence by one of the century's grand masters, Graham Greene, from an early (1935) novel, England Made Me. She might have been waiting for her lover.

question: Repeat a key word in your lead to underscore the detail that matters.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Did you note that repeating the word 'umbrella' underscored Sorbino's walking out with someone else's purse? That technique—repetition for effect—increases the dramatic impact of what's being described.

question: Start with a scene the reader can see, and begin it as close to its climax as is feasible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If your aim is publication, your best bet is to start with a scene that the reader can see. Where do you start that scene? As close to its climax as is feasible if your aim is to involve the reader quickly.

question: Keep a conventional opening if you like, but season it with just enough that is unconventional to rouse the reader's curiosity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A craftsman like Cheever will season even the most conventional beginning with just enough that is unconventional to rouse the reader's curiosity.

question: Open with an injunction of secrecy or a promise of revelation that makes the reader want what is being withheld.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: 'You must not tell anyone,' my mother said, 'what I am about to tell you.'

question: Give your subject a small observed action to picture him.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Head-ducking is not much of an action, but a reporter who is a keen observer of small detail would have the advantage of the novelist in picturing Brucell and giving him an action, however small, like ducking his head:

question: Introduce sound into your lead to make it better.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: George Brucell, a tall man, had to duck his head as the chairman ushered him into the meeting room to loud applause. Better because of the introduction of sound.

question: Open by spotlighting a single individual, characterized however briefly, performing an eccentric and somehow beautiful act.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Burns helps us see a besieged city by focusing on a single individual performing an eccentric and somehow beautiful act. Spotlighting an individual who is characterized, however briefly, is an excellent way of involving the reader's emotions.

question: Plant an early surprise that unsettles the reader's expectation.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Our curiosity is aroused when a surprise unsettles our expectation.

question: Pair an unexpected subject with an unexpected attitude in your first sentence to be both surprising and a touch amusing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I have long been an admirer of the octopus. Octopus? Admirer? That opening is both surprising and a touch amusing.

question: Introduce a visual element into your lead to perk it up.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A visual element can almost always be introduced to perk up a lead.

question: Open with a visual parallel that connects two incongruous elements.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Andy Warhol, draftsman of shoes, is dead, and the people viewing his remains are mostly wearing scuffed white sneakers. Note the visual parallel.

question: Present your narrator's core problem through a concrete visual image rather than an abstract statement of it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: That visual opening presents the narrator's problem—the wrong parents!—in an attention-grabbing way. How abstract the beginning would have sounded had the author started, 'I was born to the wrong parents.'

question: Check your action sequences: replace anything that is mere motion with action, which is what people do and say.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In fiction, action consists of what people do and say. Hemingway said it perfectly: “Never mistake motion for action.”

question: Re-read your scene for the sound of your own voice and cut it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Writers are directors of what transpires on the other side of the glass. They are not one of the actors.

question: Elaborate your static descriptions so each one does more than one job.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Cheever’s description is not static. It is part of the storytelling, and that is a key to description as it is used by our better writers: It has more than one function.

question: Rewrite flat exchanges as adversarial dialogue: combative words between characters excite readers' emotions more than sword-play.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Adversarial dialogue is action. Combative words can excite readers’ emotions more than sword-play.

question: Test each scene of your piece: could a camera film it? If not, rework it until it happens visibly before the reader.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: An immediate scene happens in front of the reader, is visible, and therefore filmable. That’s an important test. If you can’t film a scene, it is not immediate.

question: Find the places where you tell offstage events in summary, and rewrite them as immediate scenes.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: These clumps of narrative summary are not experienced by today’s readers with the immediacy and excitement of a witnessed event.

question: Wherever your scene needs information, find a way to have it come naturally out of the characters in the scene instead of stating it baldly in your own voice.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Instead of finding a way to have the information come naturally out of the characters in the scene, he states the information baldly. The author’s voice interrupts the scene.

question: Cut the transitions between your scenes: jump straight from one scene into the next.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Fiction and reporting have now borrowed a film technique called “jump cutting,” moving from one scene into the next with no transition for time to pass or locales to change.

question: Cut description that stops the story, and keep only what moves the narrative forward.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: My advice to writers yearning for publication is to minimize description, and be sure you don’t stop the story while describing. You are a storyteller, not an interior decorator.

question: Go through your nonfiction and convert whatever you can into immediate scenes.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The nonfiction writer who learns to use immediate scenes wherever he can will also find a dramatic improvement in the reception of his work.

question: Read your piece as a reader and cut everything that interrupts the experience: static description, offstage summaries, any glitch that breaks immersion.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We have to train ourselves to detect and remove interruptions of the reader’s experience. Static descriptions interrupt the story. So does a summary of what has happened offstage between scenes or elsewhere.

question: Find summaries of repetitive action and rewrite them as one specific, concrete instance the reader can picture.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The reader cannot see “endless cups” of anything. A summary of repetitive action does not create a clear image.

question: Where two scenes must be linked, bridge them with a few words of narrative summary.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If the scenes must be linked, brief narrative summary can do the linking.

question: Show a character's arrogance through action, not speech.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If he is arrogant, what does he do that will make the reader feel he is arrogant without his saying a word? An arrogant action, I find, works better than arrogant speech.

question: Characterize two people at once: write a description so it reveals the speaker as much as the person spoken about.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Can you characterize more than one person at a time? Of course you can. You characterize the speaker as well as the person spoken about.

question: Build your story from a character rather than a plot.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: There’s a book called Characters Make Your Story that you don’t have to read because the title says it all: Characters make your story. If the people come alive, what they do becomes the story.

question: Combine a physical and a psychological attribute in one portrait so each amplifies the other.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Physical and psychological attributes can also be combined for purposes of characterization:

question: Probe your character across contrasting situations — the differences reveal who they are.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Does he behave differently toward strangers than he does to members of his family? Such a difference is revealing. Would my character behave differently when he met an old friend who is now famous than when he bumped into another friend of the same vintage who is down on his luck and ashamed?

question: Cut the clichéd physical catalogue — facial features, breasts, hips, broad shoulders, chiseled features — it is top-of-the-head, thoughtless writing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Another error of inexperienced writers—or journalists in a hurry—is to confine characterization to the obvious physical attributes. For females, facial features, breasts, hips, buttocks, legs. For males, broad shoulders, strong arms, chiseled features, and so on. That’s top-of-the-head, thoughtless writing.

question: Cut the excess: stop piling on details and search for the single word or phrase that characterizes best.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If there is a common error among inexperienced writers, it’s that they say too much, they try to characterize with an excess of detail instead of trying to find the word or phrase that characterizes best.

question: Cut overused generalizations and similes — “She shuffled like a bag lady,” “She carried herself like a queen” — they pass on information but evoke nothing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You’ll want to avoid generalizations or similes that have been overused, such as “She shuffled like a bag lady” or “She carried herself like a queen.”

question: Add dramatic contrast between what your character is doing and what they are saying to themselves.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It adds to the drama to have contrast between what the character is doing and what he is saying to himself.

question: Characterize with deliberate exaggeration.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Exaggeration is another technique for characterizing: Laverne weighed two tons naked. Nobody believes for a second that Laverne weighed four thousand pounds. In speech we hear it said about an object that “it weighed a ton.” We exaggerate constantly. It’s a way of communicating quickly, and often effectively.

question: Put exaggerations in a character's mouth rather than the narrator's.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: That’s not the author talking, it’s a character talking, and therefore an acceptable exaggeration. It also characterizes the speaker.

question: Show how a character uses their eyes instead of giving their color or shape.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What inexperienced writers often do is give us the color or shape of eyes. That’s not as effective as conveying how the character uses his eyes.

question: Characterize through at least five channels — physical attributes, clothing, psychology, actions, and dialogue — not just one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: There are at least five different ways to characterize: 1. Through physical attributes. 2. With clothing or the manner of wearing clothing. 3. Through psychological attributes and mannerisms, 4. Through actions. 5. In dialogue.

question: Replace clichéd exaggerations in dialogue with a fresh line that characterizes.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: “I’ve been waiting forever for you” is an exaggeration—and also a cliché. It doesn’t characterize. Here’s how an experienced writer, Rita Mae Brown, did it in her novel High Hearts: “Girl, my fingernails could grow an inch just waiting for you.”

question: Replace a wimpish protagonist: imagine an intruder who barges into your study and tells you to shut up.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I ask the writer to imagine that he is in his study with the door closed. A person outside wants to come in. The writer orders the intruder to stay out. I ask the writer to imagine a second person outside his door who says to the first, “Get out of my way,” then comes into the writer’s study without asking. The writer starts to object and this second intruder says, “You shut up and listen for a change!” I urge the writer to listen to the character, rude as he is, and then compose a letter from that new non-wimp character to the writer that is assertive, candid, and at least a touch eccentric.

question: Write a letter from that rude, assertive, candid, slightly eccentric character to you.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I ask the writer to imagine that he is in his study with the door closed. A person outside wants to come in. The writer orders the intruder to stay out. I ask the writer to imagine a second person outside his door who says to the first, “Get out of my way,” then comes into the writer’s study without asking. The writer starts to object and this second intruder says, “You shut up and listen for a change!” I urge the writer to listen to the character, rude as he is, and then compose a letter from that new non-wimp character to the writer that is assertive, candid, and at least a touch eccentric.

question: Keep characterization visual whenever possible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Characterization should be kept visual whenever possible: “He walked against an unseen wind” is visual.

question: Listen to your character's dialogue: do their figures of speech and expressions characterize them strongly?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When I’m planning a character, I also try to listen to his or her dialogue as if the character were in the room with me. Do they use figures of speech and expressions that characterize strongly?

question: Never stop your story to characterize — let the reader see your characters talking and doing things.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Don’t ever stop your story to characterize. Avoid telling the reader what your character is like. Let the reader see your characters talking and doing things.

question: Give your character one item of clothing that stands out in the reader's mind.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As to a character’s clothing, I try to focus on one item that will stand out in the reader’s mind, for instance the fact that my character always wears a raincoat even when the sun is shining.

question: Introduce your characters before the catastrophe: let readers know the people in the car before they see it crash.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: From those experiences I am convinced that we need to know the people in the car before we see the car crash. The events of a story do not affect our emotions in an important way unless we know the characters.

question: Characterize a character at rest: give them a posture or bearing that conveys personality without motion.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The character needn’t be in motion. Posture can provide personality: He had the bearing of a man who had been a soldier a long time ago.

question: Make your protagonist assertive: they want something, want it badly, and want it now.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Let’s face it, readers aren’t interested in wimps. They are interested in assertive characters who want something, want it badly, and want it now.

question: Characterize through psychological attributes that connect to the story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Characterizing through psychological attributes can be rewarding because they often connect to the story: He dealt with his friends as if they were employees. He talked and they listened.

question: Give a small role to a real, recognizable person, using only a trace of them to jog the reader's memory.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One of the devices used by successful thriller writers is to give a small role to a real person, usually a high officeholder. Writers who use this technique do not attempt to characterize famous individuals in depth. A trace to jog memory is enough.

question: Set your character on first appearance: if a trait defines them, introduce it the moment they appear.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you develop a characteristic that’s especially pertinent to your character, or original, it’s a good idea to use it on the character’s first appearance, to “set” the character.

question: Imagine your character with reason to shout: what would you hear? If they would never shout, what thought are they repressing?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We know that people reveal themselves more when they raise their voices than when they speak normally. If my character had reason to shout, what would we hear? Or if my character is the kind of person who would never shout, what thought is he repressing?

question: Find the single word that carries a character's judgment of another, and let it reveal the speaker, not the person described.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The word “accent” characterizes not Koch but the speaker Thomassy.

question: Choose physical characteristics that relate to your story, and invert them to convey an antisexual trait.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Instead of clichéd attributes, consider using physical characteristics that relate to your story.

question: If your story starts from a theme that obsesses you, keep your allegiance to character: imagine characters whose lives involve the theme.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If their allegiance is to character, their theme-originated story has a better chance of survival.

question: Find every trait you state outright and convey it through an action the character performs, so the reader feels it instead of being told it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The man is not just tall, he is being characterized through an action. Again, the writer is not just describing; he is characterizing by an action.

question: Characterize every participant in a love triangle fully: a one-note third character fails to come alive.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The novel wasn’t working because the husband and wife were characterized successfully, but the mistress seemed to be all sex, a one-note characterization that failed to make her come alive. A triangle doesn’t work unless all three participants are characterized fully.

question: When a character feels one-note, describe them with an unexpected comparison, and carry those traits through the work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: He said he saw her walking across the room like a young lion—a male simile that opened up a new way of characterizing the mistress.

question: Make your villain mean-spirited, not merely badly behaved.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As to villains, bad behavior on its own is not as effective as mean spiritedness, deriving satisfaction and even pleasure from hurting the hero or preventing him from attaining his goal.

question: Open a characterization with a visual image and close with the character's conclusion.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Note that the paragraph starts with a visual image—the parents standing next to their car at the bus station—and ends with the character’s conclusion. Had the order been reversed, the effect would be lessened.

question: Don't default to 'walk': choose the verb whose nuance both characterizes and conveys a visual image.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A writer who always has his characters “walk” is missing opportunities. Variants on walking should be used with caution, however. Their overuse annoys readers. In considering the possible variations for walking, you have been doing what writers should do every day—reflect on the meanings of individual words.

question: Make reflecting on word meanings a daily habit.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A writer who always has his characters “walk” is missing opportunities. Variants on walking should be used with caution, however. Their overuse annoys readers. In considering the possible variations for walking, you have been doing what writers should do every day—reflect on the meanings of individual words.

question: Have a character characterize a whole class of people through a snapshot of one person.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Also note that Jane is characterizing not only her mother but a whole class of people.

question: Give your antagonist a slightly disturbing physical mannerism whose repetition grates on readers.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Can he have a physical mannerism that would be at least slightly disturbing to most people, for instance an involuntary blinking of one eye? Or sniffing? Frequent nosewrinkling? Earlobe-pulling? Elbow-scratching? It is the repetitive nature of such mannerisms that grates on readers.

question: Decide how your antagonist behaves toward people they've never met.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: How does your antagonist behave toward people he’s never met before? Does he effuse charm, is he overly deferential, or is he discourteous, uninterested, openly bored, arrogant? All of these are characteristics that would help form the reader’s attitude toward your villain.

question: Have your character complain bitterly about something and listen.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Another way is to have your character complain bitterly about something. In life, complaining is more effective when it is done in a normal voice, the words speaking for themselves. However, bitter complaining connotes an emotional overload. At such times, your character is speaking, as it were, from the gut or the heart rather than the head. Listen to the character in that state. It will help you with the part of characterization that is normally hidden from public view.

question: Make your character's change surprising but consistent with what the reader knows of them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: These are just a few examples of how a character might change in the course of a novel. The writer has to ask, is the change consistent with the character as portrayed? A change can be surprising, but it should not seem out of sync with what we know about the character.

question: Explore the full span of meaning of personality, disposition, temperament, individuality, and eccentricity for your character.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: My students find that their work in characterization improves markedly after they’ve considered the full span of meaning of those terms. ... Personality refers to the distinctive traits of an individual, a set of behaviors, attitudes, manners, and mannerisms that identify a person.

question: Imagine your adult character secretly dressed in children's clothes and ask why, but take the character's answer, not yours.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Imagine your adult character secretly dressed in children’s clothes. Why is he doing that? What you want is not your answer, but the character’s answer to that question. The child in an adult character may have a poignant memory of a lasting hurt. Or a marvelous secret to reveal.

question: Imagine a conversation between your character and a character you love from a classic; listen to what one says and how the other answers.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As you are readying yourself for sleep, imagine a scene in which that character and the character you are working on have a conversation about the story of your book. Imagine what one says and how the other answers. In due course, let yourself sleep. You might find that in the first moments of wakefulness the next morning, you’ll want to reach for a pad and paper at your bedside to record some thoughts about your character, enriched by his or her conversation with a character you loved.

question: Rephrase top-of-the-head descriptions of your character’s clothing into visual images that say something particular about them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Characterizing through unusual clothing or the manner of wearing clothing is another often neglected possibility. What it requires is to avoid the easy description that first comes to mind. ... The first description doesn’t say anything particular about either Ellen or the gown. The second is visual and tells us how Ellen and the gown came across in a way that made them both look good.

question: Characterize through contrast — give a character a behavior that clashes with their appearance.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Contrast is a useful technique for characterization. It sometimes has the extra virtue of surprise. ... What helped characterize her for me was the contrast between her appearance and her nose-picking.

question: Give a character attributes that go against their dominant behavior in the scene to come.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: An important technique that is used too seldom by novelists is to give a character life by introducing attributes that go against the character’s dominant behavior in the scene to come.

question: Ask whether your antagonist is curable — bad will work, but evil will provide a more profound experience.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You need to ask yourself about your antagonist, Is he curable? Is he bad but can be straightened out? Bad will work, but evil will provide a more profound experience for the reader.

question: Cut characterization so extreme it makes the character seem like a cartoon.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Beware of characters who are so extreme as to seem like cartoon characters. Some characters in Charles Dickens’s novels seem wildly exaggerated. Such characters are difficult to make credible to readers of mainstream fiction today.

question: Cut protagonists who are psychotic or habitual drunks.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Eccentric behavior is sometimes said to be nutty behavior, implying strange behavior, which is perfectly suitable for fiction. But “nutty” can also mean crazy, which is not intended here for an important reason. There are two types seldom seen in fiction: people who are psychotic and habitual drunks. Readers find it difficult to identify with their behavior.

question: Define your character’s disposition — their customary emotional response to the people and places of their world.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The disposition of a person is her attitude toward the people and places of the world, her customary response, particularly her emotional response.

question: Make your character just different enough to interest the reader without seeming 'special,' so readers can identify with their plight.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I made the Browns just different enough to interest the reader, but it was important that they not seem “special.” Therefore, when calamity hits the Browns, readers from any walk of life can identify with their plight, which is critical for the story. Stephen King usually has quite ordinary-seeming characters get involved in extraordinary circumstances. In most instances, however, you’ll want to make your characters as distinctive as possible rather than “ordinary.”

question: Think of the most eccentric person you know, imagine your character doing their most eccentric thing, then adjust it to a variation that stays in character.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Think of the most eccentric person you know. What makes him (or her) eccentric? What is the most eccentric thing they have ever done? What might they do that would seem even more eccentric? Then think of your character doing that very thing! Unlikely? Unreasonable? Surprising? All of the above? If such behavior would be out of character ... for your protagonist, then what variation of it would be in character?

question: Give your character an offbeat manner of behavior, dress, or speech that is peculiar to them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Eccentricity is an offbeat manner of behavior, dress, or speech that is peculiar to a person and greatly dissimilar to the same characteristics of most other people.

question: Ask whether your character is capable of any important eccentricity — if not, readers won't find them interesting.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If your character isn’t capable of any important eccentricity, you may have picked a character who will not be greatly interesting to readers.

question: Decide which emotions you are manipulating in the reader when you pit characters against each other.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What the writers have been doing with this character all along, of course, is manipulating our emotions, which is exactly what your role is when you are pitting characters against each other to create a story.

question: Make your character's extraordinary quality evident almost immediately after they appear, unless the story's thrust is their gradual unveiling.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The extraordinary quality of a character should usually be made evident almost immediately after he or she appears in the story, unless the thrust of a story is to have the gradual unveiling of a character’s unusual habits or ambition.

question: Make your characters extraordinary rather than 'perfectly ordinary.'

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: People who are exactly like other people probably don’t exist. But people who seem like most other people litter our lives, and we don’t usually seek their company because they are boring. Readers don’t read novels in order to experience the boredom they often experience in life. They want to meet interesting people, extraordinary people, preferably people different from anyone they’ve met before in or out of fiction.

question: Check that your character's oddity is individual behavior, not conformity to a widespread group mode.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When a great number of young men take to wearing an earring, that is not eccentricity. When young women iron their hair as many did in the sixties, that is not eccentricity. They are conforming to a widespread group mode.

question: Rephrase your character's quirk as others see it, not as the character sees it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The idiosyncrasies of a person are, of course, as seen by others rather than that person, who often believes his or her idiosyncrasies to be “perfectly normal.”

question: Describe your character's singularity with the particulars of concrete detail.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A writer describes a character’s singularity with the particulars of concrete detail. These are the characteristics by which an individual is recognized by others. Her differentness is her identity. It can be said that the individuality of a person marks her off, singles her out, sets her apart, and ultimately defines her.

question: When you have trouble improving a characterization, view your character from a different perspective.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Somerset Maugham said, “You can never know enough about your characters.” When you have trouble improving a particular characterization, you need to know more. The remedy may lie in viewing your character from a different perspective.

question: Characterize a minor character in a few words through a single action.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The priest was young and blushed easily. ... In just seven words, the priest is visible even before his special uniform is described. Note that blushing is an action that characterizes,

question: Use a minor character to characterize a major player and to advance the plot at the same time.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Minor characters can not only help characterize the major players in a story, but can also advance the plot.

question: Cut minor-character detail that fools the reader into expecting a larger role.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I’ve seen minor characters given too much characterization, fooling the reader into thinking they had some larger role to play. Sometimes all you want is for the reader to be able to see the minor character. Here’s how Nanci Kincaid does it:

question: Select one memorable characteristic that singles each minor character out from the rest of humanity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The most efficient technique for making minor characters come alive is to select one memorable characteristic that singles them out from the rest of humanity. This is particularly true for fleeting characters, those that appear and vanish, not to return.

question: Characterize a minor character through the eyes of an important character.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Characterizing a minor character through the eyes of an important character is a valuable technique.

question: Imagine your character in the nude, honestly and in detail — people in the nude become especially vulnerable, and a person seen realistically in the nude is immediately credible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Last, imagine your character in the nude. This one almost always works if you portray your character in the nude honestly and in detail. People in the nude become especially vulnerable.

question: Unfetter your imagination — see your character doing something out of the ordinary.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Unfetter your imagination. Can you see your character flapping arms, trying to fly? Or trying to kiss everyone at a party? Or walking in the snow without shoes? Readers are interested in the out-of-the-ordinary. All these questions involve the character in action, the ideal way to characterize.

question: When introducing a character who holds power in a scene, suggest their vulnerability before they exercise it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A common fault in fiction is the portrayal of characters as all good or all bad. Therefore, when introducing a character who will be in a position of power in a scene, suggest that character’s vulnerability before the character exercises power. Conversely, when introducing a character who will be hurt emotionally or physically in the scene to come, show the character’s strength at the outset.

question: When introducing a character who will be hurt, show their strength at the outset.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A common fault in fiction is the portrayal of characters as all good or all bad. Therefore, when introducing a character who will be in a position of power in a scene, suggest that character’s vulnerability before the character exercises power. Conversely, when introducing a character who will be hurt emotionally or physically in the scene to come, show the character’s strength at the outset.

question: Plan how your protagonist changes by the end of the novel.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In a novel it is common and desirable for the principal character to change by the end of the book. If the protagonist is a risk taker, he may step into adulthood by learning that some kinds of risks are foolhardy.

question: Give your protagonist will — desire reinforced by ambition.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We have seen that wimpishness is off-putting in a protagonist. We have a sense that will—desire reinforced by ambition—is what makes protagonists drive us through their stories.

question: Characterize through self-contradiction — a character explaining himself in contradictory terms fascinates readers.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Dostoevsky’s opening of Notes from Underground has a character explaining himself. He is so self-contradictory that when I read this opening aloud to students, they invariably laugh:

question: Scope your short story to one event or episode with room for a change of attitude toward something specific.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In a short story there is usually time for only one event or episode. ... There is room for a change of attitude toward something specific. Most often there isn’t room in a short story for a character to experience enough to cause a profound change.

question: Visualize your character as suddenly rather old, and carry something of that into the present-age characterization.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Yet another way is to visualize your character as suddenly rather old. How would that change her appearance, dress, walk? Is there anything that you can incorporate in your characterization at your character’s present age? Some people preserve characteristics of their childhood, others seem prematurely old in some way. So do some characters.

question: Define your character’s temperament — their characteristic way of confronting a new day or a new development.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Temperament is a person’s manner of behaving, thinking, and particularly reacting to people and circumstances, his characteristic way of confronting a new day or a new development.

question: Weave your characters’ traits into the story as part of an action — keep your explanations out of it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: To weave individual characteristics into a story, as much as possible let them come out during or as part of an action. The object is to avoid holding up the story and to keep the writer’s explanations out of it.

question: Rewrite how you describe a character's tastes as a distinctive verbal habit.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Martin referred to men who wore shirts and ties all day not as people but as “suits.”

question: Give your villain a human side so the reader meets the person behind the evil.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: That’s the key, of course. Uck is human. We meet his wife and child. He can be charming if he wants to. Nevertheless, he is fundamentally evil in the way he attaches himself to the life of the protagonist and won’t let go. He is not just getting a lift in the rain, he is the leech that cannot be pulled off the skin. Uck has taken the first step in pushing himself into the protagonist’s life and has begun the process of forcing the

question: Make your villain seem like a normal human being whose villainy is an ineradicable part of his nature.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Once upon a time, readers tolerated mustache-twirling villains with no countervailing virtues in their makeup. Today’s readers can be roughly divided into two groups, those who accept the fantasy villains of childhood, as in the James Bond stories and Arnold Schwarzenegger films, and those who insist on credibility. In life, villains do not uncurl whips and snarl. They seem like normal human beings. But normal humans are not villains. What distinguishes the true villain is not just the degree to which he hides his villainy under an attractive patina to snare his victims, but his contact with evil.

question: Write what other people think but don't say.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A writer cannot be a Pollyanna. He is in the business of writing what other people think but don’t say,

question: Ask yourself whether the conflict you've invented involves the best possible thing that could happen to your protagonist; if not, raise what is at stake.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you have some concern about the intensity of your plot, ask yourself, Does the conflict you’ve invented involve the best possible thing that could happen to your protagonist?

question: If your conflict is small, enlarge it until it resonates: does it lead to profound unhappiness, injury, or death, or turn on an object exceedingly valuable to the main character or on an important life decision?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When planning your story, it is important to remember that small clashes result in stories that seem relatively trivial. Larger clashes resonate for the reader. Ask yourself these questions: Does the conflict you are working on lead to profound unhappiness, injury, or death? Or is the conflict over an object that is exceedingly valuable to the main character? Is the conflict over an important life decision—to move far away, to change one’s career, to leave for another partner, to follow a hazardous opportunity, to avoid intolerable circumstances?

question: If your character needs to get somewhere right away, introduce any unexpected, uncontrollable event.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: For instance, your character needs to get someplace right away. The car breaks down. (In a melodrama, the breakdown may have been precipitated by the villain or an accomplice.) Or the weather changes drastically and impedes progress. If the weather won’t do, think of any unexpected, uncontrollable event.

question: Give your characters a want that motivates them and drives their actions.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We are driven through life by our needs and wants. So must the characters we create be motivated by what they want. The driving force of characters is their desire.

question: Relate your character's deepest desire to their fundamental difference from other characters, especially the antagonist.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: To carry the point a step further, I suggest relating the character’s deepest desire to the character’s fundamental difference from other characters, especially the character of the antagonist.

question: Cause a character to be embarrassed: it will almost always create an interesting plot development.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Experiencing a character’s embarrassment involves the reader. Causing a character to be embarrassed will almost always create an interesting plot development.

question: For each important incident in your plot, have the exact opposite of what the reader expects happen next.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Surprises are not difficult to create. Look at each important incident in your plot and see what you would normally expect to happen next. Then have the exact opposite happen. At least half the time an idea will suggest itself that will surprise your characters as well as yourself.

question: Even when your plot deviates from the norm, keep the protagonist's fierce desire and the conflict engendered by obstacles.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The wellread writer will be familiar with complex plots that deviate from the norm. What they do not deviate from is the fierce desire of the protagonist and the conflict engendered by obstacles.

question: Make your characters want something right away, even if it's only a glass of water.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: “When I used to teach creative writing, I would tell the students to make their characters want something right away even if it’s only a glass of water. Characters paralyzed by the meaninglessness of modern life still have to drink water from time to time.”

question: Make your conflicting wants connected significantly and over something the reader will view as important, not just meaningful to the characters.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The essence of dramatic conflict lies in the clash of wants. You need to be certain that the conflicting wants are connected significantly and are over something that the reader will view as important.

question: Check that your clash seems inevitable to the reader.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Ask yourself, will the clash between your protagonist and your antagonist seem inevitable to the reader? Have you avoided coincidence as the cause of their clash? Will the clash take place in a highly visible environment so that the reader will see the action?

question: Ensure that coincidence is not the cause of your clash.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Ask yourself, will the clash between your protagonist and your antagonist seem inevitable to the reader? Have you avoided coincidence as the cause of their clash? Will the clash take place in a highly visible environment so that the reader will see the action?

question: Make your clash take place in a highly visible environment so the reader sees the action.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Ask yourself, will the clash between your protagonist and your antagonist seem inevitable to the reader? Have you avoided coincidence as the cause of their clash? Will the clash take place in a highly visible environment so that the reader will see the action?

question: Think of what would most thwart your protagonist's want, then give the antagonist the power to thwart it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One way to plan is to think of what would most thwart your protagonist’s want, then give the power to thwart that want to the antagonist.

question: If a scene isn't exciting enough, introduce a new character into it who has something important at stake.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If any scene seems not yet exciting enough, think of introducing a new character into it, which always generates possibilities for conflict, especially if the new character has something important at stake in what is happening in that scene.

question: Create obstacles beyond the villain—someone blocking the protagonist for reasons of their own.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It’s common to think of the obstacles of all being generated by the villain, but we’ve seen that acts of nature can also be obstacles. And there are always other people butting in. You can devise an unwanted intervention by someone who wants to help but makes things worse. Or you can have an unwanted intervention by someone unrelated to the villain who wants to block the protagonist for reasons of his own. You can have a previously absent person return who causes problems because she is not up on what has transpired during her absence.

question: Prepare a list of every obstacle you plan to use in your plot.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Writers who feel the need of discipline in plotting can sometimes benefit by preparing a list of every obstacle they plan to use in their plot. They then can ask themselves, is the first obstacle strong enough to hook the reader? Do the obstacles build?

question: Ask whether the first obstacle is strong enough to hook the reader.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Writers who feel the need of discipline in plotting can sometimes benefit by preparing a list of every obstacle they plan to use in their plot. They then can ask themselves, is the first obstacle strong enough to hook the reader? Do the obstacles build?

question: Ask whether your obstacles build.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Writers who feel the need of discipline in plotting can sometimes benefit by preparing a list of every obstacle they plan to use in their plot. They then can ask themselves, is the first obstacle strong enough to hook the reader? Do the obstacles build?

question: Make each obstacle greater than the last: as each obstacle is faced and overcome by the protagonist, an even greater obstacle must present itself.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Do the obstacles build? That means as each obstacle is faced and overcome by the protagonist, an even greater obstacle has to present itself.

question: If your protagonist wants little or has largely given up wanting, give them a want they actively pursue.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Inexperienced writers, sometimes ill read in the great works of their own and previous times, often try to write novels with a relatively passive protagonist who wants little or has largely given up wanting.

question: When you're stuck for character-derived plot ideas, study the classified personal ads: their writers want a relationship badly enough to advertise for it, and in describing the person they want to meet they are unknowingly describing themselves.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I counsel them to examine the classified personal ads, which frequently have the following characteristics: They are written by people who want a relationship so badly that they are willing to advertise for it. What they want is a mate, which is a high category of desire and the subject of much fiction. The ad writers are doing two things at once: they are trying to describe the kind of person they want to meet; they are describing themselves (sometimes unknowingly).

question: Plant your obstacles ahead of time so they don't seem like arbitrary devices of the author.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One caution. Some obstacles need to be planted ahead of time so as not to seem arbitrary devices of the author.

question: Make your character want something badly enough that readers root for them to attain it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If your character doesn’t want anything badly enough, readers will have a hard time rooting for him to attain his goal, which is what compels readers to continue reading. The more urgent the want, the greater the reader’s interest.

question: Put your protagonist's desire and antagonist's desire into sharp conflict.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Which brings us to the essence of plotting: putting the protagonist’s desire and the antagonist’s desire into sharp conflict. If the conflict isn’t sharp, the tension will be lax.

question: Generate a character's fear from small things, not just mortal danger.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Experiencing a character’s fear creates enormous tension. It can be fear of mortal danger, of course, but experienced novelists generate fear from small things.

question: Shape your conflict so it results in a verbal or physical struggle in which your characters clash.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Would the conflict you have described result in a verbal or physical struggle? Would that struggle call for strong scenes in which your characters clash in an exciting way?

question: Make the want and the opposition to it important, necessary, and urgent.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Those are the three keys: the want and the opposition to the want need to be important, necessary, and urgent. The result should be the kind of conflict that interests readers.

question: If you write popular fiction, give your protagonist a less personal, more melodramatic want.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: For them and other writers of popular fiction, the following wants were paramount: Defeating the plans of a national enemy. Blocking an assassin out to kill an important person. Rescuing someone close to the hero. Solving an important crime.

question: Give your conflict two-way urgency: the protagonist wants their important desire fulfilled as soon as possible, and the antagonist wants to wreck that chance just as soon.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: And be certain there is a two-way urgency: your protagonist wants a particular, important desire fulfilled as soon as possible, and the antagonist wants to wreck the chance of that happening, also as soon as possible.

question: If your character's want is too specialized, replace it with one close to universal: gaining or losing a love, achieving a lifetime ambition, seeing justice done, saving a life, seeking revenge, or accomplishing a task that at first seemed impossible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It is easier for the reader to identify with a want that is close to universal and not too specialized (a stamp collection is relatively specialized). The wants that interest a majority of readers include gaining or losing a love, achieving a lifetime ambition, seeing that justice is done, saving a life, seeking revenge, and accomplishing a task that at first seemed impossible.

question: Pick an unusual locale, place a character unlikely to be there, and imagine how other characters react.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You can surprise yourself (and your readers eventually) by picking an unusual locale that you know well enough to depict accurately. Then choose a character you have already created who is most unlikely to show up in that locale. Put that character in that locale. Imagine what happens when the character shows up there, and other characters react.

question: Transfer the worst thing you imagined to the character in your story and ask whether it creates a suitable obstacle in your plot.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Now imagine the same worst thing happening not to your best friend but to the character in your story. Would that create a suitable obstacle in the plot you are developing?

question: Think of the worst thing that could possibly happen to you right now, and don't censor: a writer disciplines himself to uncover, where a layman instinctively covers up.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Think of the worst thing that could possibly happen to you right now. Don’t censor. A layman instinctively covers up. A writer disciplines himself to uncover.

question: End most chapters of your book so that they point toward the next chapter.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If it is a book, does the end of most chapters point toward the next?

question: Start with the character rather than a preconceived plot.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thou shalt not sprinkle characters into a preconceived plot lest thou produce hackwork. In the beginning was the character, then the word, and from the character’s words is brought forth action.

question: Characterize a character as capable of his bizarre conduct before he does it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If this were a story about an eccentric who behaves unpredictably, Tom’s strange conduct would require planting. If Thomas’s action is not to seem ludicrous, he would have had to have been characterized as someone who could do something as zany as going out dressed up without his pants.

question: Let your characters do things readers crave rather than keeping them meek.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thy characters shall steal, kill, dishonor their parents, bear false witness, and covet their neighbor’s house, wife, manservant, maidservant, ox, and ass, for reader’s crave such actions and yawn when thy characters are meek, innocent, forgiving, and peaceable.

question: Distinguish a closed environment from a crucible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The location is a crucible, but as yet there is no overwhelming relationship that keeps him there.

question: Add an overwhelming relationship that keeps the characters in the locale.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The location is a crucible, but as yet there is no overwhelming relationship that keeps him there.

question: Treat every coincidence in your story as a credibility risk.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If this happened in a story, the skeptical reader would say that the author is responsible for the coincidence and that it isn’t believable.

question: Convert summaries into visual events the reader can see.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you summarized material that would make interesting visual passages if you converted the summaries to events the reader could see? If there are summaries you cannot or don’t want to convert to scenes, can you shorten them in order to avoid losing the reader’s attention? If you want to “jump-cut,” the reader will go along with you.

question: Shorten the summaries you keep so the reader doesn't lose attention.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you summarized material that would make interesting visual passages if you converted the summaries to events the reader could see? If there are summaries you cannot or don’t want to convert to scenes, can you shorten them in order to avoid losing the reader’s attention? If you want to “jump-cut,” the reader will go along with you.

question: Audit every action central to your story: is its motivation credible at the moment it happens? A major act, like kidnapping, must seem motivated as it takes place or the story reads as made up.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The worst mistake that a story writer can make is to have unconvincing motivation for actions that are central to the story.

question: If your locale does not add crucible stress, change it so one participant finds it hard to leave, or add background that links the characters.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If the locale you have chosen for a particular scene does not add the stress of a crucible, can you change the location of the scene, making it difficult for one of the participants to leave? Or is there anything that you can add to the background of either or both characters that would link them in a crucible and thereby raise the stress of their relationship?

question: Form a crucible for your plot: an environment that bonds your characters and holds them together.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A crucible is an environment, emotional or physical, that bonds two people.

question: Make your characters' motivation to keep opposing each other greater than their motivation to run away, or place them where they cannot run.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The key to the crucible is that the motivation of the characters to continue opposing each other is greater than their motivation to run away. Or they can’t run away because they are in a prison cell, a lifeboat, an army, or a family.

question: Ask whether your beginning provokes sufficient curiosity and how soon after the start the reader decides not to stop reading.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Before you settle on a beginning, ask yourself if it provokes sufficient curiosity in the reader. How soon after your beginning will the reader comes upon the “engine” of your article or book, the place at which the reader decides not to stop reading?

question: Go after most adjectives and adverbs and all flab as an editor, not as the writer.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you eliminated most adjectives and adverbs, and the unnecessary words we call flab? Go after them as an editor, not as the writer. Cut every cliché you come across. Say it new or say it straight. Can you spot any similes or metaphors that show signs of strain and should now be cut?

question: Cut every cliché.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you eliminated most adjectives and adverbs, and the unnecessary words we call flab? Go after them as an editor, not as the writer. Cut every cliché you come across. Say it new or say it straight. Can you spot any similes or metaphors that show signs of strain and should now be cut?

question: Cut similes or metaphors that show signs of strain.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you eliminated most adjectives and adverbs, and the unnecessary words we call flab? Go after them as an editor, not as the writer. Cut every cliché you come across. Say it new or say it straight. Can you spot any similes or metaphors that show signs of strain and should now be cut?

question: Read your manuscript as if you were its editor and it was written by someone else: identify the weakest part, cut it, or condense it if it can't be cut entirely.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you were the editor of your manuscript and it was written by someone else, what would you choose as the weakest part? Look at that section now and see if you can eliminate it. If you can’t cut it entirely, can you condense it? Is there anything you can add to the beginning of that section that would arouse the reader’s curiosity?

question: Add something to the weakest part's beginning that arouses the reader's curiosity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you were the editor of your manuscript and it was written by someone else, what would you choose as the weakest part? Look at that section now and see if you can eliminate it. If you can’t cut it entirely, can you condense it? Is there anything you can add to the beginning of that section that would arouse the reader’s curiosity?

question: Cut clichés that are out of character.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The next step is to check if the lines spoken by each character are consistent with that character’s background. Then I remove clichés that are out of character.

question: Check that every line spoken fits the character's background.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The next step is to check if the lines spoken by each character are consistent with that character’s background. Then I remove clichés that are out of character.

question: Rewrite a flat exchange so the talk turns tough, combative, or adversarial.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When talk is tough, combative, or adversarial it can be as exciting as physical action.

question: Rewrite dialect without odd spellings or phonetic pronunciations.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Spelling out pronunciations (for instance, “Anyone see my seester?” as an attempt to indicate a Latino accent) is almost always a bad choice. I would also like to caution against a use of dialect in which speech is differentiated from the standard language by odd spellings.

question: Choose each character’s words for their effect — “May I know your name?” signals polite formality, “You, what’s your name?” impolite aggression.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Even the simplest of examples demonstrates how diction can differentiate one character from another. “May I know your name?” comes across as a polite and perhaps excessively formal marker. “You, what’s your name?” sounds impolite and aggressive.

question: Cut echoes from your dialogue—replies that mirror the question back.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Talk is full of echoes. Echoes don’t belong in dialogue.

question: Elaborate an ethnic character's speech through content and small errors rather than phonetic spellings.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: For many kinds of ethnic characters, in addition to word order and rhythm, errors in speech, particularly the omission of words, are useful: “How you get so big?” In addition, you can use the wrong verb, leave out the articles “the” and “a,” devise incomplete or slightly malformed sentences, use vocabulary oddities, and the occasional foreign word that would be understood in context.

question: Rewrite an exchange so a few lines imply the speakers' shared, unresolved past.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Characters don’t need to make speeches at each other. From just four lines the reader learns that these two people have probably had a relationship in the past that is not resolved, and at least for one of them the relationship is filled with bitterness.

question: Write dialogue as a semblance of speech, not a record of it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thou shalt not forget that dialogue is as a foreign tongue, a semblance of speech and not a record of it, a language in which directness diminishes and obliqueness sings.

question: Write historical dialogue as invention, not mimicry, keeping it intelligible to today's reader.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: John Fowles, whose novel The French Lieutenant’s Woman takes place in the nineteenth century, points out that writing dialogue for an earlier era involves invention, not just research and mimicry.

question: Turn the conversation with an incidental remark and let the response carry the plot in a new direction.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Tension can now be increased not only by the substance of their relationship but also by incidental matters. For instance: HE: It’s beginning to rain. SHE: What do you suggest?

question: Test each line of dialogue by asking what the speaker is trying to accomplish with those exact words.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What the reader gets from your fiction is the meaning of words. And most important, the emotion that meaning generates.

question: Cut jargon in dialogue to a touch.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Jargon is a marker of stuffiness. One must be careful in its use. A touch is plenty. A surfeit of jargon quickly becomes caricature instead of characterization.

question: Cut filler from dialogue so every word left counts toward characterization, story, or emotion.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: “Uh” is totally useless to a writer. Dialogue is a lean language in which every word counts.

question: Differentiate each character's speech with markers so no two characters sound alike.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The richest means of such differentiation are speech markers, signals that are quickly identifiable by the reader. Vocabulary is an important marker. Throwaway words and phrases are markers. Tight or loose wording is a marker. Run-on sentences are markers. Sarcasm is a marker. Cynicism is a marker. Poor grammar is a marker. Omitted words are markers. Inappropriate modifiers are markers.

question: Write dialogue for the effect of what is meant, not what is said.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We’ve learned that what counts is not what is said but the effect of what is meant.

question: Rewrite first-person monologue so it reveals character instead of sounding like answers to a questionnaire of biographical facts.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Monologue, or direct address to the reader by a character speaking in the first person, uses the same principles as dialogue, though in self-characterization there is a great danger of making a character sound as if he or she were answering a questionnaire instead of talking.

question: Read your dialogue aloud in a flat monotone; rewrite any line whose words cannot do the job without expression.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: the best way to judge dialogue read aloud is to read it in a monotone without expression. The words have to do the job.

question: Rewrite your dialogue so characters answer obliquely, not directly.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Dialogue, to the contrary, is indirect. The key word to understanding the nature of dialogue is that the best dialogue is oblique.

question: Rephrase a direct question so it opens the gate for an oblique answer.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A simple change in the question can open the gate wide for an oblique response: “What’s this third degree?”

question: State the purpose of each dialogue exchange.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What is the purpose of this exchange? Does it begin or heighten an existing conflict?

question: Check whether the exchange begins or heightens conflict, stimulates curiosity, creates tension, or builds to a climax or a change in the relationship.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What is the purpose of this exchange? Does it begin or heighten an existing conflict?

question: Treat dialogue as a semblance of speech, not a recording.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Dialogue, contrary to popular view, is not a recording of actual speech; it is a semblance of speech, an invented language of exchanges that build in tempo or content toward climaxes.

question: Invent exchanges that are leaner than real talk and build toward a climax.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Dialogue, contrary to popular view, is not a recording of actual speech; it is a semblance of speech, an invented language of exchanges that build in tempo or content toward climaxes.

question: Cut throwaway words and phrases unless you keep them deliberately as a character's verbal tic.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: “Actually,” “basically,” “perhaps,” “I dare say,” “I don’t know what to think,” “it occurs to me,” “you see,” “anyway” are all words that can be cut unless you are choosing to use them as verbal tics of a particular character.

question: Signal a character's education or pretension with just a word or two of distinctive vocabulary that fits the character.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Polysyllabic words like intricate, oxymoron, and antediluvian indicate the speaker is well educated or pretentious, depending on the context. The point is that the character’s speech can be differentiated from others’ with just a word or two. Be warned. The words have to fit the character you’ve created. Otherwise, the special vocabulary will jar the reader.

question: Break a stretch of dense prose with dialogue.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: P.S. An often overlooked advantage of dialogue in novels and stories is this simple: it provides white space on the page that makes the reader feel that the story is moving faster because the reader’s eyes move quickly down the page.

question: Cut the manner verbs from your dialogue tags so the words themselves carry their own decibels.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thou shalt not mutter, whisper, blurt, bellow, or scream, for it is the words and not the characterization of the words that must carry their own decibels.

question: Choose each word for its precise meaning and its sound.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Diction involves the choice of words for their precise meaning and sound, the arrangement of those words, and their selection for effect. Excellence in diction is the most important characteristic of fine writing.

question: Arrange your words deliberately.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Diction involves the choice of words for their precise meaning and sound, the arrangement of those words, and their selection for effect. Excellence in diction is the most important characteristic of fine writing.

question: Select your words for effect.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Diction involves the choice of words for their precise meaning and sound, the arrangement of those words, and their selection for effect. Excellence in diction is the most important characteristic of fine writing.

question: Diminish a coincidence by arranging concrete detail around it so the meeting lands as a true surprise.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A coincidence still? Yes, but the way the author arranged it with detail—the special store, Sally peering in to avoid Howie, the revolving door—all help to make their coincidental meeting a true surprise.

question: Strive toward a distinctive voice or style — precision, freshness, insight, and resonance are the shared interests of writers who produce durable work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Those novelists and nonfiction writers who strive to produce durable work share an interest in precision and freshness in the use of words, in insights into human nature and the physical world, and in resonance. These writers usually develop a “voice” or style that is distinctive.

question: Replace the material you would freely show friends and family with the picture you are reluctant to show.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Readers don’t want to see your photo album. They have their own. They want to see what’s in the picture you’re reluctant to show.

question: Elucidate the background of a major action before it happens so the reader is not left guessing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What in the engineer’s background would have made it possible for him to pick a stranger’s child out of a carriage and take it away?

question: Rewrite the places where you convey your own emotion so they instead stimulate an emotion in the reader.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Poetry and fiction share certain characteristics. In fashioning poetry, a common beginner’s mistake is to emote instead of to evoke, to convey the writer’s emotion rather than to stimulate an emotion from the reader.

question: Imagine the snapshot the person you truly dislike carries and would never want you to see, and take the second thing that comes to mind, not the first.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Everyone except liars has at least one person he truly dislikes, maybe even hates. What kind of snapshot would he carry that he wouldn’t want you to see? Don’t tell me the first thing that comes to mind. Maybe the second.

question: Instead of describing your character's terror, create the circumstances that make the reader feel the terror directly.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Less is more when it comes to stimulating strong emotions in the reader. One of the mistakes made by some of the popular thriller writers is that they describe the terror of characters instead of letting the reader feel the terror as Kafka does.

question: Describe a character's clothing with one distinguishing item and let the reader imagine the rest.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A more common error is detailing the clothing worn by a character as if preparing a missing persons bulletin, when one distinguishing item would suffice and allow the reader to imagine the rest.

question: When you give your reader detail, choose the single most effective detail and err on the side of too little rather than too much.

source.author: Sol Stein
