source.quote: A technique for stepping up pace in fiction that isn’t used enough is flipping forward past a scene that never appears in the book.

question: Skip the routine steps of an action and jump from one significant beat to the next — “skipping for effect” — even if that eliminates two thirds of the words.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: He washed his body, shaved his jaws, drank his coffee, and missed the seven-thirty-one. Eliminating about two thirds of the words steps up the pace brilliantly. I call this “skipping for effect.”

question: Rewrite for particularity: replace the merely concrete with the particular.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Once the word from editors was “be concrete.” But to be specific is not as precise as to be particular, which is much more advantageous to the creative writer.

question: Give a character a methodical, particularized action — like moving his gaze deliberately from eyes to hair to chin to ears — that disconcerts others and reveals his nature.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thomassy moved his gaze from Roberts’s confident eyes to Roberts’s blond hair, then Roberts’s chin, then Roberts’s left ear, then Roberts’s right ear. The four points of the cross.

question: Characterize an individual through particularity — how they look, dress, or speak — without resorting to clichés or generalizations.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: To characterize, particularity is used to show how an individual looks, dresses, or speaks without resort to clichés or generalizations.

question: Audit a passage of your writing for detail that individualizes; where the detail is generic, particularize it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It is not just detail that distinguishes good writing, it is detail that individualizes. I call it “particularity.”

question: Let dialogue particularize a character: give a character a line that reveals a trait.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In addition, the dialogue also particularizes one of the characters. Joe, for instance, has a sense of humor.

question: Go word by word through a passage and demand precision of meaning.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The requirement is precision of meaning, le mot juste, exactly the right word.

question: Convey a trait through particularized evidence — how he coughs, how others treat him — rather than stating the generalization.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Vernon coughed from the ground up. When a waitress heard Vernon’s voice she always guided him to the smoking section without asking.

question: If you deal with a character's hands, give them something particular to do instead of leaving them at a loss.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you’re going to deal with a character’s hands, give them something to do, as this author did:

question: Find the two most particular words in your sentence and make sure the sentence would turn ordinary without them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The crucial words, of course, are “bald pink knees,” a particularization that makes the character and the place instantly visible and in the reader’s experience unique. If we were to eliminate the words “bald” and “pink” how diminished that opening sentence would be:

question: Turn an ordinary appearance sentence into one that characterizes through a measurable, comparative particular.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Cecilia wore short skirts. It doesn’t take much to turn that ordinariness into a sentence that characterizes and particularizes: Cecilia’s skirts were three inches shorter than her age allowed.

question: Particularize through your viewpoint character's perception: instead of saying a smile is like an implant, have the character think it is an implant.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Note the use of metaphor to particularize. It doesn’t say Roberts’s smile is like an implant, Thomassy thinks it is an implant.

question: Sweep the abstractions out of your prose, for readers are attracted by particularity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Thou shalt not saw the air with abstractions, for readers, like lovers, are attracted by particularity.

question: If an ordinary object matters to your story, particularize it — its location, size, color, how it moves — so the reader's attention is called to it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If an ordinary object is important to a story, particularization will help call attention to it.

question: Revise an opening that lacks particularity: make people, locale, and objects distinctive and visible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Use actions if possible. If people are in your opening, have them talk or think in particulars. Make locale, objects, and people distinctive and visible. Use other senses if appropriate. And make it ominous if you can.

question: Work on one paragraph at a time; perfect a single paragraph of particularity and use it as the model for the whole book.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You work on one paragraph at a time. If you perfect a single paragraph, you have a model for a book.

question: Replace a general statement about a place by stretching out its particulars so the reader experiences it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: By stretching out the particulars (the echo of the agent’s voice, the height of the ceiling, the carved plaster angels), the reader experiences the place along with the characters.

question: Practice particularizing in your letters and personal correspondence, replacing generalizations and clichés, so the habit carries over into your work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you work at particularizing in all of your personal correspondence, the recipients will enjoy what you write much more—and you will be practicing what you need to perfect to get your books published and to build an audience for your writings.

question: Audit every detail you have added: none should be waste words; each must have a purpose, such as making a transaction credible. Cut the particulars that merely decorate.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The details do not consist of waste words; they have a purpose in making the transaction credible.

question: When a character repeats an action like laughing within a few pages, particularize each instance instead of repeating "She laughed" — make each laugh distinct.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Particularizing is also useful if you have occasion to repeat something—like a character laughing—and don’t want to bore the reader by repeating a phrase like “She laughed” several times within the same few pages:

question: When a cliché offers itself, sharpen it with an unexpected, precise phrase.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The lazy writer’s cliché would have been “Pickpockets wait until the last second.” Instead, the journalist avoided the cliché and sharpened the meaning by calling it “the exquisitely perfect last second.”

question: Resist the pressure to clip language short when your aim is to provide an experience; keep the extra words that make the experience possible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: However, simplification is not necessarily appropriate if one’s aim is to provide an experience for the reader. “The apartment was large” doesn’t do it. Nor does putting an envelope in front of somebody. The extra words are not wasted because they make the experience of the action possible and credible.

question: Choose adjectives and adverbs for the particular sound of words — branches that swoosh and thump, gravel that pops — rather than cutting them all on principle.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Adjectives and adverbs, which normally should be cut, are all over the place. They are used to wonderful effect because she uses the particular sound of words.

question: When a person comes into view, don't describe him all at once: delay part of the description, start at a distance, then notice more; use the same technique for places.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When a person comes into view, the writer’s temptation is to describe him all at once. It’s more effective to delay part of the description. Start at a distance, then notice more. It enhances the tension. The same technique of particularizing in stages works for places as well as people.

question: Catch yourself writing top-of-the-head — the cliché or the generalization that comes first — and replace it with a sentence that particularizes in an interesting way.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The temptation is always to use either a cliché or a generalization, what I call “top-of-thehead writing.” In this chapter we are trying to fashion sentences that are writerly, that particularize in an interesting way.

question: Improve your work beyond the requirements of your editor or the public — hunt precise nuances and listen to the sound of words instead of stopping at good enough.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Fiction writers who don’t improve their work beyond the requirements of their editors or the public do not have an interest in perfection because they are deaf to the sound of words and have no instinct or training to hunt precise nuances.

question: Plant a character’s motivation ahead of time before she acts for your convenience — if the plot needs her at the mall, her reason for going must be planted in advance.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: For instance, if a character suddenly gets up to go shopping for the convenience of the author because something is going to happen in a shopping mall, the events in the mall may not be credible unless the motivation for the character going to the mall is planted ahead of time.

question: Decide which of your actions would seem unconvincing without ground, and plant only those.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Planting is necessary when a later action might seem unconvincing to the reader. Not all actions require planting. For instance, if Todd trips Andrew and Andrew then punches Todd, Todd’s action does need planting, Andrew’s punch does not.

question: Before a character performs a feat of strength, plant the physical capability earlier.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If a writer’s concerned about the quality of his writing and needs to say that “Tiny picked him up bodily and threw him over the railing,” he will have planted earlier that Tiny is six foot three and a weightlifter.

question: Plant a character's motive in a single line of dialogue with a touch of humor.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The planting can be simple enough through a touch of humor: “I’m not going to go on a shopping spree ever again. After today.”

question: Check your point of view discipline: have you avoided telling how a character feels and relied on actions to make the reader experience the emotion?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you avoided telling us how a character feels? Have you relied on actions to help the reader experience emotion?

question: In first person, rewrite any line that sounds like you the author rather than the character speaking.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The author of a first-person story must constantly be on guard against telling the reader something that will sound like the author rather than the character.

question: Write first-person narration as the character making a case for himself — his view of himself, the others, the world — not as neutral reporting.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Think of it this way: the character talking to the reader is not only conveying everything the reader gets to know, the character is making a case for himself. It’s his view of himself, the others, the world.

question: Use first person when your protagonist does horrible things — it can draw the reader's emotions, even empathy, into the character despite his acts.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Another advantage of first person is that it can involve the reader’s emotions—even empathy—with a protagonist who does horrible things.

question: Test your scene's point of view by converting it: third person is first person with "he" or "she" substituted for "I" — see whose eyes the scene is really seen through.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The simplest way of understanding third person is that it is the same as first person except that you have substituted “he” or “she” for “I.”

question: Limit how many characters' POVs the reader enters in a short span — too many shifts in quick succession make the experience dizzying.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The problem was that in the first twenty-eight pages, I counted seven characters into whose point of view the reader was admitted for a short period. It was a dizzying experience.

question: Develop the "I" character until he is sufficiently different from you.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is the “I” character sufficiently different from you?

question: Check every image against your POV character's physical position — cut or rewrite any description from a vantage the character cannot have.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: From the driver’s point of view, would a twisting road ever look “like a carelessly abandoned garden hose”? The image is forced.

question: When each chapter uses a different character's POV, choose for each scene the character most affected by that scene's events.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you adopt a loose form of third person in which, say, each chapter is seen from a different character’s POV, be sure to choose for each scene the character who is most affected by the events of that scene.

question: When your first-person narrator reads another character's feelings, mark the report as his interpretation — what he believes, not the other character's view.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: He sees what he believes to be in the eyes of his friends Blair and Cynthia, but it is not their view of how they feel, it is his view.

question: Make your narrator the protagonist or a principal character directly involved in the action — he can even be the villain of the piece.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Today, a narrator is more often the protagonist or a principal character directly involved in the action. He can even be the villain of the piece.

question: Reveal a first-person narrator's looks without the mirror cliché: let him think about his looks or changes in them, or have another character remark on them in dialogue.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A character seeing himself in a mirror is a cliché. However, a first-person character can think about his looks, or changes in his looks. Or another character can say something like: “Are you dyeing your hair?”

question: Do not mix points of view within the same scene, chapter, or novel — sticking to one point of view intensifies the reader's experience.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In general, I advise the less-experienced writer not to mix points of view within the same scene, chapter, or even the same novel. It is unsettling to the reader. If you mix points of view, the author’s authority seems to dissolve. The writer seems arbitrary rather than controlled. Sticking to a point of view intensifies the experience of a story.

question: Cut the preface: readers skip it and miss essential information — develop that material skillfully inside the story itself.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In general I advise against the use of prefaces in fiction. Some readers skip them, and in doing so, miss essential information. I have found that the essential material of prefaces can almost always be skillfully developed in the story itself.

question: If your first-person narrator takes the reader into his confidence, don't let him withhold an essential secret — the reader will feel cheated.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If the character takes the reader into his confidence, the character can’t “forget” to provide the reader with an essential secret or other important piece of information. When the reader learns that something was withheld, he will feel cheated.

question: Before writing objectively, know that complete objectivity is sterile of emotion — reserve it for stories that are mainly action.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Complete objectivity tends to be sterile of emotion, particularly the kind of intimacy that readers enjoy in literary novels, but it is useful in stories that are mainly action.

question: When your first-person narrator reports an offstage scene he didn't witness, motivate the reporting and keep the report visual.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The point to remember is that you have to motivate the reporting of offstage scenes. And whenever possible keep the report visual.

question: In omniscient POV, rewrite any passage where the reader hears the author talking instead of experiencing the story — the mode lacks discipline, so guard your credibility.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The danger of the omniscient POV is that the reader will hear the author talking instead of experiencing the story. The omniscient POV lacks discipline.

question: Choose the omniscient POV only if your authorial voice has personality, authority, some wisdom, and ideally a fresh sense of humor — the author must be quite a character to manage it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The omniscient POV allows the author to speak in his own voice, to say things that would be inappropriate for any of his characters to say. The author’s voice, however, should have personality, authority, some wisdom, and ideally a fresh sense of humor.

question: Choose first person when your protagonist is highly intelligent or perceptive, so his complex thoughts reach the reader directly and intimately.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The first-person point of view is valuable, for instance, if you’ve drawn a character who is highly intelligent or perceptive. His or her complex thoughts can be conveyed much more directly and intimately to the reader.

question: Establish the limitation of your third-person POV and stick to it — the restraint becomes an advantage, a discipline.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Once the author establishes the limitation of the third-person point of view, he must stick to it and the limitation becomes an advantage, a restraint, a discipline.

question: In first person, reveal the narrator's good qualities through his actions and other characters' speech, not through self-description.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Therefore, in the first-person POV the author relies on action and the speech of other characters to reveal things—particularly good thingsabout the “I” character.

question: If your draft isn't satisfying you, set it aside and rewrite it from another point of view — third to first, omniscient to third or first.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One advantage of understanding point of view is that if your work isn’t satisfying you, you can always put the draft aside and rewrite it from another point of view. If you’ve used third person, try first. If you’ve used omniscient, try third or first. Or both.

question: Cut scenes your first-person character wasn't a witness to — he can't know what goes on beyond his ken.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You can’t have scenes your first-person character isn’t a witness to.

question: Shelve the second-person point of view: involve the reader emotionally through identification with a character, not by addressing him as "you."

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Second person is used so rarely that I suggest just shelving it. I think of it as the crackerbarrel mode, the storyteller seeking to involve the reader in the story as if he were a character. The fact is that the reader is quite prepared to be involved emotionally in the story not as himself but through identification with one or more of the characters.

question: If you shift point of view between parts or chapters, establish and clearly identify the new point of view at the outset of each part or chapter.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It was only after my confidence increased that I started using multiple first-person points of view in different parts or chapters, with the point of view established and clearly identified at the outset of each part or chapter.

question: Scan your story for any slip in point of view and correct it — one slip can hurt a story badly, and several can be fatal.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It can be said that one slip of point of view by a writer can hurt a story badly, and several slips can be fatal.

question: When your first-person character is reluctant to reveal a secret, have another character strip the secret from him in heated conversation.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The most dramatic way of handling information that the character is reluctant to convey is for another character to strip the secret from him in heated conversation:

question: Before choosing first person for a story about surviving life-threatening dangers, weigh the lost suspense: the narrator must survive to finish the story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A point sometimes overlooked by beginners is that if a story centers on the narrator’s ability to survive life-threatening dangers, some suspense will be lost in the first person because the character will have to survive to finish the story!

question: Focus on the POV of one character at a time and sustain it; if readers must know what everybody thinks, use the looser omniscient form instead.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Whatever genre you write in, my recommendation is that you focus on the POV of one character at a time, and sustain it, or you’re likely to get into trouble. If you’ve got to let your readers know what everybody thinks, you’d probably be better off using the omniscient point of view, the loosest of forms.

question: Write third person consistently from one character's point of view at a time, though you may report what any character hears, smells, touches, or tastes.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Third person works best when the story is seen consistently from the point of view of one character at a time, though the author is free to report what any of the characters hear, smell, touch, and taste.

question: Don't put thoughts into a character's head that are beyond that character's intelligence or capabilities.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Similarly, if the author is writing about people less intelligent than himself, he must be careful not to put thoughts into a character’s head that are beyond that character’s capabilities.

question: Decide whose story this is and focus on individuals — the reader wants to know whose story he is following, and a story about everybody is a story about nobody.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A story about everybody is a story about nobody. Before he’ll let himself become involved, the reader wants to know whose story this is. He expects the writer to focus on individuals.

question: Break up any quoted speech that runs more than three sentences — insert something visual, however slight, between the chunks.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you quote anyone for more than three sentences, that’s a speech. Break it up with something visual.

question: Edit quoted material toward the color of the speaker’s words — expletives and grammatical howlers included — neither a verbatim transcript nor a straightened-out version.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I wasn’t arguing for a verbatim transcript of the tapes but for a retention of their color, which I succeeded in getting, and which all writers who deal with the spoken words of others should strive for.

question: If you find yourself inventing dialogue in nonfiction, redirect that instinct into a play, novel, or movie, where invented speech belongs.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you find yourself inventing dialogue, write a play, novel, or movie.

question: Break a long quote with a seemingly inconsequential physical detail: a cough humanizes the speaker, a pointed glance implies conflict.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The first interruption humanizes the speaker and adds to the reality. The second—a glance at the mayor—invokes a suspicion of conflict by seeming to blame the mayor for the problems the speaker is talking about.

question: Cut reported speech freely: you are not obligated to reproduce every word, only to preserve the speaker’s meaning.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In reporting spoken words, it is not a writer’s obligation to reproduce all of the words as long as the speaker’s meaning is preserved.

question: Never intentionally misquote and never invent dialogue: fabricated attributed speech is a highly visible sign of untrustworthy writing.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Never intentionally misquote. And never invent dialogue.

question: Keep quoted speech rough: few people speak in complete grammatical sentences, and perfectly formed sentences come across to the reader as made up.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Few people speak in complete and grammatical sentences. Moreover, perfectly formed sentences often come across to the reader as made up. In quoting, the writer has to beware of cleaning up a speaker’s sentences.

question: Cut excess quotation from an interview: keep only what reveals the character of the speaker or defines the subject matter.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When you’re reporting the results of an interview, you will likely end up with too much quotation. You want to keep those parts that reveal the character of the speaker or that define subject matter. You want to preserve comments that are confrontational, colorful, or especially appropriate, and ditch the rest.

question: Treat dialogue as a danger in nonfiction: use only direct quotes that sound real and can be substantiated.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: For the writer of articles and books as well as journalism, dialogue is a danger unless one uses direct quotes that sound real and can be substantiated.

question: After fixing the larger problems and hunting down the smaller ones, take time away from the manuscript, then read it as a reader rather than an editor.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Now that you’ve fixed the larger problems and hunted and killed the smaller ones, take some time away from the manuscript and then read it as a reader, not an editor. But keep an editorial pencil handy, just in case.

question: Audit what you read for pleasure: the field and the quality of language you require of books is what you will write.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In the end, you write what you read. If you read literary fiction with pleasure, that’s what you will attempt to write. If you read thrillers or romances, you will in all likelihood end up writing for the audience of which you are a part. The same is true for nonfiction—not merely the field of interest, but the quality of language and insight you require of your books, read or written.

question: Do not expect your work to succeed in a field you don't habitually read for pleasure.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In the end, you write what you read. If you read literary fiction with pleasure, that’s what you will attempt to write. If you read thrillers or romances, you will in all likelihood end up writing for the audience of which you are a part. The same is true for nonfiction—not merely the field of interest, but the quality of language and insight you require of your books, read or written.

question: Bring the snapshot image back at each danger your protagonist faces, so the reader carries it through the whole story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: With every danger the decoy faced, the reader thought of the sleeping child. The reader, full of emotion now, read the novel not as an interesting plot but as a moving experience.

question: Remove the padding—unnecessary digressions and overly extensive patches of description—from your manuscript.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As you work along as an editor, do you see any places where the author might have padded the manuscript with unnecessary digressions, overly extensive patches of description, or anything else that strikes you as filler? You always strengthen text when you remove the padding.

question: Instead of narrating an unmotivated action — he went for a walk — rephrase it as a line of dialogue that gives the character a reason, like: “These new shoes are not going to get broken in if I sit around the house.”

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Or you simply need to get a character out of the house. Instead of an unmotivated walk, he could say.

question: Give your work resonance through reverberations of other times, places, important events, or influential people.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Does your work have reverberations of other times or places, of important events or influential people? The most mundane subjects can be given a lift by the use of resonance.

question: Put aphorisms in a character's dialogue only if the character is the kind who would spout them on occasion.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If they are in a character’s dialogue, as in the case of Louie, you had better be sure the character you’ve created is the kind who could and would spout aphorisms on occasion.

question: Put an aphorism in the author's voice in the third-person or omniscient point of view, never a character's first-person point of view.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: There are two points to remember about the use of aphorisms: If they are in the author’s voice, the point of view has to be either the third-person or the omniscient author’s point of view, not the first-person point of view of a character.

question: Choose names and phrases that carry built-in associations — biblical or otherwise — so they resonate before the story explains them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We have seen how the opening words of Moby Dick, “Call me Ishmael,” have instant resonance because of the biblical associations of Ishmael. The same would be true of other memorable names from the Bible, whether used for characters or in appropriate phrases.

question: Open with a bold philosophical statement so its resonance carries into what follows.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The world is what it is; men who are nothing, who allow themselves to become nothing, have no place in it. That first sentence lends resonance to the sentence and paragraphs that follow, perhaps to the book as a whole.

question: Name your nonfiction chapters with phrases that resonate — an allusion or a metaphor — so the effect lands twice, in the table of contents and at the chapter heads.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A greater value can be derived from naming chapters in nonfiction. Orville Schell’s 1994 book on China, Mandate of Heaven, has some chapter titles that invoke resonance twice, in the table of contents, and at the heads of chapters: “A Hundred Flowers Fade” evokes its familiar opposite, A Hundred Flowers Bloom. “The Graying of Chinese Culture” derives its effect through a metaphor that resonates.

question: Give a character the authentic, specialized thoughts of their profession so those thoughts confirm the character's reality.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The reader absolutely believes that this narrator, Kay Fischer, is an architect. She is, of course, an invention of the author. Her thoughts about architecture provide the resonance that confirms her reality.

question: Cut excessive preliminaries — author's notes, prefaces, multiple epigraphs.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: An excess of preliminaries might be interpreted as defensive. Don’t overdo it.

question: Lend importance to an ordinary day or moment by pairing it with a metaphor that draws on death or a vast, final scale.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In T. Correghessan Boyle’s 1987 novel World’s End the author lends importance to a day by the use of a metaphor drawing on the possibility of the death of the earth:

question: Choose an epigraph that conveys the larger import of your work so the work needn't become didactic.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: An appropriate epigraph can convey the larger import of a novel, without the novel itself becoming didactic.

question: Aim for resonance that comes from the writing itself — the visual sweep of the language — not only from borrowed devices.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The ideal resonance comes from the writing itself. The visual sweep introduces a work of history with resonance that stems from the skill of the writing.

question: Keep public and historical figures in your story fleeting — appearing only briefly — and cut any attempt to reproduce them at length.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Put an Eisenhower or a Kennedy into a story, and it resonates, especially if he appears fleetingly. I say “fleetingly” because most writers who try to reproduce historical characters at length, including their dialogue, usually fail.

question: Exaggerate a perception — hyperbole — to lend resonance to what might otherwise seem ordinary.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A hyperbole is, of course, an exaggeration that is not meant to be taken literally. For the novelist, it presents an opportunity to lend resonance to what might otherwise seem ordinary.

question: Open your story by invoking your protagonist’s death — or the feeling of it approaching — to give the work resonance from the outset.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In the last of his Rabbit Angstrom books, Rabbit at Rest, John Updike invokes his protagonist’s death at the outset:

question: Borrow the language of liturgy or religious ritual to lend resonance to a key scene.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: His novel Vespers draws some resonance from its title, but I would urge you to read at least the first four and a half pages of that book to see how liturgy lends stunning resonance to a scene that involves a killing.

question: Plant omens early in your narrative to seed suspense.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Omens are important in seeding suspense.

question: Title the parts of your book so the names resonate before the first sentence.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: By Naming the parts of a book. Omens are important in seeding suspense. The prolific British novelist Francis King lists five parts for his novel Act of Darkness. The first is titled simply “Omens.” It lends a touch of resonance even before the reader encounters the first sentence.

question: Make your description of a birthplace or formative setting go a long way toward explaining the person's life and work rather than merely detailing the place.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Some writers of biography will describe the subject’s birthplace in detail, but miss an opportunity for resonance.

question: Invent plausible professional-sounding theory — technobabble — to authenticate a character and their profession.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I invented Dr. Koch’s theory as resonance to authenticate Dr. Koch and his profession. In commercial fiction today, technobabble is used in a similar way.

question: Write what other people sometimes think but don’t say — or don’t allow themselves to think.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A writer needs the courage to say what other people sometimes think but don’t say. Or don’t allow themselves to think.

question: Let the characters play out the scene in front of you as you write — decide their scripts, not their lines, in advance.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Let them play out the scene in front of you as you write.

question: Plan individual scenes by giving characters clashing scripts.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: While two characters can have different scripts throughout a book, the Actors Studio technique is most valuable for planning individual scenes.

question: Plot the whole work around a crucible that binds the characters together.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: While two characters can have different scripts throughout a book, the Actors Studio technique is most valuable for planning individual scenes.

question: Jot down the script — the intent — of each character in a scene from a novel you are reading.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As an exercise, jot down the scripts of each of the characters in a given scene of any novel you may be reading.

question: Define each character's 'script' as their intent in the scene, not the actual lines of dialogue.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A “script” in this exercise is not the actual lines of dialogue, only the intent of the character in that scene. Think of the character as getting instructions from you, the writer. It is important to keep the instructions brief.

question: Keep each script instruction brief.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A “script” in this exercise is not the actual lines of dialogue, only the intent of the character in that scene. Think of the character as getting instructions from you, the writer. It is important to keep the instructions brief.

question: Before you write a scene, make a note of each character's script and make sure the scripts are different and at odds.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Before you write the scene, make a note as to the “script” or tack (keep it simple) of the first character and then of the second character. Make sure the scripts are different and at odds. Only you will be privy to the scripts of both characters. Let them play out the scene in front of you as you write. And if you have a third character in the scene, give that character a script different from the other two.

question: If a third character enters, give that character a script different from the other two.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Before you write the scene, make a note as to the “script” or tack (keep it simple) of the first character and then of the second character. Make sure the scripts are different and at odds. Only you will be privy to the scripts of both characters. Let them play out the scene in front of you as you write. And if you have a third character in the scene, give that character a script different from the other two.

question: Give the characters in each scene different scripts — different intentions — so their goals clash and the scene turns dramatic.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The secret of creating conflict in scenes you write is to give your characters different scripts.

question: Elaborate a character's feeling into a sequence of small actions and a stray thought, so it shows the feeling without naming it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Sometimes longer is better for showing: I put a yellow pad in front of me on the desk. I placed a pen on the yellow pad. This is ridiculous, I’ m not going to write anything, just call. That’s a character about to make an important phone call. The reader isn’t told he’s nervous. The character is given a nervous action.

question: Rewrite your backstory: show what happened before the story began rather than telling it in narrative summary or in a flashback.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What happened before the story began, sometimes called “backstory,” should be shown rather than told about either in narrative summary or in a flashback. What happens offstage can also be brought onstage and shown.

question: Bring offstage events onstage and show them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What happened before the story began, sometimes called “backstory,” should be shown rather than told about either in narrative summary or in a flashback. What happens offstage can also be brought onstage and shown.

question: Show a condition or a change of mood through color alone, the way “the color of cold is blue” shifting to black deep beneath the Arctic water makes the change ominous.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Beyond the Arctic Circle, the color of cold is blue. But deep beneath the Arctic water, the color of cold is black.

question: Cut any passage that interrupts the reader's experience to convey a character's background or anything else the author seems to be supplying.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If that experience is interrupted in order to convey a character’s background, or anything else that the author seems to be supplying, that’s telling, not showing, a major fault because it intrudes upon the reader’s experience.

question: Rewrite a flat action so it gives the reader a sense of what the character desperately wants.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: He walked as if against an unseen wind, hoping someone would stop him shows most of all because it gives the reader a sense of what the character desperately wants.

question: Check every passage: does it give an experience, or does it merely pass on information from the author?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As I’ve repeated often, what we as readers want from writing is to experience it. Receiving information from the author doesn’t give us an experience.

question: Treat what a character feels as the chief danger area for telling: make sure feelings are shown, never reported.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The late John Gardner, in his excellent book On Becoming a Novelist, insisted that the one danger area for “telling” is what a character feels. That may be the most important, but it’s not the only hazard.

question: Find any line where one character tells another what the second already knows and rewrite it — unless it is an accusation.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One character should never tell another character what the second character already knows—unless it’s an accusation.

question: When information in your work sounds like the author’s intervention, come up with a simile or a metaphor that shows what you are trying to tell.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When you stumble upon information in your work that sounds like the author’s intervention, try to come up with a simile or a metaphor that shows what you’re trying to tell.

question: Change your mind-set: stop telling what happened elsewhere and start creating an experience by showing what happened.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: All of these early exposures to offstage happenings contribute to the belief that stories are told. They can be a liability to writers later in life because the writer has to change his mind-set from telling what happened somewhere else to creating an experience for the reader by showing what happened.

question: Replace an emotion name with the action that shows it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: He was nervous tells. He tapped his fingers on the tabletop shows.

question: Replace a general statement like “She boiled water” with particular, visual actions — putting the kettle on the stove, filling it from the faucet, humming until the whistle cuts her short — since the key to the improvement is particularity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: She boiled water tells. She put the kettle on the stove begins to show. She filled the kettle from the faucet and hummed till the kettle’s whistle cut her humming short shows.

question: When you shape your showing image, prefer the compression of a metaphor over the comparison of a simile.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Note that Updike didn’t say “her hair was like kelp” (a simile), but “the kelp of her own hair” (a metaphor), an excellent example of particularity.

question: Scan your manuscript for passages where you are, consciously or not, reporting a story instead of showing it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One of the chief reasons novels are rejected is that the writer, consciously or not, is reporting a story instead of showing it.

question: Ask yourself of the passage: are you allowing the reader to see what's going on?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Are you allowing the reader to see what’s going on? Is the author talking at any point? Can you silence the author by using an action to help the reader understand what a character feels? Are you naming emotions instead of conveying them by actions? Is any character telling another what that character already knows?

question: Is the author talking at any point?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Are you allowing the reader to see what’s going on? Is the author talking at any point? Can you silence the author by using an action to help the reader understand what a character feels? Are you naming emotions instead of conveying them by actions? Is any character telling another what that character already knows?

question: Can you silence the author with an action that shows what a character feels?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Are you allowing the reader to see what’s going on? Is the author talking at any point? Can you silence the author by using an action to help the reader understand what a character feels? Are you naming emotions instead of conveying them by actions? Is any character telling another what that character already knows?

question: Are you naming emotions instead of conveying them by actions?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Are you allowing the reader to see what’s going on? Is the author talking at any point? Can you silence the author by using an action to help the reader understand what a character feels? Are you naming emotions instead of conveying them by actions? Is any character telling another what that character already knows?

question: Show what your character sees, hears, smells, touches, and tastes through actions rather than describing them, and convey feelings through actions above all.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What a character sees, hears, smells, touches, and tastes can be shown through actions rather than described. And feelings, of course, are best shown through actions.

question: Rephrase the information you need to plant so it arrives subtly through a natural-sounding remark between characters.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If this kind of telling intrudes, it is really a dodge for the author to convey information, which can be done subtly. For instance: “Do you think Henry would look more like a doctor if he grew a beard?” That is sufficient for the reader to learn that Henry is a doctor and sounds like something that one parent might say to another.

question: Audit your passage for the three areas where telling most intrudes: what happened before the story began, what a character looks like, and what a character senses.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: There are three areas in which the writer is particularly vulnerable to telling rather than showing: when he tells what happened before the story began; when he tells what a character looks like; and when he tells what a character senses, that is, what he sees, hears, smells, touches, and tastes. Those are all places where the author’s voice can intrude on the reader’s experience.

question: Rewrite every sentence that states a character's trait as a visible action that shows the trait without being told.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Helen was a wonderful woman, always concerned about her children, Charlie and Ginny. There is nothing for the reader to see, therefore the reader feels that he is being told about Helen.

question: Transform information passed on in a nonfiction vein into a visual scene so the author is no longer telling.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: conveying the information with visual detail (the blush on Beth’s freckled face, the too-small crown, two hairpins) showed the scene to the reader. No longer is the author telling.

question: Test whether a passage is showing rather than telling by determining if it is visual.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One clue to whether a writer is showing rather than telling is to determine if the passage is visual.

question: Reread your draft for spots of bare-bones writing that could be improved by a simile or metaphor, and add one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In examining your work, can you find spots of “bare bones” writing that could be improved by a simile or metaphor that you hadn’t thought of when you were getting your early draft onto paper?

question: Find comparisons in your draft that are clichés from overuse and rephrase them into fresh ones.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Simile: He felt like a million dollars. Metaphor: It was food for thought. Those examples are clichés, tired from overuse.

question: Read each simile and metaphor in your draft and ask whether it deflects attention from the story to the words on the page; if it does, cut or replace it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Inaccurate similes and metaphors have the effect of deflecting the reader’s attention from the story to the words on the page.

question: Find a flat, adverb-driven statement in your draft and rewrite it as a simile that connects two things previously unconnected, so the comparison keeps its savor.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We identify a jack-in-the-box popping up with suddenness, but if it said “She sprang up suddenly,” we’d lose the savor of the comparison.

question: Scan your manuscript for similes and metaphors that show strain or are inaccurate, and cut them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Try, fly, experiment, but if it shows strain, if it isn’t accurate, cut it.

question: Find a scene that relies only on sight and sound and rewrite it so your characters also touch, taste, and smell.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Then, as writers, we let three of our senses atrophy, as if our characters had lost part of their humanity and didn't need to touch, taste, and smell.

question: Listen to the sounds in your scene and write them as you actually hear them, not as clichés — find a sound that is recognizable but has never been seen in print.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: There's no point to your using Joyce's sound or the cliché meow. Listen to your cat and see if you can't come up with something that your readers will recognize but perhaps will never have seen in print before.

question: Mark where sound stops in your scene and write the pauses, the momentary silences.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Sound, of course, is not continuous. It is interrupted by pauses, by momentary silences, the absence of sound that makes music possible.

question: Render smells accurately: particularize what each place or object smells like instead of leaving the sense vague.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It is important not only to be aware of and use smells, but to be accurate in rendering them. Rubber bands have a marked odor. An old book smells musty. Unseen wind has a smell.

question: Use smell to help establish a setting: choose an odor that draws someone into the room.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A writer can use the sense of smell to good effect in many ways, for instance, to help a reader experience a setting: I could tell we were coming to the kitchen. The odor of fresh-baked bread drifted into the hallway like an invitation to follow where it led.

question: Give a character a habitual scent that does the characterizing for you — a signature perfume that signals they use too much of it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Characterization can benefit from the use of smell: Sally fluttered in, enveloped in her newest perfume. This tells us that Sally habitually uses too much perfume.

question: Look for the smell absent from your scene and use that absence to carry meaning.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The absence of smell is also useful to a writer: "They've bred the smell out of roses," Gloria said.

question: Blindfold yourself, empty your pocket or purse onto a table, and describe each object by touch alone, as if to someone from another planet.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Feel each object with your fingertips, describing it as best you can as if to someone from another planet who wouldn't know what those strange objects are that you carry everywhere you go. You can't say a credit card feels like plastic. You have to particularize.

question: Go through every scene you write and use the sense of touch at least once.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Your writing can only gain if you attempt to use the sense of touch at least once in every scene.

question: From memory, describe the foods of your last meal to a guest who has never tasted them, inventing similes and metaphors so their taste buds pop.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You wouldn't feed cardboard meals to guests. Don't feed cardboard meals to your characters. Make your reader's taste buds pop, even if he's from outer space.

question: Write a moment where a character senses something beyond the five senses — a door closing when there is no wind, someone in the room who is not there — in mainline as well as mystery and suspense fiction.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A writer can make excellent use of a "sixth sense" in mainline fiction as well as in mystery and suspense fiction. You are alone in the house, and you hear a door close. Is it the wind? But there is no wind inside the house.

question: Look again at a person or place for the distinguishing detail, the particularity — the thing nobody has seen quite that way before — since your first impression is usually a cliché.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The first thing you see is usually a cliché. We see the tall man, the attractive woman, the room full of people, the clean-cut lawn. These are the easy images that leap to mind. The writer's job is to look for distinguishing detail, the particularity, in visualizing what his reader is to see: the man whose wavy hair wouldn't stay under his cap

question: Switch the sense to make a metaphor: describe what is seen through another sense.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A technique used too seldom involves changing the sense: Zalatnick led me into the shop not as if I was a fellow looking for a job but as if I was a friend of a friend. I was sure the men in the shop could smell the difference. "Smell" isn't meant to be taken literally. Switching the sense from seeing to smelling creates a metaphor that gets the point across to the reader quickly.

question: Check your sensory characterizations: each one must be an action, somebody doing something — never stop the story to characterize.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you look at those examples again, you'll note that each of the characterizations is an action. Somebody is doing something. There's no need to stop a story to characterize or to use the senses.

question: Test your snapshot: would you carry it in your wallet or purse? If yes, it is not secret enough.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Please answer truthfully: would you carry that snapshot in your wallet or purse? If your answer is “yes,” perhaps it’s not so secret. The snapshots that work best are embarrassing, revelatory, or involve a strong and continuing stimulus to memory.

question: Value-test your snapshot: would its owner pay to keep you from seeing it, and would you pay to see it?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Would your enemy pay to keep you from seeing that snapshot? If not, try another that’s really private. How much would you pay to see a snapshot from your actual enemy? Nothing? Not much? Then it’s not a good snapshot. If you’d pay to see it, maybe people will pay to buy your book.

question: Check whether any friend or neighbor could have a snapshot just like yours; if so, change it to one that only you have.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is your snapshot such that any of your friends or neighbors might have one just like it? If so, change it to one that only you have. Your writing is going to be yours, not writing that could come out of anyone else’s closet.

question: Listen to the sound of your words as you write literary fiction.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In commercial fiction, the sound of words is rarely considered except for the occasional—and inaccurate—“splat” or “rat-a-tat-tat.” In literary fiction, the sound of words can contribute to the effect, though that is rarely noticed by readers.

question: Give an object a human characteristic with a single word — compress a metaphor to one word.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The most famous poem of Delmore Schwartz, “In the Naked Bed, in Plato’s Cave,” mixes ordinary description (“A fleet of trucks strained uphill, grinding”) with fresh metaphor (“The street-lamp’s vigil”). The street-lamp is given a human characteristic—vigilance—with a single word.

question: When a character's life crisis demands immediate action, make certain the action backfires and prolong the crisis.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: • If a character’s life crisis requires an immediate action, make certain that the action backfires. Prolong the crisis.

question: Audit every chapter ending except the last: does it arouse interest anew and thrust forward into the next chapter?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When each chapter of a novel (except the last) ends, the reader’s interest should be aroused anew, thrusting him forward in the novel.

question: Review your chapter lengths: keep chapters short so the story seems to move faster, but avoid any chapter under three printed pages.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: • Short chapters make a story seem to move faster. • Normally avoid chapters of fewer than three printed pages. They may not be long enough to engage the reader’s emotions.

question: Scan your novel for narrative summaries of offstage happenings between scenes and cut them.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One of the frequent failings of novelists is the inclusion of material between scenes. This usually takes the form of a narrative summary of offstage happenings.

question: Look at your list of scenes, find the weakest where your own interest flags, and cut it; then repeat with the next weakest.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Look at your list of scenes and find the weakest one, where your own interest flags. If you eliminate your weakest scene, you will strengthen your book as a whole. It takes guts, but do it!

question: Set up something that cries for resolution, then deliberately dance away from it, dealing with other things and prolonging the desperate need for resolution.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The writer’s duty is to set up something that cries for a resolution and then to act irresponsibly, to dance away from the reader’s problem, dealing with other things, prolonging and exacerbating the reader’s desperate need for resolution.

question: Check your scene against these sources of anxious uncertainty: an immediate danger to a character, an unwanted confrontation, an old fear about to become real, or a life crisis demanding immediate action.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: • A prospective danger to a character. • An actual immediate danger to a character. • An unwanted confrontation. • A confrontation wanted by one character and not by the other. • An old fear about to become a present reality. • A life crisis that requires an immediate action.

question: Find an action that is urgently wanted, then delay it by having the character think about the past before acting.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The reader wants the young sailor to climb the rigging to free the bird. That action is delayed by the young sailor’s thoughts about the past. The delay causes tension in the reader.

question: When your character overcomes an immediate danger, don't eliminate the danger—make them face an even greater one instead.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: • Don’t eliminate the prospective danger to a character. • Don’t let the character overcome the immediate danger without facing an even greater danger.

question: Recast the outcome of each major turn so it goes somewhere unexpected.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The key is not to take the reader where he wants to go.

question: Put your protagonist in serious trouble, then refuse to rescue them — leave them hanging as long as the story can bear.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Your job is to avoid rescuing the hero as long as possible. You leave him hanging.

question: If your character is apprehensive about an unwanted confrontation, hold it off as long as possible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: • If your character is apprehensive about an unwanted confrontation, make sure you hold off that confrontation as long as possible.

question: Open your story and find the moment that arouses curiosity about what will happen next; then hold that curiosity unresolved for as long as you can.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Suspense is achieved by arousing the reader’s curiosity and keeping it aroused as long as possible.

question: Count the lines of suspense running through your book: are two or three characters in unresolved trouble at once, each in a different location?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: All of these events are in the same town, but by starting each scene in a different location and focusing each on a different character, we now have three lines of suspense going at the same time.

question: Reorganize your chapters in any order that accelerates suspense, keeping time moving only forward and avoiding shifts that disturb.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Your chapters are not cemented in place. You can reorganize them in any fashion that accelerates the suspense of the whole. Watch out for time shifts that would disturb the reader. Try to keep moving only forward in time until you’ve had a good deal of experience.

question: Chart each scene on its own line: its location (different from the preceding scene, if possible), its principal character, and the action in brief.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: On each line, note the location (different from the location of the preceding scene, if possible), the principal character in the scene, and, briefly, the action that takes place there. Be brief. (Keep in mind that if there is no action, you don’t really have a scene.)

question: End a scene with your character in serious trouble, then start the next in a different location with a different character, leaving the first unresolved.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: We leave the reader in suspense and go to the next location, Chicago, where we see a scene with a different character, say the hero’s fiancée, getting into trouble.

question: Study a suspense or thriller you couldn't put down: note how each chapter ending is suspenseful and throws forward into the next.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Pick up any well-known suspense or thriller writer’s work and look at the chapter endings. You’ll see how most of the time each chapter ends on a suspenseful note and throws the reader forward into the next chapter.

question: In literary fiction, keep the suspense subtle but still ensure each chapter ending arouses curiosity about what happens next.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In literary novels, of course, the suspense is often more subtle. All forms of fiction have one thing in common: the chapter endings arouse the reader’s curiosity about what will happen next.

question: End each chapter with your hero or heroine in unresolved trouble, so what happens next is wanted.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: • Ideally, each chapter might end the way the movies used to end their weekly serials: with the hero or heroine in unresolved trouble.

question: Find a moment when something wanted isn't happening yet — or something unwanted won't stop — and build the scene around that delay.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Suspense builds when the reader wants something to happen and it isn’t happening yet. Or something is happening and the reader wants it to stop, now. And it doesn’t.

question: When a character's old fear is about to become a present reality, don't relieve it; make the situation worse than the character anticipated.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: • When an old fear is about to become a present reality, don’t relieve the fear. Make the situation worse than the character anticipated.

question: Consciously create moments in which the reader feels tension. Remember that your job is to give readers stress, strain, and pressure—readers love in fiction what they hate in life.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Their job is to give readers stress, strain, and pressure. The fact is that readers who hate those things in life love them in fiction.

question: Distinguish tension from suspense in your pacing: use tension in brief bursts that last seconds or minutes, and let suspense carry the long arc of the work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Suspense can last over a long period, sometimes for an entire book. Tension is felt in seconds or minutes.

question: Create tension by causing friction: have a character resist a demand or order, and keep the resistance going.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I quickly point out that the way to create tension is to cause friction (ordering “Stand up!”) and to have the recipient of the order not stand up; the tension will continue only as long as the disobedience.

question: Cut the immediate relief of your character’s pressing problem: don’t resolve it at once, but stretch the tension out as long as possible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In examining the manuscripts of hundreds of writers over the years, a common fault I’ve observed is that the writer creates a pressing problem for a character and then immediately relieves the pressure by resolving it. That’s humane but not a writer’s function. His mission is to manipulate the emotions of the audience, and when it comes to moments of tension, to stretch them out as long as possible.

question: Rewrite your opening to note a single chilling 'fact' — something concrete and precise — that alarms on its own.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A common way to create tension in a novel is to simply note a “fact” that is likely to chill any reader.

question: Place the first moment of tension as close to the beginning of your work as possible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The most important moment of tension in a novel is its first use, which should be as close to the beginning of the book as possible. It puts the writer in charge of the reader’s emotions.

question: Once your early pages have fastened a character to the story, create moments of tension for that character as soon as possible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The closer writing gets to literature, the more likely it is that what fastens us to the early pages is our interest in a character. And then, as soon as possible, the writer creates some moments of tension for that character.

question: Describe a character's dangerous work in minute detail so tension mounts with every turn of the screw.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The author describes what the man is doing in minute detail. The reader, aware of the man as a human being, aware also of the five-year-old watching from a distance, feels tension mount with every turn of the screw.

question: Give the scene a deadline and show it closing in until the last-moment arrival.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: At four o’clock the hero, Frank, has not yet arrived, and Molly, glancing at the time, is tense. So is the reader. At five o’clock Molly is beginning to panic. At two minutes to six, the reader’s tension is extreme. At one minute to six, Frank arrives breathless.

question: Put your character in an unavoidable meeting with a dangerous figure from their past, and make it instantly tense.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The elevator stops on the fifth floor, and the dangerously neurotic man she jilted gets on. The reader becomes instantly tense.

question: Pile one tense moment on another, adding to the tension toward a climax instead of ending the confrontation at once.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What we’ve done is add one tense moment to another, piling up the degree of tension toward a climax.

question: Before the confrontation pays off, insert a complication that stretches the tension out.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The temptation for the inexperienced writer is to have the older man go in and shoot the crazed animal right off. That makes short shrift of the tension. By adding the element of the younger volunteer and the flashlight, we add to the tension, stretching it out.

question: Build moments of high tension even when the outcome is already known: stretch out the moments in which the character might stop, change course, not go through with it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: This isn’t suspense because he told us at the outset that he committed the crime. But there are moments of high tension, stretched out.

question: Relocate a sentence in your scene—transpose it to a later position and re-paragraph around it—to increase tension without changing a word.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I transposed one sentence and created two new paragraphs. Note the increase in tension, though no words have been changed.

question: Write dialogue that sparks with friction, generating the tension it does in life.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One of the easiest ways to create tension is by means of dialogue. The best dialogue sparks with friction, generating tension in the reader as it does in life.

question: When a word is overused in your text, consult a thesaurus that offers near misses and far-off synonyms, and use them to add color as well as diversity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: My other online thesaurus came up with no fewer than twenty-one “synonyms”—some near misses and some pretty far off—that enabled my student to add color as well as diversity to her text.

question: Diminish a coincidence by having a third character stage the “accidental” meeting at an event that third character arranges.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: For instance, a third character can arrange for Sally and Howie to meet “accidentally” at an event staged by the third character.

question: Check whether your title insulates your book from the public; if it does not arouse interest or promise a rich experience, revise it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: I have met many talented writers who insulate their books from the public with titles that are not likely to arouse a reader’s interest or to promise a rich experience.

question: Study the titles of books by authors you don't know; note which tempt you to pick them up and which don't, then judge your own title by the same standard.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You’ll see how many books don’t tempt you to pick them up because of their titles, and which titles intrigue you enough to want to take them down off the shelf and read the flaps.

question: Look past the short-description title for your nonfiction work and find the more imaginative title that appeals.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What many nonfiction writers neglect is the appeal more imaginative titles hold for readers.

question: Look for your title in the lines of poems and songs that resonate with your book’s theme and audience.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Many effective titles have come from poems and songs, and I thought of a song that would likely be remembered by a prime audience for the book, the tens of thousands of infantry officers of World War II.

question: Choose a title early that people respond to, and let that response spur you to complete the work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: A title that people respond to can spur completion of the work.

question: Make your title a metaphor: put two things together that don't ordinarily go together, so the title intrigues and exercises the imagination.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: All seven of those titles are metaphors. They put two things together that don’t ordinarily go together.

question: Title your novel with the leading character’s name plus an energizing factor rather than the bare name.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One way of enticing a reader is to title a novel with the name of the leading character plus an energizing factor.

question: Consider each word of your title carefully: test synonymous rewordings against each other.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Though the words mean the same, the latter title for the same novel might have quashed the book’s chances in the marketplace.

question: Remember that a title’s primary function is not to convey meaning but to sound enticing and exude resonance; test your title against that standard.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The point to remember is that the primary function of a title is not to convey meaning as much as to sound enticing and if possible exude resonance.

question: Look forward to rewriting: treat your first draft as material to excise and improve, not as finished.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The biggest difference between a writer and a would-be writer is their attitude toward rewriting. The writer, professional or not, looks forward to the opportunity of excising words, sentences, paragraphs, chapters that do not work and to improving those that do.

question: Remove any self-imposed limit on how much rewriting you will do.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you set a limit on how much rewriting you will do, you are merely devising an artificial barrier between your work and success.

question: Do not revise front-to-back: sort the problems in your manuscript and attend to major matters first.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Their order can be changed, as long as the principle is maintained: major matters are attended to first.

question: Print a hard copy of your manuscript to consult while revising, and reprint each section after major changes so you work from clean copy.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Even if you use a computer, I recommend that you have a hard copy of your manuscript to consult for the simple reason that seeing what you wrote on paper will give you a fresh impression of your work.

question: Test your main characters: if you cannot think of an important character in situations away from the story, that character needs more work.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Do you find yourself thinking about them in situations that are not in your book? If so, good! That means your characters are alive in your mind and should come alive in the minds of your audience. If you can't think of an important character in situations away from the story, that character may need more work.

question: If your protagonist is too like yourself, give the character a distinctive trait — positive or negative — that you are sure you do not have.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If it is, that may be a symptom of the autobiography trap, creating a character that is too like yourself, which hurts the distance that every author needs from his creations. One way to ameliorate the problem is to give the character a distinctive trait—positive or negative—that you are absolutely sure you don't have.

question: Add some sparkle to your main character — an interesting eccentricity, a personality characteristic that makes his company enjoyable.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You are asking your reader to spend a good number of hours with that character. You may need to add some sparkle to your character, some interesting eccentricity, perhaps a personality characteristic that will make his company more enjoyable.

question: Imagine you have just won a two-million-dollar lottery and your character hears about it on the news; use his reactions to make him more interesting.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One way to find out is to imagine that you have just won a lottery jackpot of two million dollars. Your character doesn't know you've been playing Lotto, but he is likely to hear about it on the news.

question: Humanize your characters by giving them the kind of thoughts people have in life — not always "nice" thoughts.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: This method of revision makes certain that you have humanized your characters by giving them the kind of thoughts—not always “nice” thoughts—that people have in life. The danger is portraying a person that nobody wants to spend time with.

question: Make your protagonist undergo change in the course of the novel; if yours does not, revise it so that it does.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In a story the length of a novel, it is essential that the protagonist undergo change. If yours at present does not, it isn't too late.

question: Keep to a single villain or antagonist.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Note that I use the singular—“villain” or “antagonist.” If you have more than one, you may be diffusing the impact of the character's villainy by spreading it.

question: Deepen the degree of your antagonist's villainy: is he morally bad rather than just badly behaved, malicious rather than mischievous?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is your antagonist morally bad, not just badly behaved? Does your antagonist enjoy doing wrong to people? Is your character not just mischievous but malicious?

question: Give your villain something that charms or entices people — charm, charisma, position, or wealth.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: No villain can attract victims unless he has charm, charisma, position, or wealth.

question: If your villain is hard to make charming or interesting, try seeing him through the eyes of someone who loves him.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you're having difficulty making your villain charming or interesting, try seeing him through the eyes of someone who loves him. Or at least cares a lot about him. The villain will be a more effective adversary if he has been humanized.

question: Do not model a villain on an enemy from your life: create characters more interesting than the nasties you know.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Novels are not a place to get even. Think of yourself as in the business of creating characters who are more interesting than the nasties you know in person.

question: Give each minor character one special characteristic, or characterize them through one of the senses you have neglected.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Just one special characteristic can make a difference. An easy way to help characterize minor players is to use one of the senses you may have neglected.

question: Make sure you have a credible conflict between protagonist and antagonist.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The next step is to be sure you have a credible conflict between your protagonist and the antagonist. Stories from time immemorial have consisted of people overcoming obstacles against high odds and strong adversaries.
