If you've followed a different course, your plot may not be strong enough to sustain the reader's interest.

question: Name your most memorable scene without looking at the manuscript — if you can't remember it, it isn't memorable — then name your least memorable one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: What is the most memorable scene in your book? Don't go to your manuscript for clues. If you can't remember the scene, it isn't memorable!

question: Cut your least memorable scene; if cutting it removes needed information, convey that information in an existing scene instead.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Don't be disappointed if you can't think of a radical revision of your least memorable scene. The usual remedy is to cut it! If cutting it removes some piece of information the reader needs, find some other way of conveying that information in an existing scene.

question: Subject the new least memorable scene to the same scrutiny: would the book be stronger without it? Keep cutting until every remaining scene contributes.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Once you've revised or done away with your least memorable scene, you now have a new least memorable scene! You need to subject it to the same tough scrutiny. Would the book be stronger without it?

question: If you cannot find a weak scene, put the manuscript aside for a week, a month, or longer, then look again.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Put the manuscript aside for a week, a month, or longer (the longer the better), then look again. The weakest scene will jump out at you, staring you straight in the eye until you decide whether to let it live or die.

question: From memory, jot down the three most important actions in your novel and test whether each is motivated in a way you would accept if someone else told the story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: First, from memory, jot down what you believe to be the three most important actions in your novel. Is each action motivated in a way that you would accept if this story were told by somebody else?

question: Establish the motivation of an action by planting it ahead of the scene in which the action takes place.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Motivation can usually be established by planting it ahead of the scene in which the action takes place.

question: Plant an object like a gun much earlier than its use, so the use becomes almost inevitable; derive suspense from its not being used when expected.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If a gun is seen in the hands of someone who is not known to carry a gun and then almost immediately fired, it will seem as if the author's heavy hand is at work. If the gun is planted much earlier, the use of it becomes almost inevitable. In fact much suspense can be derived from its not being used when the audience thinks it will be.

question: Replace coincidence with motivated action: motivation is not an option but a necessity.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Motivating actions takes work, and using coincidence is much easier. But coincidence is the mark of transient works, and I have met few novelists who are satisfied to think of their work as merely temporary entertainment.

question: Review every significant action for character consistency; fix any action not in keeping with the character, or that sounds farfetched, by planting a motive in a prior scene.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is there any action in your manuscript that is not in keeping with the character? Is there any action that under examination sounds farfetched? It might be fixed by planting a motive in a prior scene.

question: Read the first page as if it were written by a contemporary author you admire, then ask: is there a compelling reason to go on to page two?

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Now read the first page as if it were the other author's manuscript. After reading the first page, would you go on to the next page? If there isn't a compelling reason to go to page two, it usually means that you haven't sparked the reader's curiosity.

question: Read the manuscript from page one to the end as a reader and an editor, not as a writer.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Embarking on a general revision calls for starting on page one and working through the manuscript to the end, reading as a reader and an editor, not as a writer.

question: When in doubt about a change, do not make it; note it for later consideration.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If in doubt about a change, don't make the change. Instead, make a note to yourself for later consideration. I find that when I look at such notes days or weeks later, many of those questionable ideas for revision get discarded.

question: Tighten the manuscript: overwriting in first drafts is normal — the skill is recognizing on a later reading what can be eliminated and having the guts to cut it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: It is perfectly normal to overwrite in first drafts. The test of a writer's skill is in recognizing on later reading what can be eliminated, and then having the guts to do the cutting.

question: When unsure whether a paragraph contributes, block-move it to the end of the manuscript; later, restore only the paragraphs that earn their place.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Every time he came to a paragraph he wasn't sure contributed to the book, he marked it and with a block move transferred it to the end, after the last page. When he finished he found that he had transferred dozens of paragraphs and that only one or two, in modified form, deserved a place in the text.

question: Eliminate between-the-scenes material — the offstage recounting of actions not seen — or make such material active and interesting in itself.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Your second objective is to watch out for the between-the-scenes material, especially the offstage recounting of actions not seen. Try to eliminate as many of these as you can, or make them active and interesting in themselves.

question: Cut whatever seems not absolutely necessary, and watch for places where your own attention flags.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In your general revision, cut words, phrases, sentences, or paragraphs, pages, or whole scenes that seem not absolutely necessary. Watch for places where your own attention flags. That's usually a sign that something needs to be revised or cut.

question: Vary the length of your sentences; ideally follow an especially long sentence with a short, even abrupt one, but avoid a mechanical short-long-short-long pattern.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If your sentences are all approximately the same length, the effect will be monotonous. Vary the length of sentences. Ideally, follow an especially long sentence with a short, even abrupt sentence. Don't do this all the time. A pattern of short-long-short-long can get almost as monotonous as all long or all short sentences.

question: Break an unbroken mellifluous cadence — a lovely rhythm, if kept up, lulls to sleep.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: An unbroken mellifluous cadence, lovely for a few sentences, if kept up will put a reader to sleep.

question: Be relentless in moving the story forward; where it bogs down and you cannot see an immediate fix, mark the place, write down what may be wrong, and come back to it later.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Unless you are consciously trying to slow things down between fast-moving scenes, be relentless in moving the story forward. If you find it bogging down at any point, it could be for many reasons: perhaps too slow a pace, not enough happening. If you don't see an immediate fix, mark the place in the margin and write down what you think might be wrong.

question: Mark any section where you catch the author talking or a mix of points of view, and revise it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you catch the author talking at any point, or a mix of points of view, mark the section so that you can return to Chapter 13 for guidance.

question: Keep your characters under stress from time to time, and make the stress increase.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Are your characters under stress from time to time? Does the stress increase? Keep reminding yourself that fiction deals with the most stressful moments of the characters' lives.

question: Cut every unessential adjective and adverb; cut "very"; make every word count.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As you go through, cut every unessential adjective and adverb. Cut “very.” Cut “poor” for everything but poverty. Make every word count.

question: If you have said the same thing twice in different words, cut the weaker one; swap a repeated uncommon word for a synonym; and mark every cliché for excision.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you've said the same thing twice in different words, pick the better one and cut the other. If you find yourself using the same uncommon word twice within a few pages, use your thesaurus to pick a synonym. And in your read-through, mark every cliché for excision.

question: Put the speaker identification first ('George said') whenever there is any chance the speaker is unclear; otherwise let it follow or omit it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If there is any chance that the reader won't know who is speaking at that point, the “George said” should come first. If it is clear who is speaking, “George said” can follow what he says or be omitted.

question: Transpose the order of words, phrases, or clauses in a sentence to let its emphasis fall where you want it.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In my own work, I make transpositions hundreds of times in a book-length manuscript. Sometimes it is to let the emphasis of a sentence fall in a different place.

question: Transpose words when their order could make the sentence misread, so the first reading is the correct one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Because readers will undoubtedly have had experience with a pulse being taken at the wrist, they may suppose that immediately on reading the word “pulse.” Immediately, they read “in the neck” and have to change their first view. That kind of glitch can momentarily disturb the reading experience. To avoid it, I simply transposed a few words.

question: Remove conspicuous passages you love — images and sentences that jump off the page and interfere with the story — and save them in a special box to look into years later.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When you “love” certain images or sentences, they are frequently so conspicuous as to interfere with the story. If they are, save them in a special box that you'll look into five years from now, and thank me for having asked you to remove them from your manuscript, though it may have hurt at the time.

question: Root out sentimentality — an excess of response to a stimulus — and underplay to evoke emotion.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Root out sentimentality, which is an excess of response to a stimulus. It makes writing “flowery.” Your job is to stimulate emotions in the reader. An excessive response turns off the reader, just as it does people in life:

question: Make sure there is something visual on every page: mark V in the corner of pages that have a visual element and NV on pages that do not, then return to introduce a visual element on every NV page.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Until you are in the habit of making sure that there is something visual on every page, while reviewing the draft put a small V in the lower right corner of every page that has something visual on it. This provides a discipline as you develop the experience of reading with an editor's eye. If a page has nothing visual, mark NV and return to it later to introduce a visual element.

question: If your characters usually speak in complete sentences, fix it so they don't.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In dialogue sequences, if your characters usually speak in complete sentences, fix it so they don't.

question: Break up any dialogue that runs longer than three sentences with an interjection, thought, or action, and make responses oblique at least from time to time.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If any dialogue runs longer than three sentences, break it up with an interjection from another character or a thought or action. Check to see that responses in dialogue are oblique, at least from time to time.

question: Catch every place a character "muttered" or "screamed" instead of "said," and substitute "he said" and "she said" — the dialogue, not the tag, should tell how lines are spoken.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In your general revision, catch the places where a character “muttered,” “screamed,” and the like instead of “said.” Substitute “he said” and “she said” for language that tells the reader how the lines are spoken. That's the dialogue's job.

question: Make a checklist of everything to catch during your general revision; if you cannot do it all in one pass, save some items for a second pass.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you are new to the process, you'll want to make a checklist of all the things I've suggested catching during general revision. If you find that you just can't do everything in one pass, save some things for a second pass later on.

question: Consider whether bringing a strong scene forward would provoke more curiosity than the scene that presently starts the book.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You may want to ask yourself, if you were to bring a strong scene forward, would that provoke the reader's curiosity more than the scene that presently starts the book?

question: Make the ending of your book a high point of satisfaction; if it is not, consider whether another scene or circumstance would make a better ending.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You might consider at this stage whether the ending of your book is a high point of satisfaction for the reader. If not, is there another scene or circumstance that might make a better ending?

question: For a final read-through, work with a clean manuscript in which your changes are not visible, and fix anything that momentarily makes you see words on the page and takes you out of experiencing the story.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: For your next read-through, work with a clean manuscript in which the changes you've made are not visible as changes. (One of the great advantages of working on a computer!) This time, as you read, watch for anything that momentarily makes you see words on the page and takes you out of experiencing the story.

question: Replace vague phrases like 'a regular guy' — verbal trunks into which a hundred people pile their own meanings — and say exactly what you mean.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Did they mean Schwarzkopf was what in colloquial parlance we call “a regular guy”? And if so, what is meant by “a regular guy”? It’s a verbal trunk into which a hundred readers would pile many meanings relating to their own experience.

question: Make sure something visible appears on every page: pencil a V in the corner of each page that has something visual, and on pages without a V, create something visual.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Is there something visible on every page? If you are reviewing what you wrote in hard copy, pencil a V in a lower corner of every page that has something visual, and on pages without a V, see if you can create something visual, even if it is a leaf falling from a tree.

question: Ask whether your opening is sufficiently visual; if not, make it visual.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Also ask yourself if your opening is sufficiently visual to be seen by the reader.

question: Create suspense by raising a question and withholding the answer for a while; find a place in the piece where you can do this now.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Have you created occasional suspenseful interest by raising a question and withholding the answer for a while? Can you recall any place where this might be done now?

question: Attend to the individual meaning and resonance of every word and show respect for the reader's intelligence — that attention separates literary writing from commercial.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The most distinguishing difference between “commercial” writers like Grisham and literary writers is the attention paid to the individual meanings and resonance of words and the respect shown for the reader’s intelligence.

question: Bring two words together that have not been together before — achieve precision by creating a new grouping of words.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One way to a reader’s emotion is to bring two words together that have not been together before. Therefore precision is achieved in poetry by the creation of a new grouping of words rather than by using each word for its exact meaning.

question: Write down what you see in your most secret snapshot — and if you’re tempted to fudge or invent one, change it to the snapshot you’re actually hiding.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: One of the ways is to write down what you see in your most secret snapshot. If you’re tempted to fudge, don’t. If you’ve decided to give us a made-up snapshot, you’ll serve your writing better by changing it to the snapshot you’re hiding.

question: At a chapter ending, cut any line that is excessively sentimental or too abstract to leave the reader with the right closing emotion.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In revising, I thought the sentence “What does a mother do with her love?” excessively sentimental. And “Why did God do nothing?” was too abstract to leave the reader with a suitable emotion at the end of the chapter. I cut both sentences.

question: Rephrase a flat, over-described sentence so that some word or group of words in it makes the reader ask “Why?” or “How?” and wants to keep reading.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Any word or group of words that makes the reader ask “Why?” or “How?” also serves as an inducement for the reader to go on.

question: Cut any modifier whose meaning the surviving head word already carries, so the remaining word alone says all you need.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The word “life” encompasses private and public. “Over the last fifteen years” provided unnecessary information that weakened the sentence.

question: Consider whether the ending of your book is a high point of satisfaction for the reader; if not, ask whether another scene or circumstance would make a better ending.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: You might consider at this stage whether the ending of your book is a high point of satisfaction for the reader. If not, is there another scene or circumstance that might make a better ending?

question: Cut any passage where your own attention flags while you read; that flag is a sign the passage needs revision or cutting.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Watch for places where your own attention flags. That's usually a sign that something needs to be revised or cut.

question: When certain images or sentences are so conspicuous you love them, cut them from the manuscript and save them in a box to look at years later.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: When you "love" certain images or sentences, they are frequently so conspicuous as to interfere with the story. If they are, save them in a special box that you'll look into five years from now, and thank me for having asked you to remove them from your manuscript, though it may have hurt at the time.

question: Eliminate the between-the-scenes material, especially offstage recounting of actions not seen; cut as many of these as you can or make them active and interesting in themselves.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Your second objective is to watch out for the between-the-scenes material, especially the offstage recounting of actions not seen. Try to eliminate as many of these as you can, or make them active and interesting in themselves.

question: Recognize on a later reading what can be eliminated, then have the guts to do the cutting.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The test of a writer's skill is in recognizing on later reading what can be eliminated, and then having the guts to do the cutting.

question: Block-move every paragraph you're not sure contributes to the book to the end of the manuscript, then see how few deserve a place back in the text.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Every time he came to a paragraph he wasn't sure contributed to the book, he marked it and with a block move transferred it to the end, after the last page. When he finished he found that he had transferred dozens of paragraphs and that only one or two, in modified form, deserved a place in the text.

question: If in doubt about a change during revision, don't make it — note it for later consideration, and let days or weeks discard most of those questionable ideas.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If in doubt about a change, don't make the change. Instead, make a note to yourself for later consideration. I find that when I look at such notes days or weeks later, many of those questionable ideas for revision get discarded.

question: Look for imprecision where the word you used is not exactly the word you needed, and consult a dictionary and a thesaurus.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: As you read through, look for imprecision, when the word you used is not exactly the word you needed. Consult a dictionary. Consult a thesaurus.

question: Put the "he said" identification before the quotation when there is any chance the reader won't know who is speaking; let it follow the speech or be omitted when the speaker is clear.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If there is any chance that the reader won't know who is speaking at that point, the "George said" should come first. If it is clear who is speaking, "George said" can follow what he says or be omitted.

question: Catch the places where a character "muttered," "screamed," and the like instead of "said," and substitute "he said" and "she said" — the dialogue itself should tell how the lines are spoken.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: catch the places where a character "muttered," "screamed," and the like instead of "said." Substitute "he said" and "she said" for language that tells the reader how the lines are spoken. That's the dialogue's job.

question: If you've used the same uncommon word twice within a few pages, use your thesaurus to pick a synonym.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: If you find yourself using the same uncommon word twice within a few pages, use your thesaurus to pick a synonym.

question: Transpose a few words when their order makes readers form a wrong first impression that they then have to correct on a later word.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: That kind of glitch can momentarily disturb the reading experience. To avoid it, I simply transposed a few words:

question: Move a phrase to a location where it is immediately comprehensible.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: In my opinion, the phrase "I won't have anywhere" is not immediately comprehensible in its present location. Transposed, it works well:

question: Transpose a phrase to the end of a sentence to shift where the sentence's emphasis falls.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: That puts the emphasis on rock music. I transposed the phrase "her son was a reader" to the end of the sentence, since that was where I wanted the emphasis to fall:

question: Improve a paragraph by transposing its final sentence to the beginning.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: The thought was improved by transposing the last of the three sentences to the beginning of the paragraph, so that it read:

question: Rephrase an overblown expression of emotion as understatement; the underplayed line evokes more feeling than the gushing one.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Underplay to evoke emotion in the reader: I looked at her eyes. They were dry. Given the right context, that would evoke more emotion than something overblown like "She was ready to cry her heart out."

question: Vary the length of your sentences; follow an especially long one with a short, even abrupt sentence, without falling into a predictable short-long-short-long pattern.

source.author: Sol Stein
source.quote: Vary the length of sentences. Ideally, follow an especially long sentence with a short, even abrupt sentence. Don't do this all the time. A pattern of short-long-short-long can get almost as monotonous as all long or all short sentences.

question: Don't make a bad guy your protagonist—readers will invest him with positive qualities he doesn't deserve.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: novices often want to write narratives with bad-guy protagonists, but bad guys seldom work as narrative protagonists.

question: Build your story on the protagonist-complication-resolution model: a sympathetic character encounters a complicating situation that he confronts and solves.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A story consists of a sequence of actions that occur when a sympathetic character encounters a complicating situation that he confronts and solves.

question: Search for the person who makes things happen and make that active player your protagonist.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: when you're looking for a protagonist search for the person who makes things happen.

question: Make sure the complication you choose is consequential enough to justify a story, not a minor irritant that merely sets the action in motion.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Any problem constitutes a complication, but only certain complications justify a story.

question: Stay in tune with your emotional responses as you report and collect the details that produce them to pass along to readers.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As he reported the story, he was in tune with his own emotional responses, targeted the details that produced them, and collected those details so that he could pass them along to readers.

question: Hold your audience by showing readers how much is at stake and launching action sequences that keep them wondering what will happen next.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The reaction testiﬁ ed to Tom's skill at showing readers how much was at stake and launching action sequences that put them on the edge of their seats as they wondered what would happen next.

question: Immerse readers in another world by combining strong action lines with artful scene-setting that lets them join the story's characters.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Writers accomplish that kind of diversion by combining strong action lines with artful scene- setting, reproducing realities where readers can join the story's characters.

question: List the plot points in your piece so you can plan its trajectory and know what to include and leave out.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: One of the most valuable things I do when coaching a writer is to list the plot points.

question: If your protagonist seems like a loser, find the constructive way he copes with his disappointment.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But that's because losing athletes, as well as losers in love, elections, workplace competitions, and the like, must ﬁ nd some constructive way to cope with their disappointments.

question: Know which forms don't need a resolution: an explanatory narrative can follow a flat action line with no climax, and so can an essay or a vignette.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: An explanatory narrative uses an action line to explore a subject, and it requires no resolution to accomplish its purpose.

question: Turn mere narrative into plot by deliberately selecting and arranging your events so that larger meanings can emerge.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A plot emerges when a storyteller carefully selects and arranges material so that larger meanings can emerge.

question: Resolve your complication either by changing the world or by changing your character himself.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You can resolve a complication, in other words, by changing the world or changing yourself.

question: Make the resolution a product of the character's own efforts.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: They, he insists, “absolutely and without exception, must be products of the character’s own efforts.”

question: Let your resolution carry a lesson the audience can take away and apply to their own lives.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It contains the lesson that the audience carries away, the insight that the story's readers or viewers or listeners can apply to their own lives.

question: Match the size of your complication to the size of the story you want.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The bigger the complication, the bigger the story.

question: Train yourself to recognize the universal ingredients of story in real-world situations before you commit to pursuing one.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A sharp eye for story comes from understanding that its basic ingredients are universal and learning how to spot them in the real world.

question: Draw each line of plot as an arc on scrap paper, an A at one end (a question) and a B at the other (its answer).

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I ﬁ nd it helpful in the planning stages to draw each line of plot as an arc on a piece of scrap paper. Put an A at one end and a B at the other. A is to be a question; B is its answer.

question: Diagram the line of your story, charting its simplest natural path of unfolding; if you can't diagram it, you haven't yet figured out the structure.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: make a diagram, charting the line of the story. I look for the simplest way to let it ﬂ ow, the most natural path of unfolding. Usually, if I can’t diagram it, that means I haven’t ﬁ gured out the structure yet.

question: Drop the roman-numeral topical outline for your story and reach for a visual diagram instead.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The kind of roman numeral outline that Mrs. Grundy taught you in the fourth grade will work ﬁ ne for a news report, a thesis, or an instructional book like this one. But it won’t uncover the patterns at the heart of story.

question: Plan your story's structure before you begin writing rather than starting without a plan and drifting with your interests.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I’d start without a plan and see where my interests took me. But that method wasn’t very efﬁcient. I wasted a lot of time on dead ends.

question: Treat polish as the final coat over structure, not the core of writing: lock down your structure before fussing over word choice and syntax.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But polish, Franklin adds, is merely “the plaster on the walls of structure.”

question: When you run into something unexpected, revise your blueprint rather than abandoning planning.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If you run into something unexpected, you can always revise the blueprint—contractors do it all the time.

question: Check the overall shape of your story against the shapes narratives naturally take, and restore what you've strayed from.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Stories tend to certain shapes, and if you stray too far from them, you’ll end up with no story at all.

question: In your first draft, get the right things in the right places and worry about making each sentence perfect only after the whole structure is roughed out.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: your ﬁ rst draft should emphasize the structure—getting the right things in the right placesrather than trying to make each sentence perfect. Once you have the whole structure roughed out, you can go back and rewrite for polish.

question: Make the structural decision for your piece first, before drafting.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If you make the right decision about structure, a huge amount becomes absolutely clear.

question: Keep the structure of your piece in mind as you gather material so things have somewhere to fit, and stop collecting what you won't use.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I always keep in mind that there is a structure to this,” Mary Roach says, “and things are going to have to ﬁ t. That saves you from collecting a lot of things you won’t use.

question: Sketch a visual blueprint of your story's assembly before you write.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Structure is more visual than logical, a pattern of parts with its own rules for ﬁtting pieces together, and most experienced writers create some sort of visual guide to the assembly of a story.

question: Launch your action immediately and blend your exposition into it, submerging the backstory in modifiers, subordinate clauses, and appositives.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You launch action immediately and then blend the exposition into it, submerging it in modiﬁ ers, subordinate clauses, appositives, and the like.

question: Close each little episode of your story with a kicker that leaves your protagonist—and your audience—dangling, waiting for what happens next.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You don’t need to create literal cliff- hangers—Indiana Jones dangling from a sapling on a vertical face high above a river—but you do want to close out each little episode with a kicker that leaves your protagonist, and your audience, dangling.

question: Decide whether to begin your story just before the inciting incident and tell it chronologically, or to begin with the crisis and use its dramatic intensity to jerk readers into the story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Do you begin the story just before the inciting incident and tell it in chronological order? Or do you begin it with the crisis, using the dramatic intensity of that moment to grab readers by their lapels and jerk them into the story?

question: When you reach the falling action, answer the remaining questions and wrap things up as quickly as possible.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: So don’t push your luck. Wrap things up as quickly as possible and leave the stage.

question: Arrange the mysteries in your dramatic structure in a deliberate escalating order, using smaller questions to lead into larger ones and saving the resolution of the biggest mystery for last.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “a string of mysteries organized in a deliberate order. The mysteries will be large and small, and the writer will make good use of this variation in interest, resolving the mysteries in escalating order, using smaller questions to lead into larger ones, saving the resolution of the biggest mystery for last.”

question: Cut your backstory down to just enough to explain how the protagonist got to this place, at this time, with the wants that drive the next phase—then clear a path forward.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Hence the principle that exposition is the enemy of narrative. Good exposition provides just enough backstory to explain how the protagonist happens to be in a particular place, at a particular time, with the wants that will lead to the next phase of the story. Thorough reporting produces overwhelming detail. Good storytellers cut through it to create a clear path leading forward.

question: Rewrite each expository segment of your story so readers understand only what they must, and no more—cut anything they can do without.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The trick to writing a good expository segment is to tell readers what they must understand . . . and no more.

question: Foreshadow coming disaster subtly by showing your character's confident assumption that the worst will not happen.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Readers know full well that when a writer takes pains to tell them a character doesn’t expect the worst, she’s about to get it.

question: End your story with a kicker that sums up, surprises a little, brings things full circle, plants your protagonist in their new status quo, and leaves no doubt the story has ended.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A good one will sum up, surprise a little, perhaps bring things full circle, ﬁrmly planting your protagonists in their new status quo. It will leave absolutely no doubt that the story has ended.

question: Before you add extensive flashbacks or flash-forwards, apply KISS—stay as close to the action as possible and resist jumping out of the chronology.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: No matter how experienced you are, you’re well advised to apply KISS anytime you consider extensive ﬂ ashbacks or ﬂ ash- forwards. ... “Beware the extended ﬂashback, the ornate ﬂ ash- forward, the so- called expert dragged forward to ‘explain.’ Stay as close to the action as possible.”

question: Make sure each new development in your story grows from the one before it, each twist leading inexorably to the next.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “There is no moment in a play,” Lajos Egri says, “which does not grow from the one before it.”

question: Even without a true psychological transformation, ask yourself what event sets up the resolution of the crisis and treat that as your point of insight to visualize your story's full structure.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Ask yourself, “What event sets up the resolution of the crisis?” Consider that your point of insight. ... having such a point helps you visualize its full structure.

question: Give your rising action the rhythm of hope rising and falling—let your protagonist win some points and lose others so the outcome stays uncertain.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Good narrative also follows the rise and fall of hope, another characteristic of effective rising action.

question: Check each plot point in your rising action and make sure most of them create new problems for your protagonist.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Most of those plot points will create new problems for the protagonist. As Ted Conover reminds us, “A narrative is when things go wrong.”

question: Open your narrative by teasing readers with a pronoun that lacks an antecedent or some other glaring loose end, and let the little mystery drive the story forward.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Often it’s simply a matter of teasing readers with a pronoun that lacks an antecedent or some other kind of glaring loose end. ... What happened? What sound? The standard newspaper report reveals all immediately. But little mysteries drive the narrative forward.

question: Write in the dramatic point of view as a series of relatively pure scenes that stick to externally verifiable reality, zeroing in on key moments and cutting the tedious daily life that connects them.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Because it sticks to an external reality that can be veriﬁed by independent observers, it’s the most objective and journalistic of third-person viewpoints. Narratives with the dramatic point of view often are structured as a series of relatively pure scenes, divided typographically and other than brief bits of necessary background—unsullied by digressions. Readers experience the story as any onlooker would, although the writer manipulates the scenic construction to zero in on key moments. It’s reality without boredom, pivotal places and times without the often tedious daily life that connects them.

question: Remember that first person limits you to your own perspective: you can't slip into another character's mind or voice unless you filter his comments through your own experience.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: For one thing, ﬁrst person limits you to your own perspective. You can’t slip into another POV character’s mind or voice unless you ﬁlter his comments through your own experience.

question: Keep a first-person viewpoint looking outward at the events around you, telling the story without making the author the story and without the look-at-me pyrotechnics of the self-absorbed narrator.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: his viewpoint looked outward, at the events happening around him. His unobtrusive prose lacked the look-at-me pyrotechnics of the New Journalism. And unlike, say, Hunter Thompson’s Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas, it told the story without the author becoming the story.

question: Limit point-of-view changes to a few: in a magazine piece focus on no more than two or three principal characters, with just a few supporting characters.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A few point-of-view changes are ﬁne, but don’t make readers dizzy by spinning through a dozen viewpoints. In a magazine piece, you’re wise to focus on no more than two or three principal characters, with just a few supporting characters.

question: Write in the memoir voice, reporting what you see, hear, smell, and feel as you move along the action line.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The author tells the story in what Peter Rubie calls “the memoir voice,” telling you what he or she sees, hears, smells, and feels while moving along the action line.

question: Determine whose story it is, then distinguish the POV character (the vehicle through whose eyes and ears readers move with the story) from the narrator who actually tells it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It has to be somebody's story, and one of the first questions any narrative writer has to answer is “whose?” ... A third-person narrative may follow a single character from the beginning of the narrative arc until the end without that character ever speaking directly to the reader. But readers move through time with the POV character, seeing what that character sees and hearing what the character hears.

question: Determine your point of view by answering three questions: through whose eyes does the reader experience the story, from which direction, and from what distance?

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: point of view boils down to the answers to three questions: Through whose eyes do we experience the story? From which direction? From what distance?

question: Use second person sparingly in narrative, as a stylistic device to put readers inside a scene rather than as actual direct address.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Second person does occasionally show up in narrative, usually as a stylistic device intended to put readers in a scene. In that context, it’s more of a literary device than actual direct address.

question: Write in third-person limited: report only the world visible to your POV character, but go inside the character's head to convey what he or she thinks as that world unfolds.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You mainly report external reality, and you report only the world visible to your POV character. But you also have the right to go inside your character’s head, to convey what he or she thinks as that world unfolds around him.

question: Claim third-person omniscience: give yourself the power to see everything, everywhere, anytime, and include anything that advances the story, so long as you investigate it and report it accurately.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Give yourself the power to see everything, everywhere, anytime you choose. Slip into the ultimate third-person option—third-person omniscient. ... So long as you take the time to investigate it and accurately report what you ﬁnd, you’re free to include anything that advances the story.

question: Exploit third person's range: turn yourself into a movie camera framing external images, peek inside characters' heads, and rise above a scene to see into past and future.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: In third person you can turn yourself into a movie camera, using vivid detail to frame external images of scenes and characters. Or you can violate the laws of nature by peeking inside the heads of characters. You can rise high above a scene to report what’s going on at the same moment in distant places. You can even claim the prerogative of seeing into past and future with you-are-there immediacy.

question: Choose the stance for each scene — the place you position your camera and the direction you point it — to give readers the best angle on the unfolding story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Bias aside, you ordinarily pick a stance to give readers the best angle on the unfolding story.

question: Climb the ladder when you want meaning and comprehensiveness, trading the ability to form concrete images for knowledge that applies across a larger class of things.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You gain comprehensiveness as you climb the ladder, but you lose the ability to form concrete images.

question: Keep readers unconsciously secure about where they stand by maintaining a coherent visual frame for continuous action, avoiding jump cuts that jar by butting inconsistent bits together.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: To immerse readers in a story, you want them unconsciously secure about their various positions for viewing it. The point is to let them see the action as though they were there themselves. That means they need a coherent visual frame, creating a stage for continuous action. You want to avoid what videographers call “jump cuts,” sudden breaks in the unfolding narrative that jar viewers by butting inconsistent bits of action together.

question: Write on the lowest rungs of the abstraction ladder to put readers in the scene, letting them see, hear, and sometimes smell what a firsthand observer would.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The lowest rungs of the ladder put you in the scene. Hence the notion of scenic narrative. You see it. You hear it. Sometimes, you even smell it. So you can react as a ﬁ rsthand observer would. You feel the fear as the Green Wall approaches. You share the horror when Byars’s body appears. Emotion originates on the ladder’s lower rungs.

question: When you weren't there for a scene, quiz an eyewitness about exactly what they could see from their position until the scene assumes a detailed, coherent shape.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: So, I asked, “What can you see when you look into the kitchen from the living room?” Tom described the arched doorway. He mentioned the kitchen table. I quizzed him about what hung on the walls, the mother’s appearance, and the veggies. The scene assumed a more detailed, coherent shape.

question: Think of your story on a ladder of abstraction that rises from the most concrete level of any concept up through ever-larger categories, and place each sentence on the rung it belongs to.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The ladder, one of the most useful concepts for any writer, rises from the most concrete level of any concept through an increasingly abstract series of categories.

question: Open a scene not with a summary lead but with a sequence of specific actions that unfold moment by moment.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: To describe the Highway 23 accident scenically, a storyteller might begin not with a summary lead, but with a sequence of speciﬁ c actions

question: Watch for the tunnel vision that report-writing can give you, which traps you on the middle rungs of the abstraction ladder and cripples your ability to tell a story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But reports can give you tunnel vision, trapping you on the middle rungs of the abstraction ladder and crippling your ability to tell a good story.

question: Shift your stance as the story unfolds, moving the camera to whichever position captures each phase of the action best rather than locking it in one place.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: So Stu’s stance—his camera position—is inside the patrol car with McGowan, watching as the pickup crosses McGowan’s ﬁeld of view. But that stance won’t work for all the action that follows, and Stu moves his camera several times before he ends the yarn.

question: When a situation offers enough story elements — a protagonist, a complication, a series of plot points — tell it as a story that emphasizes process rather than outcomes.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But stories offer rewards beyond raw information, the kind that yield meaning by recreating life as it’s lived. Stories emphasize process, rather than outcomes. So if readers don’t need the main point immediately and if a situation offers enough story elements—ingredients such as a protagonist, a complication, and a series of plot points—a narrative might be the better way to go.

question: Recognize the two distances of narrative: write in summary narrative when you step way back from the action, and shift into scenic narrative when you shrink the distance.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When the distance is great, when you step way back from the action, you write in summary narrative. When you shrink the distance, you shift into scenic narrative.

question: Constantly shift between scenic and summary modes, ascending and descending the ladder of abstraction as you vary distance, rather than committing to show-don’t-tell alone.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Most nonﬁ ction narrative writers constantly shift between scenic and summary modes, varying distance with each oscillation. They ignore the writing gurus who harp at them to “show, don’t tell,” knowing that good writing constantly ascends and descends the ladder of abstraction. They show and tell.

question: Adopt a persona — a distinctive stance toward your material — and ask what kind of personality you want to bring to the page.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: By adopting a persona, the writer adopts a distinctive stance toward the material, bringing an identiﬁ able personality to bear on the subject.

question: Rewrite your draft to strip the institutional tone: root out passive voice, stilted vocabulary, indirect syntax, and weak verbs that drown your individual voice.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Journalese drowns individual voice in an institutional swamp of passive voice, stilted vocabulary, indirect syntax, and weak verbs.

question: Develop a consistent voice that readers come to expect, one that emerges as you mature, relax, and become comfortable with your literary self.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: most narrative writers develop a consistent voice that readers come to expect, one that emerges as writers mature, relax, and become more comfortable with their literary selves.

question: Cut long introductory phrases and clauses that back into long, complicated sentences.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Long introductory phrases and clauses that back into long, complicated sentences immediately ﬂ ag the institutional voice we call journalese.

question: Turn to the full range of figurative devices beyond metaphor and simile — allusion, word play, and personification.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A real stylist may turn to allusion (“his Alfred Hitchcock physique”) or word play (hot dog brands engaged in “grinding competition”) or personiﬁ cation.

question: Decide whether to use first person based on your mission, not habit — first person is not voice, and voice is not first person.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But ﬁ rst person is not voice, and voice is not ﬁ rst person.

question: Match your level of diction to the subject.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: In the world of narrative writing, an author’s level of diction is one of the prime markers of his style.

question: Hunt for the right metaphor during rewrite, not the rough draft.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I’m more likely to ﬁ nd a ﬁ gure during rewrite, when puzzling over just the right metaphor doesn’t interrupt the struggle to get through the ﬁ rst version.

question: Decide where you stand as narrator — far in the background letting facts speak, near the audience adding commentary, or in front keeping focus on yourself.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: position refers to where writers stand as they narrate the unfolding story.

question: Read every piece of writing out loud in a firm, clear voice, hear the false notes, and cut verbiage and simplify syntax so it sounds like you.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The best thing any writer can do is to read every piece of writing out loud.

question: Relax and be yourself when you write — tension makes your words rigid and formal, submerging your true voice in stiffened formality.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But the ultimate secret to letting your voice sound on the page is simply to relax and be yourself.

question: As you edit, stay alert for clichés and root out hackneyed expressions, replacing them with something fresh.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As I edit, I stay alert for clichés, which signal opportunity for rooting out hackneyed expressions and replacing them with something fresh.

question: Space your figures of speech through the writing, dropping about one for every three paragraphs so readers never lose sight of the one ahead.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: you want to space the metaphors out without spreading them so far apart that readers lose sight of those ahead. About one ﬁ gure for every three paragraphs seems about right.

question: Write fast and loose in the first draft rather than agonizing over every word.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A relaxed writer is a fast writer, and fast writers sound more like themselves.

question: Salt your piece with anecdotes—stories within stories—as persuasive evidence for your take on a character.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: These stories within stories maintain reader interest by salting a larger article with little narrative arcs, each one pulling the audience inexorably forward.

question: Replace a few disembodied quotations with detail that presents your subject as a full human being.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But those few quotes are all the humanity you’re likely to find. Disembodied voices. A few formal pronouncements on the subject of the piece.

question: Let the odyssey from complication to resolution change your character profoundly.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: In the best stories, the odyssey from complication to resolution changes the character profoundly.

question: Identify your protagonist's central want, and check that it drives every action she takes and places her in each scene.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The personality, values, and desires of a protagonist produce action. And the POV character’s wants put her in a particular place, creating scene.

question: In nonfiction, choose a protagonist who has been through a struggle and experienced a point of insight.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Even though a nonfiction storyteller has no control over the content of a protagonist’s character, he does control his choice of protagonist. Finding someone who’s been through a struggle and experienced a point of insight suggests that you’re on to something worthwhile.

question: Cut any detail of appearance, anecdote, or possession that doesn’t reveal something about the story your character drives.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The purpose of character is to drive story.

question: Make the antagonist formidable enough that the opposing forces appear evenly matched and readers worry who will win.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Drama is interesting only when opposing forces appear evenly matched.

question: Cut insignificant actions included only to break up background or dialogue; every detail must advance the action line and develop character.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The point, as always, is that every word must do some work, and every detail must advance the action line and develop character. You never include detail for its own sake.

question: Give your protagonist human foibles, inconsistencies, and a capacity for change so readers see themselves and care what happens.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Human foibles, inconsistencies, and a capacity for change make protagonists sympathetic. It’s only when characters reflect the reality of human complexity that they evoke universals readers can recognize.

question: Put a direct quotation in the context of a revealing gesture or mannerism that shows what words hide.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: the reporter was savvy enough to put the direct quotation in the context of a gesture: “‘I’m tired of being the one who’s always wrong,’ she said as she crossed her arms.”

question: Show how your character speaks—tone, grammar, accent.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But how we say something reveals character, too, perhaps even more profoundly than the actual content of our words. ... The way we talk may be the most revealing detail of all.

question: Quote people as they really speak, dialect and all, to convey the color of daily life and honest emotion.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: And isn’t the rich patois of an authentic American dialect more likely to convey the color of daily life, the variety of our culture, or honest emotion?

question: Match the depth of character work to your text’s length: the longer the piece, the more room—and need—character has to grow.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The more story you have, the more room character has to grow. The longer your text, in other words, the more important character becomes in the mix of character, action, and scene.

question: Reveal character in successively deeper layers, each revelation driving the reader forward to discover more.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The narrative line reveals one layer of character and then probes further, discovering successively deeper layers.

question: Structure the arc so the protagonist fails early attempts, reaches a crisis, then achieves a point of insight that lets her finally overcome the obstacle.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Typically, the protagonist fails during early attempts to satisfy the central want. ... Then she achieves the point of insight, a new way of looking at the world that allows her to finally overcome whatever’s standing between her and her want.

question: Fill your notebook with particulars on your character’s appearance, possessions, behavior, and speech, choosing those that reveal the most about the person.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: They fill their notebooks with particulars on a character’s appearance, material possessions, behavior, and speech and choose those that reveal the most about the person.

question: Make your central character round—many faceted and capable of change—rather than flat and fixed.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A round character is many faceted and is capable of change.

question: Replace straight commentary on your subject with details that lead readers to their own inevitable conclusions about the character.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Instead, the best modern fiction and nonfiction writers let a character’s visible persona speak for itself, the method Burroway calls “direct characterization.” They may occasionally comment on character. But mostly they choose to include details that lead readers to certain inevitable conclusions about the character they are describing.

question: Record the pattern of behavior and possessions through which your character expresses—or imagines—her position in the world.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: the recording of . . . the entire pattern of behavior and possessions through which people express their position in the world or what they think it is or what they hope it to be.

question: Show your character through the larger context that defines her: her values, beliefs, behaviors, and possessions.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Human beings are the sum of their values, beliefs, behaviors, and possessions. They’re distinctive because they look a certain way, talk a certain way, and walk a certain way. We know them only when we start to tap the larger context that defines them.

question: Keep the first image of a character terse and drop more descriptive details into the action line later.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Long expository descriptions take readers out of the unfolding story. So keep that first image terse. You can drop more descriptive details into the action line later.

question: Identify the want that drives your protagonist’s story; the bigger the want, the bigger the story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: For a storyteller, the critical element of character is the want that drives the story.

question: Develop a theory of personality that guides your reporting, and ask how character explains each action you observe.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Ultimately, every nonfiction writer who successfully probes human character must develop a theory of personality that guides the reporting.

question: Describe a character with just three or four details that trigger a stored image.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Three or four details will usually do the trick. ... “Detailed descriptions tend to defeat their own purpose,” Wolfe said, “because they break up the face rather than create an image.”

question: Give your pivotal character a want so strong that she would destroy or be destroyed in the effort to attain it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: He must want it so badly that he will destroy or be destroyed in the effort to attain his goal.

question: Keep your scene-setting absolutely accurate but not exhaustive: give readers only enough detail to stimulate them to fill in the blanks themselves.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The details must be absolutely accurate, of course, but they need not be exhaustive. All they need do is stimulate readers to fill in the blanks.

question: Create a sense of narrative motion by describing the approach to a scene, moving from the long view to the scene itself.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You also can create a sense of narrative motion by describing the approach to a scene, moving from the long view to the scene itself.

question: Apply Chekhov's Rule: do not introduce an object into a scene unless it will play a part in the action that follows.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Readers expect writers to follow Chekhov's Rule—'One must not put a loaded rifle on the stage if no one is thinking of firing it.'

question: Characterize groups, neighborhoods, or whole cities with collective details—the status indicators that place human beings in social context.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: He characterizes groups with collective details, the status indicators that place human beings in social context.

question: Drop any scene you are considering that lacks conflict and emotion.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Forward momentum is the overcoming of opposition. If a scene you're considering lacks conflict and emotion, he adds, don't bother with it.

question: Make every descriptive detail meaningful; cut any detail that does not serve a larger purpose.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: the main point of description is story progression. That means details must be meaningful

question: Open with an establishing shot: a wide-angle view that takes in the entire setting that will contain the sequence of actions.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Television and movie storytellers talk about 'establishing shots,' wide-angle views that take in the entire setting that will contain a sequence of actions.

question: In an explanatory narrative, make each scene hold one of the larger, more abstract points you want to make about your topic.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: In an explanatory narrative, each scene holds some of the larger, more abstract points the writer wants to make about his topic.

question: Check each scene against these tests: does it cause a subsequent scene to occur?

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A good scene, he says, will: cause a subsequent scene to occur, creating cause and effect. be driven by the main character's needs and wants. explore various ploys by the character to get his own way. include action that changes a character's position, relative to the end of the story.

question: Check that each scene is driven by the main character's needs and wants.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A good scene, he says, will: cause a subsequent scene to occur, creating cause and effect. be driven by the main character's needs and wants. explore various ploys by the character to get his own way. include action that changes a character's position, relative to the end of the story.

question: Check that each scene explores various ploys by the character to get his own way.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A good scene, he says, will: cause a subsequent scene to occur, creating cause and effect. be driven by the main character's needs and wants. explore various ploys by the character to get his own way. include action that changes a character's position, relative to the end of the story.

question: Check that each scene includes action that changes the character's position relative to the end of the story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A good scene, he says, will: cause a subsequent scene to occur, creating cause and effect. be driven by the main character's needs and wants. explore various ploys by the character to get his own way. include action that changes a character's position, relative to the end of the story.

question: Build atmosphere by asking not only 'What happened?' but also 'How did it feel?', letting carefully chosen details add up to create mood.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Larson had the good sense to ask not only 'What happened?' but also 'How did it feel?'

question: Choose details that not only create the stage that holds the action but also help make some larger point: stay primed to spot les petits vrais, the little truths of life.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Every good narrative has a larger point, and every good narrative writer is constantly primed to spot les petits vrais—'the little truths' of life. Not every detail contributes to scene building, but the best not only create the stage that holds the action, but also help make some larger point.

question: Seize on perspective-rich images—a road winding into the snowy woods, a long stairway ascending in front of you, railroad tracks—to help flesh out the stages you create.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Lots of perspective-rich images can do the same thing—a road winding into the snowy woods, a long stairway ascending in front of you, railroad tracks. Seize on such devices to help flesh out the stages you create.

question: Think of yourself as a playwright: create a stage, a place where your story can unfold, then people it with characters who can breathe, move, and act.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When you set out to craft a nonfiction story, it doesn't hurt to think of yourself as a playwright. You must, after all, create a stage, a place where the story can unfold.

question: Remember that the scene is never an end in itself: in a story, the ultimate point is action, so let the wants and needs of your characters drive the plot forward through the scenes.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The scene is never an end in itself. In a story, the ultimate point is action.

question: Set each scene so the reader gets a feeling of volume, space, and dimension, and has a sensory experience there.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You have to set a scene so the reader gets a feeling of volume, space, dimension, and has sensory experience there.

question: Unfold each scene along the narrative arc, propelling the action line through the phases of story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Each scene should unfold along the narrative arc, propelling the action line through the phases of story. You'll want to open a story narrative with a scene suitable for exposition, which in an opening means introducing the protagonist and providing the backstory necessary for understanding the complication.

question: Open with a scene of exposition that introduces the protagonist and the backstory needed to understand the complication.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Each scene should unfold along the narrative arc, propelling the action line through the phases of story. You'll want to open a story narrative with a scene suitable for exposition, which in an opening means introducing the protagonist and providing the backstory necessary for understanding the complication.

question: Land the inciting incident in the first or second scene.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Each scene should unfold along the narrative arc, propelling the action line through the phases of story. You'll want to open a story narrative with a scene suitable for exposition, which in an opening means introducing the protagonist and providing the backstory necessary for understanding the complication.

question: Treat setting as gift wrap and story as the gift: keep description in service of the story you are telling.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Setting is the gift wrap; story is the gift.

question: Do not describe the world in all its detailed complexity: tap what is already in the reader's head by carefully selecting a few details that stimulate existing memories.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The mission is to tap what's already in the reader's head by carefully selecting a few details that stimulate existing memories.

question: Describe the scene in terms of texture: look for the elements that contrast with one another so your readers can see something other than sameness.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Look for the elements that contrast with one another, he said. You'll give your readers a richer experience if they can see something other than sameness.

question: Make every scene change the protagonist's 'value charge'—the degree to which the character is up or down relative to the ultimate goal of resolving the complication.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: each movie scene must change what he calls the protagonist's 'value charge.' The phrase refers to the degree to which a character is up or down relative to the ultimate goal of resolving the complication.

question: End each scene with a cliff-hanger, an action that portends drama in the next section and pulls the reader onward.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Underneath the boxes designating the scenes, I wrote a few words describing the action that would end the scene with a cliff-hanger, an action portending drama in the next section.

question: Never guess at what happened in a true-life narrative; interview the sources to capture the actual words and events rather than inventing them.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But you can’t guess in a true-life narrative.

question: Write the scene so the reader moves through it alongside the POV characters, rather than watching it from the distance of a theater seat.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: We see the world as the POV characters move through it, and the most involving scenes pass by as though we’re walking or driving through them with those characters, not as though we’re staring at them from a theater seat.

question: Think of your story as a series of scenic episodes and plot the scenic structure as the first step to planning the narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Once you get used to thinking of stories as a series of scenic episodes, plotting the scenic structure becomes the natural ﬁrst step to planning the narrative.

question: Show the scene through the eyes of a particular character moving through their own world, creating the illusion that the reader sees it as that character does.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But the frosting on the scenic cake is the illusion that we’re seeing a scene through the eyes of particular characters as they move through their own worlds.

question: Proceed through a series of scenes carefully selected to tell the story, instead of organizing your narrative by topic the way a report is.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A narrative, in contrast, proceeds through a series of scenes carefully selected to tell the story.

question: Make each scene substantially removed from the others in time and space, letting one scene end and another open somewhere else down the narrative arc.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: each of Barry Newman’s scenes is substantially removed from the others in time and space. One scene ends, and another opens somewhere else down the narrative arc.

question: Plan each scene and sketch out the scenic blueprint for the whole narrative before reporting.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The process guides the reporting that follows, focusing the questions and zeroing in on the story’s key moments.

question: Accumulate concrete, evocative details so that, taken together, they make your setting feel like a unique and special place.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Dogs chained outside cabins, shacks, canoes—every detail adds to a sense of Alaska as a unique and special place. Cumulatively, they add up to what literary critics refer to as “setting.”

question: Make setting a constant presence in your narrative, letting place step into the foreground with such insistence that it almost becomes a character in its own right.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: In the strongest regional writing, setting is a constant presence, and place steps into the foreground with such insistence that it almost becomes a character in its own right.

question: Build your sense of setting through the sights, sounds, and smells of the place, weaving them into the action line.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Robin Cody captures my part of the world, the Paciﬁc Northwest, as well as anybody does, largely through the sights, sounds, and smells that give a strong sense of setting.

question: Separate each major scenic unit in your narrative with a typographical device such as star-line breaks, bullets, or drop caps.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: in most print narratives typographical devices—typically star-line breaks, bullets, or drop caps—separate each major unit in the overall structure.

question: Make each scene seem absolutely real by choosing the most vivid details you can find.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Ultimately, the point of description is to create scenes that seem absolutely real, and vivid details are the most important elements in living scenes.

question: Weave your description seamlessly into the action line so it gains authenticity by appearing as the characters move, rather than standing apart from the action.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Such descriptions gain added authenticity because they’re woven so seamlessly into the action line.

question: Keep the acting subject at the start of the sentence—passive syntax cripples even the most active verb.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Contrary to widespread misconception, active voice is a matter of syntax, not just verbs.

question: Cut any aimless action from your opening and make sure it carries readers from one intriguing development to the next.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Aimless action gets you nowhere, and readers expect an opening that takes them from one intriguing development to the next.

question: Delete an unnecessary “had” where context already makes the timing clear.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But he didn’t need the “had.” The context made it clear that the attack took place earlier in the story. So why didn’t he simply delete “had”?

question: Keep the story rolling forward—even a small action that tells what happened next beats a passage that lies still.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Pulling away from the curb is not explosive action, but it keeps the story rolling forward. It tells you what happened next.

question: When you need real momentum, favor verbs that show cause and effect—motion alone, without causality, is not the most powerful action.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But because they don’t describe causality, they’re still not the most powerful action words available.

question: Once you launch the action, keep it moving—pause for explanation only when necessary and never drift into navel-gazing.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But readers won’t cut you much slack for what old newshounds derisively called “navel- gazing.” So once you launch it, keep the action moving.

question: Limit linking verbs to exposition—use them where you must explain, then return to action.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: For exposition, you usually need a few linking verbs, the weakest form.

question: Rewrite your opening lines so they immediately demand attention, crackling with enough energy to turn heads and serve as a narrative hook.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: ﬁ rst lines in the popular print media must immediately demand attention, crackling with enough energy to turn heads.

question: Rewrite your opening line so that something actually happens in it, right out of the blocks.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Something should happen in the ﬁ rst line of your narrative.

question: Replace passive voice where it strips human causality—active voice shows who affects what and advances the narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Part of the problem with passive voice is that it strips human causality from a sentence.

question: Rewrite a passive sentence so the actor appears—instead of “was released,” write “went home.”

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But those instances are relatively rare, and you can usually ﬁ nd your way around them. How about writing, “After six days in the hospital, Tashina went home”?

question: Open at the point of attack—a moment where something vital is at stake, where a conﬂ ict will lead to a crisis or a character has reached a turning point.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: An ideal “point of attack,” he added, zeros in on a moment where something vital is at stake.

question: Start your story from the protagonist’s point of view so readers feel they are facing the coming challenges themselves.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: start each story from the protagonist’s point of view. Telling a story from the perspective of the key player helps put readers in the scene, where they can recognize the coming challenges as though they themselves were facing them.

question: Open with the protagonist’s name immediately followed by a strong verb.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: the default option for any narrative opening is to begin with the name of the protagonist and to immediately follow that with a strong verb.

question: For a quiet story, open quietly—but make sure something is still happening from the first line.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Not every narrative opening demands slam- bang action. Quieter stories call for quieter openings. But it’s still essential that something is happening.
