question: Prefer simple past or present tense over past perfect or present progressive—the simple form keeps the action vigorous.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Action- oriented storytellers steer clear of tenses such as past perfect or present progressive in favor of simple past or present.

question: Recreate an action scene with a strong active verb in simple tense—drop the weak verb, the expletive, and the unnecessary perfect tense.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The writer had all the ingredients, but he cloaked their impact with a weak verb, an expletive, and an unnecessary perfect tense.

question: Open by teasing your readers—plant a detail that makes them wonder what happens next.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: you can, for example, tease your readers, making them wonder what happens next.

question: Cut forms of “to be” and sense verbs that merely state an equivalency—they carry no action.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Like the sense verbs—“smells,” “tastes,” “feels,” “looks,” and so on—“to be” merely states an equivalency.

question: Use transitive verbs to advance the story—they show action with consequences rather than just extending the narrative with a series of motions.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Transitive verbs, therefore, allow you to advance story, rather than just extending the narrative by describing a series of actions.

question: Sweep your prose for ﬂ abby verbs and weak sentence syntax—verbs carry the action, so replace the limp ones with strong, precise verbs.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Verbs signify action. And, if you’re going to keep a story moving, you’ll need lots of good ones.

question: Watch for passive constructions like "can be seen" that filter action through a third party — the refuge that dodges personal responsibility — and rewrite them as direct, firsthand description.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: This reticence drives some newspaper reporters into passive voice, the ultimate refuge for dodging personal responsibility.

question: Find every action you introduced with "began to" or a similar phrase, and cut to the chase — describe the action itself rather than its beginning.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You’re almost always better off if you cut to the chase, describing the action rather than its beginning.

question: Find the expletives in your prose — "there are," "there is," "it was," and the like — and rewrite each into an active verb that generates an image.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Why not introduce a real verb that generates an image by writing, “two airplanes taxied on the runway” or “two airplanes idled on the runway,” or even “two airplanes sat on the runway”?

question: Rather than leaving the action line, drop your exposition into subordinate clauses, modifiers, and appositives — reserve the main clauses for action alone.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Sometimes, you don’t have to leave the action line at all. Instead, you drop exposition into action sentences via subordinate clauses, modiﬁers, appositives, and other incidental elements. Reserve the main clauses for action alone.

question: Put readers directly into the scene so they experience the action firsthand, as though they were witnessing it themselves — don't filter it through a third party.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: For the great majority of narrative, your aim as a storyteller is to put readers into a scene where they can experience the action as though they were there witnessing it themselves.

question: When you find yourself writing exposition, step back and ask whether your readers really need it to understand what's going on — if not, cut it and get back to the action.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When you ﬁ nd yourself writing exposition, step back, clear your head, and ask yourself, “Do my readers really need this to understand what’s going on?” If not, desist.

question: Include plenty of highlights in your story and move readers quickly between them — leave out the parts people skip.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As a writer, you want to include plenty of highlights, and you want to move readers quickly between them.

question: Sandwich any necessary explanation between action, and place especially memorable action right after the digression.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When it’s consistently repeated, the technique trains readers to stick with you as you digress. They quickly learn that even though you’ve abandoned the action, you’ll soon be back in the thick of things. And Bill reinforces that lesson by placing especially memorable action right after any expository digression, creating little rewards that lure readers relentlessly forward.

question: Invert life's pace: speed up through the boring stretches of your story and slow way down through the best parts.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The paradox is that when you’re in the boring stuff, that’s when you need to speed up and when you’re in the best stuff where things are really moving rapidly, you slow down. The reason you slow down is so that the reader can really feel and process and really enter that scene.

question: Slow a climactic scene down by giving it more space on the page: more sentences, shorter sentences, more paragraph breaks, and the natural pauses you would normally skip over.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You allow more space on the page. You allow more sentences. You literally write in shorter sentences. You get more paragraph breaks. You use space. You ﬁ nd pauses inside the scene that occur naturally that you would normally skip over.

question: Make your story's chronology unmistakable by seeding in time markers — subtle ones like the fall colors on the trees or the height of the sun — wherever the action jumps in time.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Often, time markers can be relatively subtle. You might simply note the fall colors on the trees when you open a new scene that jumps ahead from summer to autumn.

question: Keep any digression from the main narrative to two paragraphs or less, so exposition never stalls the action for long.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Bill Blundell says his rule of thumb is to never digress from the main narrative for more than two paragraphs.

question: Attribute thought or conversation based on distant memories with phrases such as 'he recalled thinking' or 'his memory is that,' so readers know how you know what you know.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When you’re reporting thought or conversation based on more distant memories, you can attribute with phrases such as “he recalled thinking” or “his memory is that,” or “as he would later remember.”

question: Use dialogue as your primary tool for developing character, since how people speak reveals who they are.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Because we reveal so much of who we are by how we speak, what dialogue does best of all is develop character.

question: Cut dialogue that exists only for its own sake, and make sure every line of dialogue does real work, such as advancing the action.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Of course, dialogue isn’t an end in itself; it has to do some real work.

question: When you want to tell a true story, move your narrative from dropped-in direct quotations toward true dialogue in which your characters talk to one another.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But if you want to tell a true story, your readers should hear your characters talk to one another.

question: In first-person narrative, include your own part of the conversation and the action that contains it, so the other character's responses appear in a context that makes them more meaningful.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Unlike an interview, the dialogue you report includes your part of the conversation and the action that contains it. So the other character’s responses appear in a context that makes them much more meaningful.

question: Include what is going on in your characters' minds, because narrative becomes plot only when combined with motive and internal thought advances it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Only when narrative combines with motive does it become plot. So what’s going on in the mind of your characters advances plot.

question: When you plan to render a subject's inner thoughts, interview them as soon as possible after the event, before their memories degrade.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: For one thing, you interview as soon as possible after the event, before memories degrade.

question: Be extremely leery of putting remembered conversations from long ago inside quotation marks, since reconstructed dialogue is especially suspect.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Reconstructed dialogue is especially suspect, and an ethical nonﬁ ction writer will be extremely leery of putting remembered conversations from long ago inside quotation marks.

question: Weave physical action into your dialogue scenes so readers feel they are watching the scene unfold and hearing your speakers firsthand.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Note how McPhee mixes physical action—“the man shifted his weight”with the dialogue, reinforcing the sense that you’re there watching the scene unfold and hearing old Chap ﬁ rsthand.

question: Supply background information yourself as narrator and reserve dialogue for the things it does best, rather than loading background into your characters' speech.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Supply the background yourself in your role as narrator. Reserve dialogue for the things it does best.

question: Never put exposition in dialogue by having a character say something they would already know.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Savvy ﬁ ction writers have long understood that you should never make your characters say something they would already know

question: When you are not absolutely sure what was said, paraphrase rather than pretending you have the exact words by using quotation marks.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If you’re not absolutely sure about what was said, you paraphrase, rather than pretending you have the exact words by using quotation marks.

question: Use paraphrased dialogue when you want to approximate what the parties to a conversation said while slipping background information in as a stage whisper to the audience.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As the narrator, you can approximate what the parties to a conversation are saying while you slip in background information as a kind of stage whisper to the audience.

question: Limit your reconstruction of thought to dramatic highlights, the intense points in a life when memory is reliable enough to kick into high gear.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: you limit your reconstruction to things that happen at dramatic highlights, the relatively rare points in a human life when the experience is so intense that memory kicks into high gear.

question: Record more than conversation when you observe an unfolding scene, since the other action that is unfolding in the scene also yields meaning.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It’s not just what a character says that gives dialogue its power. Remember, dialogue happens in the context of a scene. So the other action that’s unfolding in the scene yields meaning, too.

question: Verify a subject's recollection of thoughts or events by evaluating it for internal consistency and face validity, triangulating multiple witnesses, and crosschecking with documentary sources.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You also can evaluate your source’s recollection for internal consistency and logical probability, what scientists call “face validity.” You can triangulate one account by interviewing multiple witnesses to an event or multiple participants in a conversation.

question: If your protagonist’s life seems alien to your audience, take special pains to demonstrate the connections to their own.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If your protagonist lives a life that seems especially alien to your audience, you must take special pains to demonstrate connections.

question: Don’t reject a theme because it is clichéd: the familiar principle becomes an eternal truth at the conceptual level.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: clichés may be an embarrassment at the sentence level, but they are at the heart of theme. “At the conceptual level,” Franklin wrote, “the cliché undergoes a strange metamorphosis: It becomes an eternal truth.”

question: Let the theme statement and outline guide your journey, then erase them when you arrive.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Then I’m off on the writer’s journey, secure in the knowledge that I know my destination. When I arrive, I erase the theme statement and outline.

question: Find the extraordinary in the ordinary: tell the tale of an ordinary person facing the challenges of ordinary living.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: part of the job is to ﬁnd the extraordinary in the ordinary.

question: Articulate the lesson your theme carries—the bigger the lesson, the more value it adds for your audience.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When you think about it, every theme incorporates a lesson. That’s the value added that draws an audience to a story in the ﬁ rst place. The bigger the lesson, the more value added.

question: State your theme, then check that every element of your action line—the plot—exists to serve it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: In a fully realized story, the action line—what we call “plot” in ﬁction—exists to serve the theme.

question: Reinforce your theme at every opportunity—in the lead, at each major turn, and especially at the last word before any page break or jump.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As the story took shape, the text reﬂected theme at every opportunity. The lead emphasized Gary Wall’s barren, postaccident existence:

question: Before writing anything, type “theme:” at the top of the file and puzzle out the noun-verb-noun structure of your statement.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Because a theme statement is so valuable, the ﬁ rst word I write on any project is always the same. I open a new computer screen and type “t- h- e- m- e.” Then I hit the colon key and sit there for a minute, puzzling over just the right noun- verb- noun structure for my statement.

question: Write a theme statement and use it to focus both your reporting and your writing.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Theme gives the audience a sense of time well invested. (What’s the point of reading unless reading has a point?) But it also focuses the reporting and writing.

question: Locate your theme inside yourself—draw it from your own convictions about cause and effect in human lives, not from the external world.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A literary theme inevitably springs from the writer’s personal values, his or her highly individual understanding of cause and effect in human lives.

question: Use your theme statement as the standard for every decision—structure, reporting, title, and especially what to cut.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: So the theme statement suggests your structure. It guides your reporting. It helps you ﬁ nd a title. If you have to cut, it tells you what can go and what must stay.

question: Don’t impose a theme on your story; find it in the material and extract it from the facts the world delivers.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “It’s not something that you bring to the story. It’s something that you ﬁ nd in the story and extract from the story.”

question: Express your theme as one clear, coherent sentence, not a single word.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “A true theme is not a word but a sentence,” McKee says, “one clear, coherent sentence that expresses a story’s irreducible meaning.”

question: Write a theme statement first and use it to find both the title and the shape of the story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: First we come up with a theme statement, and we use that to ﬁ nd both the title and the shape of the story.

question: Develop your theme statement with your editor early in the process so it becomes a shared standard for decisions about the story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Hashing one out together provides common ground, a shared standard for making decisions about a story.

question: State your theme in three parts—a character, the conflict (“leads to”), and the outcome—so it suggests the shape of your narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “Every good premise,” he said, “is composed of three parts, each of which is essential to a good play. Let us examine ‘Frugality leads to waste.’ The ﬁ rst part of this premise suggests character—a frugal character. The second part ‘leads to,’ suggests conﬂ ict, and the third part, ‘waste,’ suggests the end of the play.”

question: When a theme won’t surface, search for an overall title for the story and its parts to orient your brain toward its essence, structure, and drive.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “I’m always looking for an overall title,” he said, “as well as titles for the various parts and chapters. It’s a way of orienting your brain toward the essence of the story, also its structure and drive.”

question: Write your theme statement around a transitive verb so the sentence answers “what?” and shows causality.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Because they answer the question “what?” sentences built around transitive verbs show causality. And causality is the essence of a theme that tells readers how the world works and how they can inﬂ uence it. Hence, “Action creates (what?) identity.”

question: Find the context that links your protagonist’s life with your readers’ own.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Connecting with readers means ﬁnding the context that links the lives of your protagonists with their own.

question: Keep asking “What does this mean? Why did she do that?”—the quality of your thinking during reporting determines the impact of the details you find.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: the quality of the setting is far more important than the quality of the stone. And the quality of the setting reﬂects the quality of your thinking as you proceed through the reporting process. “What does this mean?” you constantly ask yourself? “Why did she do that?

question: Always back up your recordings with notes, and type up more complete notes at the end of the day.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote:
backing up with notes is a good idea. In any event, I don’t share the fear that tape recorders inhibit sources, producing a kind of Heisenberg effect that alters their words and behavior. Modern audio recorders are quiet and inconspicuous, and sources get used to them in the same way they get used to ﬂy- on- the- wall observers. Eventually, they’ll forget both the reporter and the recorder.

Still, a lot of narrative writers try to keep recorders and notebooks to a minimum when they’re in a scene with a source. Gay Talese occasionally pulled out a notebook for an especially juicy quote, but he also took notes when a source was out of the room. And, like Ted Conover and many others, he would type up more complete notes at the end of the day.

question: Keep your notebook especially rich in physical appearance, facial expressions, gestures, and tone of voice—the elements of direct characterization.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: especially rich in scribbled observations of physical appearance, facial expressions, gestures, tone of voice, and all the other elements of direct characterization.

question: Empathize with personalities outside your usual imaginative range—people unlike yourself—and let that openness drive your reporting.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote:
But, above all, the reporter must be able to empathize with personalities outside his usual imaginative range, mentalities unlike



<!-- PAGE 160 -->



his own, kinds of people he would never have written about had he not been forced to by encountering them inside the journalistic situation.

question: Find your way into stories from the resolution end—most news stories are endings without beginnings attached, so dig for the actions that led to the outcome.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Most news stories are endings,” he says, “without beginnings attached.

question: Have faith in the power of tiny, tiny moments—when it looks like nothing is happening, something important may be; pay better attention.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You really need to have faith in the power and importance of tiny, tiny moments,” Tom French says. “Newspaper reporters are trained so that we are really good at big moments. But the longer I do this, the more I learn to have faith that in those times when it looks like nothing is happening. In front of me something very important is happening. I just need to learn to pay better attention.

question: Report what you saw with your own eyes—firsthand observation carries a credibility that attributions and speculation undermine.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote:
Nothing beats seeing the action ﬁ rsthand. If you can tell readers you saw it with your own eyes, you carry the kind of credibility that’s admissible in court. And observational narrative—the kind generated by full- body immersionprojects authority. Your writer’s voice naturally sounds more conﬁdent when



<!-- PAGE 162 -->



it’s not undermined by attributions and speculation. “Listen to me, pal,” you seem to be saying. “I was there, and that’s the way it was.

question: Stay until familiarity breeds trust: once you disappear into the background, subjects relax and become themselves.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But familiarity breeds trust, or at least indifference. The “ﬂ y- on- the- wall” technique operates on just that principle. Once something gets familiar enough, it disappears into the background. Only then, the theory goes, will the subjects of an immersion reporter’s interest relax and become themselves.

question: Focus your reporting on motivation—a story begins when somebody wants something.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: a story begins when somebody wants something. So reporting for a story narrative should focus on motivation.

question: When reconstructing a major event, pitch survivors on the it's-your-one-chance-to-get-history-right argument—preliminary reports are often shallow and misleading.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: it’s- yourone- chance- to- get- history- right” argument. Anyone who’s been swept up in major news knows that preliminary reports of the event are often shallow and misleading.

question: Agree on ground rules with sources up front—on the record, on background, not for attribution, off the record—and treat each as an ironclad contract you can only change by renegotiating.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote:
One thing you owe your sources, whether you’re interviewing or silently observing, is an up- front discussion that explains the rules of the game. Tradi-



<!-- PAGE 166 -->



tional journalistic ground rules work well, regardless of whether you’re writing a book, shooting a documentary, or interviewing for a blog. Consider each of them an ironclad contract. Once you and a source agree to a ground rule, you’re bound to it unless you renegotiate.

question: Immerse yourself in your subject's world—being there and watching, listening, smelling, and feeling—instead of relying only on secondhand accounts.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Being there and watching. And listening, and smelling, and feeling. That’s immersion reporting.

question: For immersion reporting, breathe your subjects' air, quietly observe and hang around, learn the rhythm of their typical work, pick up their vocabulary, read their literature, and find their gurus.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote:
Breathing their air.”
- 2. “Quietly observing, hanging around.”
- 3. “Understanding the rhythm of their typical work.”
- 4. “Learning their vocabulary.”
- 5. “Reading their literature”—texts, guidebooks, professional publications.
- 6. “Finding their gurus.

question: Hold face-to-face interviews in informal settings—avoid sitting across a desk; ask to move to the kitchen table.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Most good reporters agree that face- to- face interviews are best and that informal settings help to loosen up sources. I’ve always tried to avoid sitting across a desk from a source, even for a conventional news interview. Richard Ben Cramer doesn’t like interviewing in living rooms, because “that’s where you sit with your hands folded.” He asks sources if they can move to the kitchen table.

question: Show genuine interest in your sources—people want to tell their stories, but only to someone who is truly interested in them.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: people want to tell their stories. But only if you’re interested in them, which I am.

question: Let dramatic action speak for itself—let the theme emerge from the flow of life, showing rather than stating it from a soapbox.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: they are free to let dramatic action speak for itself.” When Tom Hallman told Gary Wall’s story, he never once stepped back and baldly stated that “action creates identity.” The story unfolded naturally, showing rather than telling.

question: Stay patient during long immersion reporting and be willing to live without knowing the outcome while the story unfolds.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Patience is a huge part of it,” Conover has said. “Being able to live ‘without knowing’ is crucial to the method.

question: Break the world down into the universals of story—look for a good conflict, recognize a good protagonist, and you'll find a good story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Look for a good conﬂ ict, and chances are you’ll ﬁ nd a good story. Recognize a good protagonist, and chances are you’ll ﬁ nd a challenge that will interest an audience.

question: Weave modern technology's records—cell-phone and surveillance video, searchable eyewitness databases—into a you-are-there narrative line.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It’s surprising how often modern technology produces records that good reporting can weave into a you- are- there narrative line. Cell- phone and surveillance cameras capture scenes that would have been lost not many years ago.

question: Mine letters, newspaper accounts, court records, diaries, memoirs, and private papers for detail—no document is worth overlooking.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: he used letters, newspaper accounts, court records, diaries, memoirs, and collections of private papers to craft Devil in the White City as vividly as though he were actually there for the 1893 Chicago World’s Fair. “No document,” he says, “is worth overlooking.

question: Keep any judgmental reaction out of your eyes and your questions during an interview, or the source will close down.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If you have a judgmental reaction in your eyes during an interview, or a judgmental nuance as you pose a question, people will close down.

question: Fill your reporting notebook with visual details, anecdotes, action sequences, and smells—a quote-filled notebook is death for narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: visual details, anecdotes, action sequences, smells, and the like.

question: During an interview, ask a question you don't really care about so you can jot down physical appearance, clothing, and surroundings while the source talks.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: ask a question you don’t really care about so that you can jot down details of physical appearance, clothing, and surroundings while the source drones on.

question: Match technique to need: observe a subject while they act, and interview them when you want general information.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You observe a doctor when she’s treating your patient. You interview her when you want general information about a disease or a treatment.

question: Assume everything is on the record in the absence of any agreement to the contrary, even in situations ordinarily considered private.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: everything is on the record in the absence of any agreement to the contrary, even in situations ordinarily considered private.

question: For a major project, conduct a psychological interview: start with childhood memories, then work through the protagonist's life targeting key decisions and what went into them.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: He starts by asking about childhood memories, looking for the genetic and behavioral roots of motive. Then he works his way through the protagonist’s life, targeting key decisions and the elements that went into them.

question: Reconstruct a past event by interviewing witnesses, searching documents, and retracing the action line—working backward from a known destination guarantees a satisfying outcome.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: reconstructing a past event by interviewing witnesses, searching documents, and retracing the action line. Because you’re working backward from a known destination, you guarantee yourself a satisfying outcome.

question: For an interview that reconstructs a scene you didn't witness, ask sources to think of their experience as a series of scenes, like a movie, and describe the details that fill each one.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You might tell them to think of their experience as a series of scenes, as in a movie, and to describe the details that ﬁll each scene.

question: Include reporting on the reporter in your notes—the questions, emotions, and internal reactions you had during observation.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: reporting on the reporter, noting any questions, emotions, or other internal reactions that occurred during observation.

question: Take the ride-along approach to observation in many different fields, not just one night in a squad car.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Police ride- alongs,” she says, “ought to happen in lots of different ﬁelds.

question: When real events don't conform to your story's original shape, look for other lessons in what actually happened—every development says something about life.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But every story development says something about life, even if it wasn’t part of the original theme statement, and you often can pull a story out of the hat even if it isn’t the one you thought you had.

question: Probe motive by noting status indicators—what your character drives, what skis they own, what they drink.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: one way you probe motive is by noting the “status indicators” that Tom Wolfe sees as so revealing. Does your character drive a Prius or a Hummer? Does the rack in his garage hold cross- country or downhill skis? Does she drink bourbon or scotch, wine or beer?

question: Once you spot someone facing a challenge, stick close, gambling that you've found a protagonist who will eventually resolve their complication.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Once he spots someone facing a challenge, he sticks close, gambling that he’s found a protagonist who will eventually resolve his complication.

question: Gain access with quiet confidence and relentless determination—if you fail once, try again, and again.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Barging into other people’s lives takes quiet conﬁ dence and relentless determination. If you fail once, you try again. And again. “Stubbornness really helps,” says Tom French, “being really, really stubborn.

question: Position yourself as a student to your source's teacher—“I am a person who doesn't know much: Can you help me?”

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I often try to position myself as a student to their teacher. I am a person who doesn’t know much: Can you help me?

question: Plan how you will talk your way into an observation point—you can't simply walk into a stranger's world and assume the fly-on-the-wall position.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You can’t just knock on a door, walk into a stranger’s house, and assume your ﬂy- on- the- wall observation point. Somehow, you have to talk your way in.

question: To collect anecdotes, prime the pump by telling a story—about yourself or your protagonist—and asking for another.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote:
To get stories,” he said, “you have to tell stories.”

That’s it! Somebody tells us an agonized tale of a disastrous travel delay, and we respond by dredging out our own misery- loves- company yarn of missed connections or lost baggage.

To get anecdotes, you prime the pump by telling a story—either on yourself or your protagonist—and asking for another.

question: Develop a theory of personality to guide your information gathering, then let the details build the theory while the theory guides the search for more details.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The details build your theory, and your theory guides the search for more details. Once you conclude you’re dealing with a neat freak obsessed with order, ask to peek in his sock drawer.

question: Select your details so readers know you have a point—set up a single detail like a Tiffany's window so it shines.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If readers know that you have a point, that you’re not just aimlessly ﬂopping around among the sights, sounds, and facts of personal history, then they’ll pay close attention to the details you’ve selected. “It’s like a Tiffany’s window,” Mary Roach says. “If there’s only one thing in there and if you really set it up, you can really make it shine.

question: Trigger sources' recall by reminding them where they were and what was going on when critical events took place—one memory can trigger another.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: one memory can trigger another. So it’s often helpful to remind sources of where they were and what was going on when critical events took place.

question: Interview witnesses for scenes you didn't observe by making them complicit helpers—“I need parts to assemble”—so they build the scene with you.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I want you to work with me, please, as though we are two carpenters. I need parts to assemble.’ They aren’t haplessly yammering while I take things down but become complicit helpers in building the scene. They create the story with me.

question: Before you write even a little bit, make sure you understand a lot about your subject.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You’ve got to understand a lot,” McPhee said, “to write even a little bit.

question: Narrow your focus to what a person wants and whether they will get it—will they win the game or give the speech without passing out?

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I really try to narrow the focus down to what does this person want and are they going to get it?” he says. “Are they going to win the game or get the award or give the speech without passing out?

question: Develop a minor figure into a continuing character who recurs to set up the climax and stress the doubt that heightens the drama.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But in Version 4, Welch became a continuing character. We used him to set up Kasman's Monday performance, stressing the doubt that heightened the drama.

question: Don't close a narrative with direct quotes and a status update on a character, which flattens it into a standard news feature instead of a true story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But it closed with direct quotes from Lortie and an update on his condition, which kept the focus on the injured pianist and gave the story the flavor of a standard news feature, rather than a true narrative.

question: Rough out a story draft as soon as you can, even before the narrative arc is complete, because the sooner you begin writing the sooner your brain begins processing the story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The sooner you begin writing, the sooner your brain will begin processing the story.

question: Resolve the ending's tension through a specific, electrifying image of a character's action rather than a general statement.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Most importantly, Welch gave added cachet to the ending, embodying action that created a electrifying image for readers, one that resolved tension with the power of specificity.

question: Cast cold eyes on your material and decide what sort of narrative it is, then name the tools you'll need to build it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Early in the process of launching a narrative, they cast cold eyes on their material and ask a fundamental question: "Just what sort of narrative are we talking about here, and what tools will I need to build it?"

question: Choose a kicker word for a key spot that is one syllable, has a strong consonant sound, and carries tremendous emotional content.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: "Dreads" is a terrific kicker word, I said. It's one syllable, it has a strong consonant sound, and it has tremendous emotional content.

question: Let your own authority and voice come through in the telling, offering insight from your expertise that naive readers can't supply themselves.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I urged David to let his authority and voice come through. As a storyteller, he was more than a music critic here.

question: Confine a short narrative to one or two scenes, budgeting about five hundred words as the minimum for each scene and its action line.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Short narrative writers also must confine themselves to one or two scenes. As a rule of thumb, I figure about five hundred words as a minimum for creating a scene and the action line it contains.

question: Develop your opening into a full-fledged scene that captures the atmosphere of the place where the trouble first breaks.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I urged David to develop the opening so that it functioned as a full-fledged scene that captured the atmosphere of the elegant restaurant where symphony president William Ryberg first heard that his star pianist was injured and couldn't play.

question: Include episodes that create both rising and falling tension in a narrative, not a single unbroken climb.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I argued that good narrative includes rising and falling tension, which the Tchaikovsky episode provided.

question: Focus a short narrative on the action line rather than on developing its characters.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: For that reason short nonfiction narratives focus on action.

question: Remember that a short piece lacks the running room to probe character complexity, so let it explore situation instead.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A short piece of writing lacks the running room necessary to probe the complexities of character. So a general principle of fiction—that the novel explores character and the short story explores situation—also applies to nonfiction.

question: Start a short narrative with immediate action, bursting out of the blocks, and let the arc end abruptly and precipitously.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Short story narratives also have to start faster and end more abruptly, the narrative arc spiking up and falling precipitously. I urge writers to burst out of the blocks with immediate action.

question: When the pivotal event of your story arrives, withhold its contents briefly to heighten the drama.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When the fatal phone call arrived, I suggested, David should withhold its contents, heightening drama.

question: When you can, aim for a constructive ending — the protagonist defeating the complication — rather than a tragedy, and let that choice guide which protagonist you build the story around.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: We wanted what Aristotle referred to as a comedy—a story about a protagonist defeating the complication.

question: Hold off on substantial background digression until enough of the action line has launched to put readers on the hook; only then is a long expository section safe.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: By that point enough of the action line had been launched to provide breath- ing room for more expository digression. The story had readers on the hook, and Julie could safely begin a substantial background section on the Warm Springs tribes, the history of the reservation, and the Yahtins.

question: End a section with a line that completes the central thought and foreshadows the dramatic struggle to come, rather than trailing off into summary.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: She ended the section with a beautiful line that completed the central thought and foreshadowed the dramatic struggle that was to follow:

question: Give the opening section of your story enough exposition, slipping in background on characters and setting as the action line proceeds, so readers have what they need to understand the complication.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The ﬁ rst section in any story needs a certain amount of exposition, and as the action line proceeded Julie slipped in background on the Yahtin family, giving readers the information they'd need to understand the complication.

question: Drop an expository flashback only when a hopeful development in the action gives breathing space, using it to fill in background rather than stalling a rising scene.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: That hopeful development provided a little more breathing space, and Julie seized it to drop into her second expository ﬂ ashback, a downer historical overview of Dorothy's drug- and alcohol- addicted life.

question: Build the crisis around a point of insight: a realization that changes the protagonist's understanding of the world and sets up the climax.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It was what story theorists call the point of insight, the realization that changes the protagonist's understanding of the world and sets up the climax.

question: Choose as your protagonist a character who can engage the complication, grapple with it through rising action, and resolve it through their own initiative — the captain of their own fate.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A good protagonist is, most of all, the captain of his fate. For a story to take a form that offers a valuable life lesson, the protagonist must engage the complication, grapple with it through a period of rising action, and ultimately resolve it through his own initiative.

question: Reconstruct scenes you did not witness by interviewing witnesses who saw the moment, and gather enough physical description from their accounts to ground your characterization.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: At ﬁ rst Julie's reporting was reconstructional. She interviewed witnesses who'd seen Dorothy hit her low point before she enrolled in alcohol treatment, and she gathered background on the Yahtin family. But then her reporting became increasingly observational.

question: Test whether your central character can drive the narrative arc: if nothing the character does can change their situation, they fit an explanatory narrative but cannot carry a true story narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Chesley might provide a ﬂ at action line for an explanatory narrative, but the odds were against him creating the arc of a true story narrative.

question: Shape rising action and the crisis as an oscillating curve of ups and downs rather than a steady climb, so the protagonist's fortunes swing before the climax.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As it always does in the best stories, Part 2—rising action—had its ups and downs, as did the following section, the crisis. Remember the oscillating curve of rising action and crisis we discussed in the chapter on story structure?

question: Pick as protagonist a rounded character with depth and complexity — and, crucially, the potential for change — rather than a flat one who cannot transform.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Dorothy, in other words, was no ﬂ at character. She had the depth and complexity Julie needed to capture a fully rounded human being. Dorothy also carried the potential for change, if only she could kick the booze and reunite with her kids.

question: Before writing a long narrative, build a scenic outline: list each scene in order and under it the beats it must hit, so the whole story is planned scene by scene.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Then she produced this scenic outline:

question: Sketch your narrative arc before writing — exposition, rising action, crisis, climax, falling action, denouement — and use the sketch to guide every scene you write.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The outline produced a perfect narrative arc, which Julie and I sketched out to guide her writing

question: Set each scene with sparse but compelling detail: open with an establishing shot, then zero in on the key objects with only a handful of carefully chosen particulars.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As she did consistently throughout the narrative, Julie set the scene with sparse but compelling detail. Scene 6 opened with an establishing shot of the reservation

question: Draft a theme statement for your narrative in the crisp form of subject, transitive verb, object — one sentence capturing the core idea that will guide your writing.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I asked Julie to prepare a theme statement. The process was new to her, and she didn't quite achieve the crisp subject–transitive verb–object form that I prefer. But what she came up with certainly captured the core idea that would guide her writing

question: Set your action scenes on the lower rungs of the ladder of abstraction where emotion rules, and place your explanation higher up where meaning holds sway.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Action takes place on the lower rungs of the ladder of abstraction, where emotion rules. Explanation takes place farther up the ladder, where meaning holds sway.

question: Structure the piece like a layer cake, progressing steadily through successive, top-to-bottom sections of scenic action and explanatory digression.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Because an explanatory narrative progresses steadily through successive, top- to- bottom sections of scenic action and explanatory digression, it assumes a structure that Michael Roberts, writing coach at the Arizona Republic, likens to a layer cake.

question: Ask the questions that bare the mechanisms turning your world: How do they do that? Where does that come from; where does that go? Who is that guy? How did this get to be such a mess? What's it like to be him or her?

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: And she offers a list of questions designed to bare the mechanisms that turn our world: How do they do that? Where does that come from; where does that go? Who is that guy? How did this get to be such a mess? What's it like to be him or her?

question: Look beyond conventional sources — talk to people at every level, read specialty journals, and hang around where relevant things take place.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: She advises that would- be explanatory journalists look beyond conventional sources, talking to janitors as well as administrators, home- care aides as well as doctors. She suggests haunting Internet bulletin boards and chat rooms, reading specialty journals related to the topic, hanging around backstage in places where relevant things take place.

question: Range farther up and down the ladder of abstraction than a typical journalist — interview and observe for revealing detail, and look for how your examples fit into larger patterns.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: To explore the bottom rungs of the ladder, they interview and observe for revealing detail—a Muslim holy man conducting a halal inspection. To climb higher, they look for ways their speciﬁ c examples ﬁ t into larger patterns—the french fry, for example, as a stand- in for growing Paciﬁ c Rim trade.

question: Preserve dramatic tension by bailing out of the action line at just the right moment — create a cliff-hanger by pausing when something hangs in the balance.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: One secret to successful digression is to preserve dramatic tension by bailing out of the action line at just the right moment. If the writer creates a cliff- hanger by pausing when something hangs in the balance, the reader will usually hang around to see what happens when the narrative resumes.

question: Digress in the middle of the action, not between actions, because that's when the reader remembers well and is happier to come back.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It's frequently best to digress in the middle of the action, not between actions, because then we remember well and we're happier to come back.

question: Use the journey you follow as a flat spine that holds the piece together, a narrative line running A to Z rather than an arc carrying a protagonist through rising action, climax, and resolution.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The journey of the fries will simply serve as a spine that holds the piece together, that gives it shape. But it's a ﬂat narrative line, A to Z, instead of an arc that takes a main character through rising action, a climax, and a resolution.

question: Track an inanimate object that moves, knowing it will touch a series of characters along the way and bring the necessary humanity into the yarn.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It could be a ship or a gun or a load of coal. But it must move, and in moving it will inevitably touch a series of characters. That brings the necessary humanity into the yarn. But it's the movement that matters.

question: Have the courage to digress, leaving the reader hanging at an intriguing point in the action line.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Then McPhee has the courage to digress, leaving us hanging at this intriguing point in the action line so that he can explore the history of ﬂood control in the Mississippi Delta:

question: Tune your brain so everything around you is a source for stories — constantly interrogate your story, step back from the case at hand, and ask 'Why does this matter? Why here? Why now?'

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You must constantly interrogate your story, she explains. To ﬁ nd a good explainer, take a couple of steps back from the case at hand, asking Why does this matter? Why here? Why now?

question: Match the length of a digression to the drama at the pause — the higher the emotional valence, the longer it should be.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: the higher the emotional valence, the longer the digression.

question: Work out an outline before you begin writing so that, once you know the structure, you can concentrate each day on one thing and know right where it fits.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Going through all that creates the form and the shape of the thing. It also relieves the writer, once you know the structure, to concentrate each day on one thing. You know right where it ﬁts.

question: Rely on observation more than conventional reporters — plunge into your subjects and practice fly-on-the-wall techniques, quietly watching and listening for nuances otherwise inaccessible.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: they rely more on observation—as opposed to interviewing and document research—than conventional reporters do. They plunge into their subjects, leaving their old realities behind. Like ethnologists, they quietly watch and listen, practicing ﬂ y- on- the- wall techniques for getting at nuances that would be otherwise inaccessible.

question: Every so often stop the action, pull the curtain on the narrative, and go off on a short exploration of the subject — an abstract explanation that adds depth.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But every once in a while, the writer stops the action, just pulls the curtain on the narrative. Then he goes off on a little exploration of the subject, an abstract explanation that gives depth and meaning to what the reader's been witnessing in the narrative.

question: In your explanatory piece, don't just follow a route — track one particular person or thing, and give close-to-the-ground specificity so readers can visualize the exact places at particular times.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: you can't just follow a route; you have to track a person or a thing. An explanatory narrative requires close- to- the- ground speciﬁcity. Readers must visualize particular places at particular times.

question: Structure an explanatory narrative as a 3+2 explainer: three narrative scenes separated by two digressions—open with the lead character and the explanatory question, digress for background, follow the character through the action line, digress to complete the explanation, then bring the action to a logical stopping place.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: creating a layer cake means you need a digression between the beginning and the middle and another digression between the middle and the end. That's the minimum, it seems to me, for a true explanatory narrative. It's a form I call the 3+2 explainer—a structure containing three narrative scenes separated by two digressions.

question: Let the characters in an explanatory narrative carry the explanation—choose people whose words and actions do the explaining rather than telling the reader what you know yourself.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The walking, talking human beings that populate most explanatory narratives are the vehicles the writer uses to explore the subject at hand. The characters, through their words and actions, do the explaining.

question: Balance an explanatory narrative so you write roughly one word of digression for every word of action, whether you weave the digressions into the narrative or break them out as separate sections.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If the writer simply weaves the digressions into the narrative, rather than breaking them out as separate sections, the ratio should remain about the same—one word of digression for every word of action.

question: When an explanatory narrative focuses on a person, you need not follow them through a full story arc—share a few brief episodes that serve as windows into their world.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: We meet the scanner head or the greatest salesman who ever lived not to follow them through a narrative arc, complete with point of insight and climax, but to share a few brief episodes that serve as windows into their worlds.

question: Use an explanatory structure to tell a true story that encompasses a complication, change, character development, and resolution—not just a process explanation.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But nothing says you can't use an explanatory structure to tell a true story—one that encompasses a complication, change, character development, and resolution.

question: Characterize economically: emphasize just a few key personality traits and bits of personal history for each person you bring onto the page.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As with most characterization, the writer emphasizes just a few key personality traits and bits of personal history.

question: Before writing, craft a detailed outline that tracks each narrative segment and digression in your explanatory narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Rich worked out his structure, crafting a detailed outline that tracked each narrative segment and digression.

question: Work a physical description of a character into the text early, and use the details of their clothes and belongings as status indicators that reveal character.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: He worked a physical description into the text early.

question: After any digression, return quickly to the moving action line so the constantly moving action keeps carrying the explanation forward.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The constantly moving action line greased the explanatory skids.

question: Keep each scene in an explanatory narrative around five hundred words, about twelve newspaper column inches, so the scene-digression-scene structure stays taut.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I generally figure on print scenes averaging about five hundred words, which translates to twelve column inches in a newspaper.

question: Write a bookend narrative by bracketing a stretch of expository material with two pieces of engaging scenic action, opening and closing with narrative that holds the duller content in the center.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: To write one, you bracket a stretch of expository material with two pieces of more engaging scenic action, opening and closing with narrative that has the power to hold the longer, duller content in the center.

question: Build a column around storytelling rather than table-pounding opinion, using narrative to attract and keep loyal readers.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: some of the most successful columns attract loyal readers with storytelling skills, rather than table- pounding opinion.

question: Aim your personal essay for a crossover: move readers from the specific to the general, then across to a new ladder of abstraction and down to the specifics of their own lives.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The ultimate payoff for a personal essay is when readers follow the writer from the speciﬁc to the general, then cross over to a new ladder of abstraction and descend it to the speciﬁ cs of their own lives.

question: Structure your personal essay inductively with three parts—a narrative, a turn, and a conclusion—moving from the particular, rising on the ladder of abstraction, and ending with a cosmic truth.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: All personal essays follow Montaigne’s lead and include a narrative, a turn, and a conclusion. They’re inductive, in other words, moving from the particular (a deformed child), then rising on the ladder of abstraction (arguing that everything born of nature is part of God’s plan), and concluding with some cosmic truth.

question: Vary your short personal essay's structure: break the narrative into pieces with intermediate conclusions along the way.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You can break the narrative into pieces, inserting intermediate conclusions along the way. You can minimize the narrative and expand the more abstract discussion of the subject. Or you can let the narrative dominate while the cosmic conclusion emerges from subtle literary cues.

question: Vary your short personal essay's structure: minimize the narrative to expand abstract discussion.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You can break the narrative into pieces, inserting intermediate conclusions along the way. You can minimize the narrative and expand the more abstract discussion of the subject. Or you can let the narrative dominate while the cosmic conclusion emerges from subtle literary cues.

question: Vary your short personal essay's structure: let the narrative dominate while the cosmic conclusion emerges from subtle literary cues.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You can break the narrative into pieces, inserting intermediate conclusions along the way. You can minimize the narrative and expand the more abstract discussion of the subject. Or you can let the narrative dominate while the cosmic conclusion emerges from subtle literary cues.

question: Stay open-minded about narrative form: if you have something that would entertain people, treat it as material for a narrative and find the form that fits it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The important thing is that you stay open- minded. If you have something that will entertain your buddies over a beer, you probably have the makings of a narrative that will sell somewhere. It’s just a matter of ﬁnding the form that ﬁts.

question: Write a narrative issue essay as a quest: carry your idea from source to source, exploring issues, poking and probing, to find information that expands the idea.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: An essay, it’s been said, is a way of “taking an idea for a walk.” In the case of narrative issue essays, the metaphor’s literally true. The essay writer’s legwork carries her from source to source, exploring issues, poking and probing, looking for information that will help expand the idea.

question: Launch your narrative issue essay with a quiet narrative action line that starts the quest by rubbing two contradictory ideas together.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The article begins with a quiet little narrative action line, launching Pollan’s quest by rubbing two contradictory ideas together.

question: Use narrative not only to explore places but also to explore systems, letting the story structure reveal how a system works.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You can use narrative, he argues, not only to explore places but also to explore systems.

question: After a narrative launch, include a nut graf: a summary that tells readers why the issue matters and what the piece will show.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: His fourth paragraph is a “nut graf,” a Wall Street Journal– style summary of why the issue’s important:

question: After your narrative opening, take a turn: climb suddenly up the ladder of abstraction to address the macrocosm that the opening scene represents.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The next paragraph constituted what’s called a “turn,” a sudden climb on the ladder of abstraction to address the macrocosm that the opening represented.

question: Shape your material into a vignette: a single scene standing alone, with an action line running through a geographical place and no complication, crisis, or resolution.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A vignette is a single scene, standing alone.

question: Make your standalone vignette work harder than an ordinary scene, offering a slice of life rich in theme that reveals some important secret to good living.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Because they stand alone, vignettes must work harder to offer a slice of life that’s rich in theme, that reveals some important secret to good living.

question: When something has emotionally affected you without your quite knowing why, write the narrative as a way of discovering your own feelings.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I puzzled about my odd reaction—I’m not given to tears over strange dogs—and ﬁ nally decided to write the narrative as a way of discovering my own feelings.

question: Treat every alteration you make when turning reality into prose as an ethical choice you must consciously justify.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Every attempt to do so alters reality in some respect, and every alteration represents an ethical choice.

question: When sources give conflicting versions of the same event, present each account with attribution rather than silently choosing one version as settled.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If three execs have three different versions of a meeting—and they will—whose version will you choose?

question: Add an author's note explaining your reporting methods so readers can judge your standards of accuracy, evidence, and fairness for themselves.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: the essay on methods he included in Devil meets my basic test of transparency. Readers can see what he did and make up their own minds about his standards of accuracy, evidence, and fairness.

question: Ask whether you are changing or inventing facts to make a better story—if so, you have crossed from nonfiction into fiction.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If you are changing or inventing facts to make a better story, you are writing ﬁ ction.

question: Cut specific sensory details no source recorded and no source could verify, rather than inventing them.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But how, I wondered, would you know about ﬂ ies on the windowsill, and how would you know that a train rumbled through the intersection at that exact moment? Those don’t strike me as the kind of details anyone would record, and Larson’s footnotes are silent on the matter.

question: Cut internal monologue you cannot verify, since you can only report a subject's thoughts if they told you.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If you ask another what she was thinking when she made an important decision, do you include that unveriﬁ able internal monologue in your narrative?

question: Scan your draft for any place you bent a fact to gain drama, clarity, or style, and restore the literal truth even at the cost of the payoff.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Don’t fudge, ever, even if a tiny departure from reality produces a huge payoff in drama, clarity, or style.

question: Do not invent dialogue in memoir; reconstruct only what you can verify or clearly flag as reconstructed.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: much of his dialogue was obviously invented and he clearly didn’t apply Walt Harrington’s standards to verify historical accuracy.

question: Remove any scene you created by suggesting an action to a source, since staging a scene alters reality.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But is it kosher to alter reality by suggesting the visit?

question: Elucidate in your draft the difference between emotional truth and factual truth, and be clear which one you are actually claiming.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Maybe you can’t get every detail right, goes the argument, but you can capture a larger meaning that’s essentially truthful.

question: When you reconstruct a scene from reasonable assumptions, flag your leaps of faith with tip-off words like 'probably,' 'perhaps,' and 'maybe.'

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But when he was reconstructing scenes based on reasonable assumptions, Preston let readers in on any leaps of faith by sprinkling his copy with tip- off words such as “probably,” “perhaps,” and “maybe.”

question: Move cumbersome in-text attributions into footnotes to document your sources without cluttering the narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Like a more traditional historian, Larson used footnotes to document his sources, a tactic that avoids the clutter caused by attributions such as “he probably thought” or “as he recalled in his memoir.”

question: Push your reporting and writing toward the closest possible portrayal of what actually happened, accepting that you will never get it absolutely right.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But the only ethical approach is to get as close as possible.

question: Keep clarifying comments a source gives you on a later call separate from the original dialogue instead of blending them into it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: If you call one of your sources back to explain an earlier conversation, can you blend those clarifying comments into the ﬁ rst dialogue?

question: Never build a composite character in nonfiction; combining real people belongs to fiction.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: “Where I came from,” he said, “a composite character was a ﬁction.”

question: Record every conversation you plan to quote in your notebook at the time or soon after, so your dialogue is exact.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: All of the conversations recorded in the book took place. I heard them (and participated in many of them) and wrote them down in my reporter’s notebook at the time or soon thereafter.

question: Protect subjects' privacy by changing names rather than altering the facts of their lives.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: I’ve changed some of the names to ensure privacy, but in only one small instance (a hometown) have I knowingly changed any facts of details about their lives.

question: Check every quotation, name spelling, and small factual detail against your reporting and correct them before publishing.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Quote exactly. Spell names correctly. Get the smallest details absolutely right.

question: Put quotation marks around only the dialogue you heard yourself; attribute reconstructed conversation to participants' memories.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: No dialogue appears within quotation marks unless Hallman heard a conversation himself.

question: Make sure readers can tell exactly where you learned each thing you claim to know.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But for me the bottom line is that readers should know exactly where you learned what you claim to know.

question: Keep yourself visibly present in scenes you witnessed rather than hiding your presence for the greater drama of an omniscient view.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When you write, do you reveal your presence or opt for the greater drama of describing the two executives bargaining nose to nose by themselves?

question: Cut invented detail until your draft stays on the nonfiction side of the line between imagination and fiction.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Too much reportage and we cross into scholarship or journalism. Too much imagination and we cross into ﬁ ction.

question: Check every verifiable fact—temperatures, elevations, dates, names—against a source you can confirm rather than relying on memory alone.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When I write that the spring water is ﬁ fty- one degrees, I have measured it with a thermometer.

question: Before using background a source shared casually, warn her that you might use it and give her the chance to take it off the record.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Or do you have to warn her that you might use it and give her a chance to take it off the record?

question: Avoid casting: don't seek out only the sources who make your point and ignore those who will muddy your theme.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Neither can you seek out sources you know will make your point and ignore those who will muddy your theme, a practice known as “casting.”

question: Resist the story's pull to credit one character with too much responsibility, inflate a minor incident's significance, or tie up loose ends more neatly than real life allows.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A complete story calls for a protagonist. So the dark side credits one character with more responsibility for resolving a complication than she deserves. A complete story calls for a climax. So the dark side invests a minor incident with more signiﬁ cance than it deserves. A complete story calls for resolution. So the temptation is to wrap up loose ends more neatly than is ever the case in real life.

question: Have a very direct conversation with sources early in a project—even trying to talk them out of the story—so both sides' expectations are clear.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: She insists on having “a very direct conversation” early on. “There have been times,” she says, “when I’ve almost tried to talk people out of doing stories.”

question: Work through a process that weighs competing interests, asks key questions, and considers all the practical alternatives instead of applying an ethical formula.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The only workable route to ethical behavior is working through a process that weighs competing interests, asks key questions, and considers all the practical alternatives.

question: Judge your reporting against the four ethical mandates: speak the truth, remain independent, minimize harm, and be accountable.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: that duty includes four ethical mandates: 1) Speak the truth. 2) Remain independent. 3) Minimize harm. 4) Be accountable.

question: Set explicit standards for evidence: rely on primary sources, avoid interest-group material, use opinion across the political spectrum, and find three examples from diverse sources for every point.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Everything they published would come from primary sources, they would avoid material from interest groups, they would use opinion from across the political spectrum, and they would ﬁ nd at least three examples—from diverse sources and regions—to buttress every point.

question: Before a narrative project, explain the ground rules going in: describe your role as a writer and how it may differ from what sources expect.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Explain the ground rules going in, says Bob Steele. Describe your role as a writer and how it might differ from what sources expect.

question: In final editing, ask whether you can vouch for the verbatim accuracy of anything in quotation marks, back up every generalization, and keep attributions clear and the chronology straight.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Can you vouch for the verbatim accuracy of anything inside quotation marks? Can you back up every generalization, or should you ratchet your claims back a notch or two? Do the attributions make the sources clear, keep the chronology straight, and reveal when you’re speculating?

question: When you're a character in your own first-person narrative, treat whatever happens to you as a legitimate part of the story.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: When you’re playing a part in your own narrative, anything that happens to you can be a legitimate part of the story.

question: Work in good faith rather than chasing absolute accuracy: check and double-check, do your best to get everything right, and never deliberately falsify anything, large or small.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: The real route to responsible nonﬁ ction is not absolute accuracy but good faith. You work hard at your craft and do your best to get everything right. You check and double- check. And you never deliberately falsify anything, large or small.

question: As a story idea forms, ask ethical questions: can you access key sources honestly, how much can you observe directly, and does your theme emerge from the reporting or get imposed on the facts?

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Can you get access to key sources honestly? How much can you observe directly, and how much will you need to reconstruct?

question: Before an immersion, explain to the people you will document that your job is to observe and write—so your presence doesn't alter the reality you're covering.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Rich’s job was to document their work without altering reality via his own involvement, a mission he explained to team members before leaving for Sri Lanka.

question: In an immersion, be a good house guest: follow your host's lead, stay polite and nonjudgmental, and disrupt the household routine as little as possible.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A good guest is polite and nonjudgmental. He follows his host’s lead, disrupting the household routine as little as possible.

question: If you let a source review a manuscript, preface it with the proviso that you're open to correcting errors but your interpretations remain your own.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: an exercise that I always precede with the proviso that I’m totally open to correcting errors but that my interpretations remain my own.

question: If your material won't support the story you want, write fiction or correctly label the work—never secretly mix fiction's reliance on imagination with nonfiction forms.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: You can write a nonﬁ ction book or produce a documentary. You can write a novel or produce a feature ﬁ lm. But you can’t secretly mix ﬁction’s reliance on imagination with nonﬁ ction forms, no matter the temptation.

question: Don't give readers the impression you witnessed something you actually reconstructed from others' reporting.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: And you can’t give the impression that you witnessed something you reconstructed.

question: Beware mindreading in your draft: cut phrases like 'seemed to feel' that claim inner states you can't know, and rewrite the moment from observable behavior.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But Hart’s markup cautioned Hallman to “be careful of statements such as ‘seemed to feel.’ We don’t want anybody accusing us of mindreading.”

question: Apply prosecutorial editing: question everything in your draft with the tough intensity a district attorney brings to a criminal defendant.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Much of the process boils down to what’s known as “prosecutorial editing,” a habit of mind that questions everything with the same tough intensity that a district attorney brings to bear on a criminal defendant.

question: Rely on the questions you ask yourself rather than a fixed ethics code to determine how ethically you operate.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It’s the questions you ask, not the answers you give, that determine how ethically you operate.

question: Edit the stumbles and false starts out of quoted speech, but never put quotation marks around dialogue you can't verify came from the source.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Editing out meaningless meandering is one thing. Putting quotation marks around questionable dialogue is something else, and ethical nonﬁction writers recognize the distinction.

question: During reporting, ask whether you use diverse sources, how sources know what they know, whether you've checked eyewitness accounts against documents, and whether anyone has a conflict of interest.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Am I using diverse, representative sources, or am I trying to make a case by casting? How do my sources know what they know? Have I double- checked eyewitness accounts against documentary evidence? Do my sources have conﬂ icts of interest? Do I?

question: On a long project, revisit the direct conversation with sources and engage them in your process as the story develops.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: On a long project, that direct conversation bears revisiting. Sensitive writers engage sources in their process.

question: Use secrecy or undercover methods only as a last resort—whenever possible, be up front with people about who you are and what you're doing.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Secrecy is something that I think a journalist or a nonﬁction writer should only use as a last resort, because whenever possible in this life it’s good to be up front with people.

question: When a story is 'too good to check,' actively hunt for evidence that contradicts it instead of protecting the story template.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: A good story is a temptation. When we take off in pursuit of one, we run the risk of ignoring evidence that might contradict it, either because we don’t want to spoil it or because we simply don’t think of possibilities outside the story template.

question: Don't alter a direct quotation, even slightly, if the change could affect the speaker's meaning.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Ultimately, I decided that I couldn’t make the change honestly and put “the” back.

question: Keep your account scrupulously accurate while pushing toward truths beyond the reach of a routine report.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: It would be scrupulously accurate, but it would reveal truths beyond the reach of an ordinary news report.

question: Ground your story in specific real-world decisions, applying abstract story principles to the actual material at hand.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Good narrative comes from speciﬁc real- world decisions made by writers and editors who not only understand the abstract principles of story, but also know how to apply them in the real world.

question: Learn enough story theory to recognize when you are forcing narrative onto material that does not call for it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Another is learning enough about story theory to avoid the fatal error of forcing narrative onto inappropriate material.

question: Care more about how well your story is told than about where it appears.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: where a story appeared is far less important than how well it was told.

question: Do not let lack of experience keep you from narrative: grasp a few core principles, find an appropriate story structure, and draft from there.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: don’t let lack of experience intimidate you. Time and again I’ve seen writers with absolutely no narrative experience grasp a few core principles, ﬁ nd appropriate story structures, and draft dramatic tales that moved readers.

question: Use immersion reporting as a core technique for your nonfiction narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: As Ted Conover demonstrated, both ethnography and nonﬁ ction narrative share immersion reporting as a core technique.

question: Master a wide variety of narrative forms rather than relying on a single one.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Mastering a wide variety of narrative forms is one key to success.

question: Match your form to your material: when a subject is best served by simple informational writing, make the key point quickly instead of building a narrative.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: But experience has taught me that most subjects are best suited to simple informational writing that makes the key point quickly.

question: When your audience needs a key point quickly, skip the long narrative windup and lead with it.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: if your neighbors want to know if their school will be closed, you’d be foolish to begin a report on the critical school board meeting with a long narrative windup.

question: Show how one action leads to another so your story makes sense of a confusing world.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Story makes sense out of a confusing universe by showing us how one action leads to another.

question: Turn the sources of your true story into characters and its topics into scenes.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Instead of sources, it would have characters. Instead of topics, it would have scenes.

question: Give your narrative strong internal structure that regulates pace and builds dramatic tension.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Strong internal structure would regulate pace and create dramatic tension.

question: Decide deliberately what to include in your narrative and what to leave out.

source.author: Jack Hart
source.quote: Help with their reporting, help with their selection of scenes, help with their descriptions of characters, and help with their choices about what to include and what to leave out.
